abstract: Traditional methods of studying neural coding characterize the en(cid:173) coding of known stimuli in average neural responses. Organisms face nearly the opposite task - decoding short segments of a spike train to extract information about an unknown, time-varying stim(cid:173) ulus. Here we present strategies for characterizing the neural code from the point of view of the organism, culminating in algorithms for real-time stimulus reconstruction based on a single sample of the spike train. These methods are applied to the design and anal(cid:173) ysis of experiments on an identified movement-sensitive neuron in the fly visual system. As far as we know this is the first instance in which a direct "reading" of the neural code has been accomplished.
authors: Robert R. de Ruyter van Steveninck

paragraphs: The paper studies neural coding from the perspective of an organism receiving spikes. Traditional analyses describe average neural responses to stimuli already known to the experimenter. The organism instead has to infer an unknown, changing stimulus from a short segment of neural activity. This reverses the direction of the central inference problem.

The authors develop strategies that culminate in algorithms for reconstructing a stimulus in real time from a single sample of a spike train. The reconstruction directly asks what information can be extracted from the activity available on one occasion. That connects the characterization of a neural code to the practical task of interpreting it.

The methods are used to design and analyze experiments on an identified movement-sensitive neuron in the fly visual system. The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first direct reading of a neural code. The key contribution is the explicit reconstruction of a changing stimulus from neural spikes, making decoding itself the basis of the investigation.
summary.tldr: The paper develops real-time stimulus reconstruction from a single spike train and applies it to a movement-sensitive fly neuron.

title: Reading a Neural Code

abstract: A patient visits the doctor; the doctor reviews the patient's history, asks questions, makes basic measurements (blood pressure, .. . ), and prescribes tests or treatment . The prescribed course of action is based on an assessment of patient risk-patients at higher risk are given more and faster attention. It is also sequential- it is too expensive to immediately order all tests which might later be of value. This paper presents two methods that together improve the accuracy of backprop nets on a pneumonia risk assessment problem by 10-50%. Rankprop improves on backpropagation with sum of squares error in ranking patients by risk. Multitask learning takes advantage of future lab tests available in the training set, but not available in practice when predictions must be made. Both methods are broadly applicable.

paragraphs: The paper addresses pneumonia risk assessment in a setting where medical decisions unfold sequentially. A clinician must judge risk using currently available information, while additional tests may become available later. Ordering every potentially useful test immediately is too expensive, so prediction must work before the full clinical record exists.

The authors introduce two complementary methods. Rankprop improves how a backpropagation network orders patients by risk compared with training using squared error. Multitask learning draws on later laboratory tests recorded in the training data, even though those results are unavailable when the deployed system must make its prediction. Later information thus contributes to learning without becoming a required input at prediction time.

Together, the methods improve the reported accuracy of neural networks on the pneumonia risk problem by 10–50%. The findings connect two aspects of the application: the importance of prioritizing patients correctly and the opportunity to learn from richer historical records. The authors describe both methods as broadly applicable, with the reported evidence coming from this risk-assessment task.
summary.tldr: Rankprop and multitask learning improve pneumonia risk assessment by refining patient ranking and learning from later tests available only during training.

title: Using the Future to "Sort Out" the Present: Rankprop and Multitask Learning for Medical Risk Evaluation

In the real world there are cases where the identity of an object is ambiguous due to the noise in the measurements based on which the classification should be made. It is helpful to re(cid:173) duce the ambiguity by utilizing extra information referred to as context, which in our case is the identities of the accompanying objects. This technique is applied to white blood cell classification. Comparisons are made against "no context" approach, which demonstrates the superior classification performance achieved by using context. In our particular application, it significantly reduces false alarm rate and thus greatly re(cid:173) duces the cost due to expensive clinical tests. • Author for correspondence. Incorporating Contextual Information in White Blood Cell Identification

paragraphs: This paper studies how surrounding objects can help identify an ambiguous object. Measurements may be noisy enough that an object's own observed properties do not clearly determine its class. The proposed technique adds context, defined here as the identities of accompanying objects, to the information used for classification.

The authors apply the approach to white blood cell identification. The central idea is that evidence about the other objects present can help resolve uncertainty about the cell being classified. This makes classification depend on both the cell's measurements and the contextual information supplied by its companions.

Comparisons with classification that does not use context show better performance when context is included. In the reported application, the method substantially reduces false alarms, which in turn reduces costs associated with expensive clinical tests. The practical significance is that improved classification changes the number of unnecessary follow-up actions. The paper thus links a general way of handling ambiguous observations to a concrete benefit in white blood cell identification.
summary.tldr: Using the identities of accompanying objects improves white blood cell classification and reduces costly false alarms.

title: Incorporating Contextual Information in White Blood Cell Identification

abstract: We consider the problem of reliably choosing a near-best strategy from a restricted class of strategies TI in a partially observable Markov deci(cid:173) sion process (POMDP). We assume we are given the ability to simulate the POMDP, and study what might be called the sample complexity - that is, the amount of data one must generate in the POMDP in order to choose a good strategy. We prove upper bounds on the sample com(cid:173) plexity showing that, even for infinitely large and arbitrarily complex POMDPs, the amount of data needed can be finite, and depends only linearly on the complexity of the restricted strategy class TI, and expo(cid:173) nentially on the horizon time. This latter dependence can be eased in a variety of ways, including the application of gradient and local search algorithms. Our measure of complexity generalizes the classical super(cid:173) vised learning notion of VC dimension to the settings of reinforcement learning and planning.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much simulated experience is needed to choose a good strategy when an agent cannot fully observe its environment. Its target is a strategy close to the best member of a restricted strategy class. The analysis assumes access to a simulator of the partially observable Markov decision process.

The authors prove upper bounds on the amount of data required. Even an infinitely large, arbitrarily complicated environment can admit a finite data requirement. In these bounds, the requirement grows linearly with the complexity of the chosen strategy class, but exponentially with the planning horizon. Thus, restricting the available strategies can control one source of difficulty even when the environment itself is enormous.

The complexity measure extends the supervised-learning idea of VC dimension to planning and reinforcement learning. The paper also describes ways to ease the horizon dependence, including gradient and local search methods. Its guarantee concerns selection within the restricted class; it does not establish that this class contains the best possible strategy for the environment.
summary.tldr: With simulator access, selecting a near-best strategy from a restricted class can require finite data even in infinitely large POMDPs.

title: Approximate Planning in Large POMDPs via Reusable Trajectories

abstract: We apply to oscillatory networks a class of learning rules in which synaptic weights change proportional to pre- and post-synaptic ac(cid:173) tivity, with a kernel A(r) measuring the effect for a postsynaptic spike a time r after the presynaptic one. The resulting synaptic ma(cid:173) trices have an outer-product form in which the oscillating patterns are represented as complex vectors. In a simple model, the even part of A(r) enhances the resonant response to learned stimulus by reducing the effective damping, while the odd part determines the frequency of oscillation. We relate our model to the olfactory cortex and hippocampus and their presumed roles in forming associative memories and input representations.

The resulting synaptic ma(cid:173) trices have an outer-product form in which the oscillating patterns are represented as complex vectors. paragraphs: The paper studies how spike-timing-dependent learning shapes networks with oscillating activity. Synaptic changes depend on activity before and after a connection, together with a timing kernel that specifies the effect of a postsynaptic spike occurring at a given delay after a presynaptic spike. The learning rule therefore incorporates the temporal relationship between connected neurons.

The resulting synaptic matrices have an outer-product structure, with oscillating patterns represented by complex vectors. In a simple model, different parts of the timing kernel have distinct effects. Its even component strengthens the resonant response to a learned stimulus by reducing effective damping. Its odd component determines the oscillation frequency.

This separates two consequences of temporal learning: how strongly a learned pattern resonates and how quickly the network oscillates. The authors relate the model to the olfactory cortex and hippocampus, discussing their presumed roles in associative memory and input representation. These biological connections frame the model's relevance, while the stated division between damping and frequency is a result within the simple model analyzed.
summary.tldr: In a simple oscillatory-network model, different components of spike-timing-dependent learning control learned resonance strength and oscillation frequency.

title: Spike-Timing-Dependent Learning for Oscillatory Networks

abstract: It has been shown that the receptive fields of simple cells in VI can be ex(cid:173) plained by assuming optimal encoding, provided that an extra constraint of sparseness is added. This finding suggests that there is a reason, in(cid:173) dependent of optimal representation, for sparseness. However this work used an ad hoc model for the noise. Here I show that, if a biologically more plausible noise model, describing neurons as Poisson processes, is used sparseness does not have to be added as a constraint. Thus I con(cid:173) clude that sparseness is not a feature that evolution has striven for, but is simply the result of the evolutionary pressure towards an optimal repre(cid:173) sentation.

paragraphs: This paper asks why sparse representations arise in models of simple-cell receptive fields in primary visual cortex. Earlier optimal-encoding accounts required an additional sparsity constraint. That requirement suggested sparsity might need an explanation separate from the pressure to represent information optimally.

The author revisits the noise assumption behind that conclusion. The earlier work used an ad hoc noise model; this paper instead describes neurons as Poisson processes, which the author regards as more biologically plausible. Under that modeling choice, sparsity no longer has to be imposed as an extra constraint. The change in the account comes from how neuronal noise is represented.

The author interprets this result as evidence that sparsity can follow from evolutionary pressure toward optimal representation, without being an independently selected objective. The key modeling lesson is that conclusions about the need for a separate sparsity principle depend on the assumed noise process. The stated evolutionary conclusion is the author's interpretation of the result obtained with the Poisson-neuron model.
summary.tldr: With a Poisson model of neuronal noise, sparse representations emerge without an additional sparsity constraint.

title: Whence Sparseness?

abstract: We introduce NashProp, an iterative and local message-passing algo- rithm for computing Nash equilibria in multi-player games represented by arbitrary undirected graphs. We provide a formal analysis and exper- imental evidence demonstrating that NashProp performs well on large graphical games with many loops, often converging in just a dozen itera- tions on graphs with hundreds of nodes. NashProp generalizes the tree algorithm of (Kearns et al. 2001), and can be viewed as similar in spirit to belief propagation in probabilis- tic inference, and thus complements the recent work of (Vickrey and Koller 2002), who explored a junction tree approach. Thus, as for prob- abilistic inference, we have at least two promising general-purpose ap- proaches to equilibria computation in graphs.

We provide a formal analysis and exper- imental evidence demonstrating that NashProp performs well on large graphical games with many loops, often converging in just a dozen itera- tions on graphs with hundreds of nodes. paragraphs: The paper introduces NashProp, an algorithm for computing Nash equilibria in multiplayer games represented by undirected graphs. Such a representation organizes the game around relationships between players. NashProp works through repeated local message passing, allowing information relevant to equilibrium computation to move through the graph over successive iterations.

The algorithm generalizes an earlier approach for tree-structured games to arbitrary undirected graphs, including graphs with many loops. The authors describe it as similar in spirit to belief propagation in probabilistic inference. This connection helps explain its design: local exchanges support a computation concerning the whole network of interacting players.

Formal analysis and experiments support its performance on large graphical games containing many loops. In the reported experiments, it often converges in roughly a dozen iterations on graphs with hundreds of nodes. This is an empirical observation rather than a universal convergence promise. The paper positions NashProp alongside junction-tree approaches as another promising general-purpose route to equilibrium computation in graphical games.
summary.tldr: NashProp uses local message passing to compute equilibria in graphical games, often converging quickly on large, loopy graphs in experiments.

title: Nash Propagation for Loopy Graphical Games

abstract: We introduce a generalization of temporal-difference (TD) learning to networks of interrelated predictions. Rather than relating a single prediction to itself at a later time, as in conventional TD methods, a TD network relates each prediction in a set of predictions to other predictions in the set at a later time. TD networks can represent and apply TD learning to a much wider class of predictions than has previously been possible. Using a random-walk example, we show that these networks can be used to learn to predict by a fixed interval, which is not possible with conventional TD methods. Secondly, we show that if the interpredictive relationships are made conditional on action, then the usual learning-efficiency advantage of TD methods over Monte Carlo (supervised learning) methods becomes particularly pronounced. Thirdly, we demonstrate that TD networks can learn predictive state representations that enable exact solution of a non-Markov problem. A very broad range of inter-predictive temporal relationships can be expressed in these networks. Overall we argue that TD networks represent a substantial extension of the abilities of TD methods and bring us closer to the goal of representing world knowledge in entirely predictive, grounded terms.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference networks extend learning from one prediction to a collection of related predictions. Conventional temporal-difference learning relates a prediction to its own later value. Here, a prediction can instead depend on other predictions at a later time, allowing the network to express a wider variety of temporal relationships.

The paper demonstrates several consequences of this extension. In a random-walk example, the networks learn predictions at a fixed time interval, a capability the authors distinguish from conventional temporal-difference methods. When relationships between predictions depend on actions, they also show a particularly pronounced learning-efficiency advantage over Monte Carlo supervised learning methods.

A further demonstration shows that the networks can learn predictive state representations enabling an exact solution to a non-Markov problem. This is a demonstrated capability on a problem, not a guarantee of exact solutions to every such problem. Together, the examples support the authors' argument that interrelated predictions substantially expand temporal-difference learning and move toward representing knowledge about the world through grounded predictions.
summary.tldr: Temporal-difference networks connect multiple predictions across time, enabling richer prediction tasks and demonstrated learning-efficiency and predictive-state benefits.

title: Temporal-Difference Networks

abstract: We present a learning algorithm for undiscounted reinforcement learning. Our interest lies in bounds for the algorithm's online performance after some finite number of steps. In the spirit of similar methods already successfully applied for the exploration-exploitation tradeoff in multi-armed bandit problems, we use upper confidence bounds to show that our UCRL algorithm achieves logarithmic online regret in the number of steps taken with respect to an optimal policy.
originalAbstract: We present a learning algorithm for undiscounted reinforcement learning. Our interest lies in bounds for the algorithm's online performance after some finite number of steps. In the spirit of similar methods already successfully applied for the exploration-exploitation tradeoff in multi-armed bandit problems, we use upper confidence bounds to show that our UCRL algorithm achieves logarithmic online regret in the number of steps taken with respect to an optimal policy.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning algorithm must choose actions while it is still learning which choices are valuable. This paper evaluates that ongoing behavior in an undiscounted setting, where future rewards are not progressively reduced by a discount factor. Its focus is performance after a finite number of interactions, rather than only the quality of an eventual learned policy.

The proposed algorithm, UCRL, uses upper confidence bounds to manage the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. The approach draws on methods used successfully for multi-armed bandit problems. Confidence bounds provide a way to make decisions that account for uncertainty, connecting the need to gather information with the goal of obtaining rewards during learning.

The authors establish logarithmic online regret in the number of steps relative to an optimal policy. Regret measures the accumulated performance shortfall against that reference. A logarithmic bound means this shortfall grows slowly as interaction continues, giving a quantitative account of the cost of learning while acting. The contribution is a finite-step performance guarantee for the presented undiscounted reinforcement learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: UCRL uses upper confidence bounds to achieve logarithmic online regret in the studied undiscounted reinforcement learning setting.

title: Logarithmic Online Regret Bounds for Undiscounted Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We usually endow the investigated objects with pairwise relationships, which can be illustrated as graphs. In many real-world problems, however, relationships among the objects of our interest are more complex than pair- wise. Naively squeezing the complex relationships into pairwise ones will inevitably lead to loss of information which can be expected valuable for our learning tasks however. Therefore we consider using hypergraphs in- stead to completely represent complex relationships among the objects of our interest, and thus the problem of learning with hypergraphs arises. Our main contribution in this paper is to generalize the powerful methodology of spectral clustering which originally operates on undirected graphs to hy- pergraphs, and further develop algorithms for hypergraph embedding and transductive classiﬁcation on the basis of the spectral hypergraph cluster- ing approach. Our experiments on a number of benchmarks showed the advantages of hypergraphs over usual graphs.

paragraphs: Ordinary graphs describe relationships between pairs of objects. The paper argues that some learning problems involve relationships among larger groups, and that forcing those relationships into pairwise form loses potentially useful information. It therefore uses hypergraphs, which can represent a relationship involving multiple objects together.

The main contribution extends spectral clustering from undirected graphs to hypergraphs. This brings a graph-based clustering methodology to a richer relational representation. The authors then build algorithms for hypergraph embedding and transductive classification on the same foundation, connecting the clustering formulation to both representation and prediction tasks.

Experiments on several benchmarks show advantages for hypergraphs over ordinary graphs. These results support the value of retaining relationships involving groups when they contain information useful for learning. The paper's broader contribution is a shared spectral approach for working with that information across clustering, embedding, and classification. The empirical comparison supports the proposed representation in the tested problems, without establishing that hypergraphs improve every task.
summary.tldr: Extending spectral clustering to hypergraphs enables clustering, embedding, and classification that preserve relationships among groups of objects.

title: Learning with Hypergraphs: Clustering, Classification, and Embedding

abstract: Empirical evidence shows that in favorable situations semi-supervised learning (SSL) algorithms can capitalize on the abundancy of unlabeled training data to improve the performance of a learning task, in the sense that fewer labeled training data are needed to achieve a target error bound. However, in other situations unlabeled data do not seem to help. Recent attempts at theoretically characterizing the situations in which unlabeled data can help have met with little success, and sometimes appear to conflict with each other and intuition. In this paper, we attempt to bridge the gap between practice and theory of semi-supervised learning. We develop a rigorous framework for analyzing the situations in which unlabeled data can help and quantify the improvement possible using finite sample error bounds. We show that there are large classes of problems for which SSL can significantly outperform supervised learning, in finite sample regimes and sometimes also in terms of error convergence rates.

paragraphs: Unlabeled examples sometimes greatly reduce the number of labels needed for classification and sometimes provide little benefit. This uneven empirical picture has been difficult to reconcile with broad theoretical claims. The paper develops a framework for specifying when semi-supervised learning can genuinely improve performance.

The analysis gives finite-sample error bounds that quantify possible gains from unlabeled data. It identifies large classes of problems where semi-supervised methods outperform supervised learning, including settings with better error-convergence rates. The framework thus examines conditions and magnitudes of improvement rather than assuming unlabeled data are uniformly useful.

The contribution connects practical success to a more discriminating theory of learnability. Its central implication is that the usefulness of the input distribution depends on the structure of the learning problem. More unlabeled observations are valuable when that structure connects them to the prediction target, and a meaningful guarantee must make those favorable conditions explicit.
summary.tldr: A finite-sample framework identifies broad problem classes where unlabeled data improve label efficiency and sometimes convergence rates.

title: Unlabeled data: Now it helps, now it doesn't

abstract: We show how to model documents as bags of words using family of two-layer, undirected graphical models. Each member of the family has the same number of binary hidden units but a different number of ``softmax visible units. All of the softmax units in all of the models in the family share the same weights to the binary hidden units. We describe efficient inference and learning procedures for such a family. Each member of the family models the probability distribution of documents of a specific length as a product of topic-specific distributions rather than as a mixture and this gives much better generalization than Latent Dirichlet Allocation for modeling the log probabilities of held-out documents. The low-dimensional topic vectors learned by the undirected family are also much better than LDA topic vectors for retrieving documents that are similar to a query document. The learned topics are more general than those found by LDA because precision is achieved by intersecting many general topics rather than by selecting a single precise topic to generate each word.

paragraphs: This paper models bag-of-words documents using a family of two-layer undirected graphical models. Different members handle different document lengths while keeping the same number of binary hidden units. Their softmax visible units share weights to those hidden units, tying the family together through a common learned representation.

Each model expresses document probabilities as a product of topic-specific distributions. Precision comes from intersecting several broad topics, which allows the learned topics themselves to remain relatively general. The authors contrast this mechanism with selecting a single precise topic to generate each word, and provide efficient procedures for inference and learning.

The reported comparisons with Latent Dirichlet Allocation show substantially better generalization in held-out document log probabilities. The learned low-dimensional topic vectors also perform substantially better for retrieving documents similar to a query document. These findings support both the model's probability estimates and its usefulness as a document representation, with the product-based combination of topics central to the proposed explanation.
summary.tldr: Replicated Softmax combines broad topics through a product model and reports better document modeling and retrieval than LDA.

title: Replicated Softmax: an Undirected Topic Model

abstract: Studying signal and noise properties of recorded neural data is critical in developing more efficient algorithms to recover the encoded information. Important issues exist in this research including the variant spectrum spans of neural spikes that make it difficult to choose a global optimal bandpass filter. Also, multiple sources produce aggregated noise that deviates from the conventional white Gaussian noise. In this work, the spectrum variability of spikes is addressed, based on which the concept of adaptive bandpass filter that fits the spectrum of individual spikes is proposed. Multiple noise sources have been studied through analytical models as well as empirical measurements. The dominant noise source is identified as neuron noise followed by interface noise of the electrode. This suggests that major efforts to reduce noise from electronics are not well spent. The measured noise from in vivo experiments shows a family of 1/f^{x} (x=1.5\pm 0.5) spectrum that can be reduced using noise shaping techniques. In summary, the methods of adaptive bandpass filtering and noise shaping together result in several dB signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) enhancement.

paragraphs: The paper examines both neural signals and the noise mixed into in vivo recordings. One difficulty is that individual neural spikes occupy different frequency ranges, making a single bandpass filter hard to optimize for every spike. The authors propose adapting the filter to the spectrum of each spike instead.

They also investigate multiple noise sources using analytical models and empirical measurements. In their analysis, neuron noise is the dominant contribution, followed by noise at the electrode interface. This suggests that concentrating major noise-reduction effort on the electronics would have limited value in the studied setting.

Measured in vivo noise has a frequency spectrum in the family 1/f^x, with x reported as 1.5 ± 0.5, rather than the conventional white Gaussian description. The authors use noise shaping to reduce this structured noise. Combined with adaptive bandpass filtering, the methods yield several decibels of signal-to-noise improvement. The findings connect noise characterization to concrete choices about filtering and where reduction efforts are likely to matter.
summary.tldr: Characterizing spike spectra and recording noise motivates adaptive filtering and noise shaping that together improve signal-to-noise ratio by several decibels.

title: Noise Characterization, Modeling, and Reduction for In Vivo Neural Recording

abstract: We consider a statistical framework in which recurrent networks of spiking neurons learn to generate spatio-temporal spike patterns. Given biologically realistic stochastic neuronal dynamics we derive a tractable learning rule for the synaptic weights towards hidden and visible neurons that leads to optimal recall of the training sequences. We show that learning synaptic weights towards hidden neurons significantly improves the storing capacity of the network. Furthermore, we derive an approximate online learning rule and show that our learning rule is consistent with Spike-Timing Dependent Plasticity in that if a presynaptic spike shortly precedes a postynaptic spike, potentiation is induced and otherwise depression is elicited.

paragraphs: The paper studies recurrent networks of spiking neurons that learn to generate patterns spread across both neurons and time. It uses a statistical framework with biologically realistic stochastic neuronal dynamics. The learning problem includes synaptic weights directed toward both visible neurons and hidden neurons, so internal network activity can participate in storing the sequences.

This makes the hidden part of the network an active contributor to how many patterns can be retained.

Its changes in synaptic strength are consistent with Spike-Timing Dependent Plasticity: a presynaptic spike shortly before a postsynaptic spike induces potentiation, while otherwise depression occurs. This connects the statistical learning procedure to a timing-based form of synaptic adaptation, alongside its results on sequence recall and capacity.
summary.tldr: Learning synapses toward hidden neurons improves spiking-network sequence capacity, with an approximate online rule consistent with timing-dependent plasticity.

title: Sequence learning with hidden units in spiking neural networks

abstract: Determining interactions between entities and the overall organization and clustering of nodes in networks is a major challenge when analyzing biological and social network data. Here we extend the Indian Buffet Process (IBP), a nonparametric Bayesian model, to integrate noisy interaction scores with properties of individual entities for inferring interaction networks and clustering nodes within these networks. We present an application of this method to study how microRNAs regulate mRNAs in cells. Analysis of synthetic and real data indicates that the method improves upon prior methods, correctly recovers interactions and clusters, and provides accurate biological predictions.

We present an application of this method to study how microRNAs regulate mRNAs in cells. Analysis of synthetic and real data indicates that the method improves upon prior methods, correctly recovers interactions and clusters, and provides accurate biological predictions.

paragraphs: Interaction networks are often inferred from noisy pairwise scores, but the properties of the entities themselves can supply additional information. This paper combines those sources to estimate relationships and discover groups jointly. Its model extends the Indian Buffet Process, a Bayesian nonparametric latent-feature framework.

The extension integrates uncertain interaction evidence with individual entity attributes. This allows network inference and node clustering to inform one another instead of being performed as disconnected steps. The application examines how microRNAs regulate messenger RNAs, where recovering the right interactions is biologically meaningful.

Synthetic and real-data analyses improve on prior methods, recover interactions and clusters, and yield accurate biological predictions. The contribution is a flexible model for sharing information between network structure and node properties. The latent representation provides a way to pool weak evidence across related entities rather than treating every candidate interaction as an independent classification problem.
summary.tldr: An Indian Buffet Process extension combines node attributes and noisy interaction scores to infer networks and latent groups, including microRNA targets.

title: Inferring Interaction Networks using the IBP applied to microRNA Target Prediction

abstract: Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) has proven to be a powerful, generic planning technique for decision-making in single-agent and adversarial environments. The stochastic nature of the Monte-Carlo simulations introduces errors in the value estimates, both in terms of bias and variance. Whilst reducing bias (typically through the addition of domain knowledge) has been studied in the MCTS literature, comparatively little effort has focused on reducing variance. This is somewhat surprising, since variance reduction techniques are a well-studied area in classical statistics. In this paper, we examine the application of some standard techniques for variance reduction in MCTS, including common random numbers, antithetic variates and control variates. We demonstrate how these techniques can be applied to MCTS and explore their efficacy on three different stochastic, single-agent settings: Pig, Can't Stop and Dominion.

paragraphs: Monte-Carlo Tree Search plans by using simulated outcomes to estimate the value of decisions. Because those simulations are stochastic, their estimates contain both bias and variance. The paper focuses on variance, which concerns fluctuations in the estimates, rather than the bias-reduction approaches that had received more attention through the addition of domain knowledge.

The authors investigate three established statistical techniques: common random numbers, antithetic variates, and control variates. Their contribution is to show how these methods can be applied within Monte-Carlo Tree Search. This connects tools from statistical simulation with a planning procedure whose decisions depend on values estimated from random simulations.

The empirical investigation covers Pig, Can't Stop, and Dominion in stochastic single-agent settings. These experiments explore the techniques' efficacy in the studied planning problems; the abstract does not assert a uniform improvement from every technique. The broader significance is to make variance reduction an explicit part of MCTS design, alongside efforts to improve the bias of its estimates.
summary.tldr: The paper adapts three classical variance-reduction techniques to Monte-Carlo Tree Search and studies their efficacy in three stochastic single-agent games.

title: Variance Reduction in Monte-Carlo Tree Search

abstract: We propose a robust filtering approach based on semi-supervised and multiple instance learning (MIL). We assume that the posterior density would be unimodal if not for the effect of outliers that we do not wish to explicitly model. Therefore, we seek for a point estimate at the outset, rather than a generic approximation of the entire posterior. Our approach can be thought of as a combination of standard finite-dimensional filtering (Extended Kalman Filter, or Unscented Filter) with multiple instance learning, whereby the initial condition comes with a putative set of inlier measurements. We show how both the state (regression) and the inlier set (classification) can be estimated iteratively and causally by processing only the current measurement. We illustrate our approach on visual tracking problems whereby the object of interest (target) moves and evolves as a result of occlusions and deformations, and partial knowledge of the target is given in the form of a bounding box (training set).

paragraphs: Filtering estimates a changing state from measurements, but outliers can make that estimation unreliable. This paper assumes that the posterior density would have a single mode without the unwanted outliers. Under that assumption, it seeks a point estimate directly, avoiding both an explicit model of the outliers and a general approximation of the whole posterior.

The approach combines finite-dimensional filtering, such as an Extended Kalman Filter or Unscented Filter, with semi-supervised multiple instance learning. It begins with a candidate set of inlier measurements. State estimation and inlier identification are then treated as linked regression and classification problems, allowing the method to update both its state estimate and its judgment of which measurements belong.

The authors show that these updates can proceed iteratively and causally using only the current measurement. They illustrate the method through visual tracking with occlusions and deformations, starting from partial target information supplied as a bounding box. The contribution is a filtering procedure that jointly tracks the target and revises the measurements considered reliable.
summary.tldr: Multiple instance filtering jointly estimates a changing state and its inlier measurements under a unimodality assumption for the outlier-free posterior.

title: Multiple Instance Filtering

abstract: Gaussian Graphical Models (GGMs) or Gauss Markov random fields are widely used in many applications, and the trade-off between the modeling capacity and the efficiency of learning and inference has been an important research problem. In this paper, we study the family of GGMs with small feedback vertex sets (FVSs), where an FVS is a set of nodes whose removal breaks all the cycles. Exact inference such as computing the marginal distributions and the partition function has complexity $O(k^{2}n)$ using message-passing algorithms, where k is the size of the FVS, and n is the total number of nodes. We propose efficient structure learning algorithms for two cases: 1) All nodes are observed, which is useful in modeling social or flight networks where the FVS nodes often correspond to a small number of high-degree nodes, or hubs, while the rest of the networks is modeled by a tree. Regardless of the maximum degree, without knowing the full graph structure, we can exactly compute the maximum likelihood estimate in $O(kn^2+n^2\log n)$ if the FVS is known or in polynomial time if the FVS is unknown but has bounded size. 2) The FVS nodes are latent variables, where structure learning is equivalent to decomposing a inverse covariance matrix (exactly or approximately) into the sum of a tree-structured matrix and a low-rank matrix. By incorporating efficient inference into the learning steps, we can obtain a learning algorithm using alternating low-rank correction with complexity $O(kn^{2}+n^{2}\log n)$ per iteration. We also perform experiments using both synthetic data as well as real data of flight delays to demonstrate the modeling capacity with FVSs of various sizes. We show that empirically the family of GGMs of size $O(\log n)$ strikes a good balance between the modeling capacity and the efficiency.

With n nodes and a feedback set of size k, exact message-passing inference has complexity O(k²n).

When the feedback set is known, exact maximum-likelihood estimation takes O(kn² + n² log n), without requiring the remaining graph structure in advance. An alternating low-rank correction method costs O(kn² + n² log n) per iteration. Synthetic and flight-delay experiments explore different feedback-set sizes, with logarithmic-size sets empirically offering a useful balance between modeling capacity and efficiency.
summary.tldr: Gaussian graphical models with small feedback vertex sets support efficient inference and structure learning with either observed or latent feedback nodes.

title: Learning Gaussian Graphical Models with Observed or Latent FVSs

abstract: In this paper, we consider a multi-step version of the stochastic ADMM method with efficient guarantees for high-dimensional problems. We first analyze the simple setting, where the optimization problem consists of a loss function and a single regularizer (e.g. sparse optimization), and then extend to the multi-block setting with multiple regularizers and multiple variables (e.g. matrix decomposition into sparse and low rank components). For the sparse optimization problem, our method achieves the minimax rate of $O(s\log d/T)$ for $s$-sparse problems in $d$ dimensions in $T$ steps, and is thus, unimprovable by any method up to constant factors. For the matrix decomposition problem with a general loss function, we analyze the multi-step ADMM with multiple blocks. We establish $O(1/T)$ rate and efficient scaling as the size of matrix grows. For natural noise models (e.g. independent noise), our convergence rate is minimax-optimal. Thus, we establish tight convergence guarantees for multi-block ADMM in high dimensions. Experiments show that for both sparse optimization and matrix decomposition problems, our algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: High-dimensional optimization often combines a data-fitting loss with penalties that encourage useful structure. This paper studies a multi-step stochastic ADMM method, beginning with one regularizer and then extending to multiple variables and regularizers. The applications include sparse optimization and decomposing a matrix into sparse and low-rank parts.

For an s-sparse problem in d dimensions, the method achieves a rate of O(s log d/T) after T steps. The authors establish that this rate is minimax-optimal up to constant factors. The matrix-decomposition rate is also minimax-optimal under natural noise models, including independent noise. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art methods for both applications. The contribution therefore includes sharp theoretical guarantees and empirical comparisons, with the optimality claim for matrix decomposition tied to the stated noise settings. Extending the analysis to multiple blocks makes the approach relevant to objectives with several interacting structural components.
summary.tldr: Multi-step stochastic ADMM achieves sharp high-dimensional convergence guarantees for sparse optimization and multi-block matrix decomposition.

title: Multi-Step Stochastic ADMM in High Dimensions: Applications to Sparse Optimization and Matrix Decomposition

abstract: This paper investigates how to extract objects-of-interest without relying on hand-craft features and sliding windows approaches, that aims to jointly solve two sub-tasks: (i) rapidly localizing salient objects from images, and (ii) accurately segmenting the objects based on the localizations. We present a general joint task learning framework, in which each task (either object localization or object segmentation) is tackled via a multi-layer convolutional neural network, and the two networks work collaboratively to boost performance. In particular, we propose to incorporate latent variables bridging the two networks in a joint optimization manner. The first network directly predicts the positions and scales of salient objects from raw images, and the latent variables adjust the object localizations to feed the second network that produces pixelwise object masks. An EM-type method is then studied for the joint optimization, iterating with two steps: (i) by using the two networks, it estimates the latent variables by employing an MCMC-based sampling method; (ii) it optimizes the parameters of the two networks unitedly via back propagation, with the fixed latent variables. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our joint learning framework significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches in both accuracy and efficiency (e.g., 1000 times faster than competing approaches).

paragraphs: Extracting an object from an image involves locating it and deciding which pixels belong to it. This paper treats those activities as linked learning tasks. It introduces two convolutional networks that work together, aiming to locate salient objects quickly and then segment them accurately without handcrafted features or sliding-window approaches.

The first network predicts object positions and scales directly from the image. Latent variables connect its predictions to the second network by adjusting the localizations used to produce pixelwise object masks. This connection makes localization part of a joint optimization problem, so the two networks are trained as a collaborative system.

The next holds those variables fixed and updates both networks through backpropagation. Experiments report substantial gains in accuracy and efficiency over competing approaches, including a speedup of 1,000 times in the reported comparisons. These findings support joint learning as a useful way to coordinate localization and segmentation.
summary.tldr: Two jointly trained convolutional networks connect object localization and segmentation through latent variables, with substantial reported accuracy and speed gains.

title: Deep Joint Task Learning for Generic Object Extraction

abstract: This work concerns learning probabilistic models for ranking data in a heterogeneous population. The specific problem we study is learning the parameters of a {\em Mallows Mixture Model}. Despite being widely studied, current heuristics for this problem do not have theoretical guarantees and can get stuck in bad local optima. We present the first polynomial time algorithm which provably learns the parameters of a mixture of two Mallows models. A key component of our algorithm is a novel use of tensor decomposition techniques to learn the top-$k$ prefix in both the rankings. Before this work, even the question of {\em identifiability} in the case of a mixture of two Mallows models was unresolved.

paragraphs: Ranking data can come from a heterogeneous population whose members follow different preference patterns. This paper studies parameter learning for a mixture of Mallows ranking models, focusing on a mixture with two components. The task is to recover the underlying models from the combined ranking data, rather than treating all observations as expressions of one common pattern.

Existing heuristics for this problem lacked theoretical guarantees and could become trapped in poor local optima. The authors present what they identify as the first polynomial-time algorithm with a proof of parameter learning for two Mallows components. Its key ingredient is a new application of tensor decomposition to recover the top-k prefixes of both underlying rankings.

Recovering these prefixes supplies an essential component of the full learning procedure. The result also addresses a foundational uncertainty: before this work, identifiability for two-component Mallows mixtures remained unresolved. Identifiability concerns whether the observed distribution determines the underlying model parameters. The contribution establishes a provable learning route for this specific mixture setting, beyond the behavior of heuristic optimization.
summary.tldr: A tensor-based algorithm provably learns a mixture of two Mallows ranking models in polynomial time.

title: Learning Mixtures of Ranking Models

abstract: The Multi-Armed Bandit problem constitutes an archetypal setting for sequential decision-making, permeating multiple domains including engineering, business, and medicine. One of the hallmarks of a bandit setting is the agent's capacity to explore its environment through active intervention, which contrasts with the ability to collect passive data by estimating associational relationships between actions and payouts. The existence of unobserved confounders, namely unmeasured variables affecting both the action and the outcome variables, implies that these two data-collection modes will in general not coincide. In this paper, we show that formalizing this distinction has conceptual and algorithmic implications to the bandit setting. The current generation of bandit algorithms implicitly try to maximize rewards based on estimation of the experimental distribution, which we show is not always the best strategy to pursue. Indeed, to achieve low regret in certain realistic classes of bandit problems (namely, in the face of unobserved confounders), both experimental and observational quantities are required by the rational agent. After this realization, we propose an optimization metric (employing both experimental and observational distributions) that bandit agents should pursue, and illustrate its benefits over traditional algorithms.

paragraphs: A bandit agent learns by choosing actions and observing rewards. This paper distinguishes that active experimentation from passively observing which actions occurred and what followed. When an unmeasured variable affects both the action and its outcome, the relationships found through observation generally differ from those obtained through intervention.

The authors show that this distinction changes what a bandit agent should optimize. Traditional algorithms implicitly pursue rewards using the experimental distribution. The paper argues that this is not always the best strategy: in certain classes of problems with unobserved confounding, achieving low regret requires both observational and experimental quantities. The claim concerns those settings, rather than every bandit problem.

The proposed optimization metric explicitly combines the two distributions, and the authors illustrate benefits over traditional algorithms. The contribution is therefore conceptual as well as algorithmic. It identifies circumstances in which information about naturally occurring actions remains relevant even for an agent that can actively experiment, and incorporates that information into the objective guiding its decisions.
summary.tldr: In certain confounded bandit settings, low-regret decisions require an objective that combines observational and experimental information.

title: Bandits with Unobserved Confounders: A Causal Approach

abstract: Despite their success, convolutional neural networks are computationally expensive because they must examine all image locations. Stochastic attention-based models have been shown to improve computational efficiency at test time, but they remain difficult to train because of intractable posterior inference and high variance in the stochastic gradient estimates. Borrowing techniques from the literature on training deep generative models, we present the Wake-Sleep Recurrent Attention Model, a method for training stochastic attention networks which improves posterior inference and which reduces the variability in the stochastic gradients. We show that our method can greatly speed up the training time for stochastic attention networks in the domains of image classification and caption generation.

paragraphs: Convolutional image models can be costly because they examine every image location. Stochastic attention models can reduce test-time computation by selectively attending to image information. Their training, however, presents a separate difficulty: posterior inference can be intractable, and sampled gradient estimates can vary substantially, complicating the learning process.

The paper introduces the Wake-Sleep Recurrent Attention Model to address these training obstacles. It borrows techniques from deep generative model learning and applies them to stochastic attention networks. The proposed method improves posterior inference and reduces variability in the stochastic gradients, targeting both the inference problem and the instability of the training signal.

The authors show that the method can greatly accelerate training for image classification and caption generation. The stated result concerns making stochastic attention networks easier and faster to train in these domains, complementing their existing computational advantages at test time. Its broader significance is that selective visual processing becomes more practical when the learning procedure is designed around the randomness of the attention mechanism.
summary.tldr: Wake-sleep training improves posterior inference and reduces gradient variability, substantially accelerating stochastic attention training in the demonstrated tasks.

title: Learning Wake-Sleep Recurrent Attention Models

abstract: Adaptive optimization methods, which perform local optimization with a metric constructed from the history of iterates, are becoming increasingly popular for training deep neural networks. Examples include AdaGrad, RMSProp, and Adam. We show that for simple overparameterized problems, adaptive methods often find drastically different solutions than gradient descent (GD) or stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We construct an illustrative binary classification problem where the data is linearly separable, GD and SGD achieve zero test error, and AdaGrad, Adam, and RMSProp attain test errors arbitrarily close to half. We additionally study the empirical generalization capability of adaptive methods on several state-of-the-art deep learning models. We observe that the solutions found by adaptive methods generalize worse (often significantly worse) than SGD, even when these solutions have better training performance. These results suggest that practitioners should reconsider the use of adaptive methods to train neural networks.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers such as AdaGrad, RMSProp, and Adam use information from earlier iterates to construct the metric guiding optimization. This paper examines how that choice affects the solution eventually learned. Its central concern is generalization: achieving a better training objective does not necessarily mean achieving better predictions on unseen examples.

The authors construct a simple, overparameterized binary classification problem with linearly separable data. In this example, gradient descent and SGD obtain zero test error, while the adaptive methods can have test error arbitrarily close to one half. The construction demonstrates a sharp possible difference in generalization caused by the optimization method’s choice of solution.

The paper also evaluates adaptive methods on several state-of-the-art deep-learning models. In those experiments, adaptive methods generalize worse than SGD, often substantially, even when they perform better on the training data. Together, the example and experiments motivate reconsidering routine use of adaptive optimizers. The evidence concerns the demonstrated construction and studied models, rather than establishing that adaptive methods always generalize worse.
summary.tldr: A constructed example and deep-learning experiments show adaptive optimizers can generalize worse than SGD despite better training performance.

title: The Marginal Value of Adaptive Gradient Methods in Machine Learning

abstract: Convolutional long short-term memory (LSTM) networks have been widely used for action/gesture recognition, and different attention mechanisms have also been embedded into the LSTM or the convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) networks. Based on the previous gesture recognition architectures which combine the three-dimensional convolution neural network (3DCNN) and ConvLSTM, this paper explores the effects of attention mechanism in ConvLSTM. Several variants of ConvLSTM are evaluated: (a) Removing the convolutional structures of the three gates in ConvLSTM, (b) Applying the attention mechanism on the input of ConvLSTM, (c) Reconstructing the input and (d) output gates respectively with the modified channel-wise attention mechanism. The evaluation results demonstrate that the spatial convolutions in the three gates scarcely contribute to the spatiotemporal feature fusion, and the attention mechanisms embedded into the input and output gates cannot improve the feature fusion. In other words, ConvLSTM mainly contributes to the temporal fusion along with the recurrent steps to learn the long-term spatiotemporal features, when taking as input the spatial or spatiotemporal features. On this basis, a new variant of LSTM is derived, in which the convolutional structures are only embedded into the input-to-state transition of LSTM. The code of the LSTM variants is publicly available.
originalAbstract: Convolutional long short-term memory (LSTM) networks have been widely used for action/gesture recognition, and different attention mechanisms have also been embedded into the LSTM or the convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) networks. Based on the previous gesture recognition architectures which combine the three-dimensional convolution neural network (3DCNN) and ConvLSTM, this paper explores the effects of attention mechanism in ConvLSTM. Several variants of ConvLSTM are evaluated: (a) Removing the convolutional structures of the three gates in ConvLSTM, (b) Applying the attention mechanism on the input of ConvLSTM, (c) Reconstructing the input and (d) output gates respectively with the modified channel-wise attention mechanism. The evaluation results demonstrate that the spatial convolutions in the three gates scarcely contribute to the spatiotemporal feature fusion, and the attention mechanisms embedded into the input and output gates cannot improve the feature fusion. In other words, ConvLSTM mainly contributes to the temporal fusion along with the recurrent steps to learn the long-term spatiotemporal features, when taking as input the spatial or spatiotemporal features. On this basis, a new variant of LSTM is derived, in which the convolutional structures are only embedded into the input-to-state transition of LSTM. The code of the LSTM variants is publicly available.

paragraphs: This paper investigates which parts of a convolutional LSTM actually help recognize gestures. It starts from architectures that combine a three-dimensional convolutional network with a ConvLSTM, then changes individual components to examine how spatial information and information across time are combined.

The evaluated variants remove convolutions from the three gates, apply attention to the incoming features, or rebuild the input and output gates using modified channel-wise attention. These comparisons probe whether the gates need spatial processing and whether attention inside them improves feature fusion. In the reported evaluations, gate convolutions contribute little, and attention in the input and output gates does not improve fusion.

The authors interpret these findings as evidence that, when spatial or spatiotemporal features are already supplied, ConvLSTM mainly contributes by combining information across recurrent steps. They consequently derive an LSTM variant that retains convolutions only in the input-to-state transition. The result offers a more targeted architectural design grounded in the evaluated components' contributions.
summary.tldr: Experiments on gesture recognition motivate an LSTM variant that keeps convolutions only in the input-to-state transition.

title: Attention in Convolutional LSTM for Gesture Recognition

abstract: Understanding how humans and animals learn about statistical regularities in stable and volatile environments, and utilize these regularities to make predictions and decisions, is an important problem in neuroscience and psychology. Using a Bayesian modeling framework, specifically the Dynamic Belief Model (DBM), it has previously been shown that humans tend to make the {\it default} assumption that environmental statistics undergo abrupt, unsignaled changes, even when environmental statistics are actually stable. Because exact Bayesian inference in this setting, an example of switching state space models, is computationally intense, a number of approximately Bayesian and heuristic algorithms have been proposed to account for learning/prediction in the brain. Here, we examine a neurally plausible algorithm, a special case of leaky integration dynamics we denote as EXP (for exponential filtering), that is significantly simpler than all previously suggested algorithms except for the delta-learning rule, and which far outperforms the delta rule in approximating Bayesian prediction performance. We derive the theoretical relationship between DBM and EXP, and show that EXP gains computational efficiency by foregoing the representation of inferential uncertainty (as does the delta rule), but that it nevertheless achieves near-Bayesian performance due to its ability to incorporate a "persistent prior" influence unique to DBM and absent from the other algorithms. Furthermore, we show that EXP is comparable to DBM but better than all other models in reproducing human behavior in a visual search task, suggesting that human learning and prediction also incorporates an element of persistent prior. More broadly, our work demonstrates that when observations are information-poor, detecting changes or modulating the learning rate is both {\it difficult} and (thus) {\it unnecessary} for making Bayes-optimal predictions.

paragraphs: People can learn as though their environment might change abruptly even when its statistics remain stable. The Dynamic Belief Model explains this tendency through Bayesian inference, but exact computation is demanding. This paper investigates whether a much simpler, neurally plausible exponential-filtering algorithm, called EXP, can reproduce the relevant predictions and human behavior.

The authors derive the relationship between EXP and the Bayesian model. EXP saves computation by omitting an explicit representation of inferential uncertainty. Nevertheless, it retains a persistent influence from prior beliefs, allowing it to achieve near-Bayesian prediction performance. The abstract identifies this persistent prior as the feature that distinguishes it from the other approximation methods considered.

EXP approximates Bayesian predictions much better than the delta-learning rule. In a visual search task, it also reproduces human behavior comparably to the Dynamic Belief Model and better than the other models examined. The broader conclusion is conditional: when individual observations convey little information, detecting changes or adjusting learning rates can be difficult and unnecessary for Bayes-optimal prediction.
summary.tldr: A simple exponential filter preserves a persistent prior, enabling near-Bayesian predictions and accounting for human behavior in a visual search task.

title: Demystifying excessively volatile human learning: A Bayesian persistent prior and a neural approximation

abstract: Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) is an important methodology for Bayesian inference when the likelihood function is intractable. Sampling-based ABC algorithms such as rejection- and K2-ABC are inefficient when the parameters have high dimensions, while the regression-based algorithms such as K- and DR-ABC are hard to scale. In this paper, we introduce an optimization-based ABC framework that addresses these deficiencies. Leveraging a generative model for posterior and joint distribution matching, we show that ABC can be framed as saddle point problems, whose objectives can be accessed directly with samples. We present the predictive ABC algorithm (P-ABC), and provide a probabilistically approximately correct (PAC) bound that guarantees its learning consistency. Numerical experiment shows that P-ABC outperforms both K2- and DR-ABC significantly.

paragraphs: Approximate Bayesian computation supports Bayesian inference when the likelihood is too difficult to evaluate directly. Existing sampling-based approaches can become inefficient with high-dimensional parameters, while regression-based alternatives can be difficult to scale. This paper introduces an optimization-based framework intended to address both obstacles through a different formulation of the inference problem.

The method uses a generative model to match posterior and joint distributions. The authors show that this matching task can be expressed as saddle-point optimization, with objectives accessible directly from samples. This gives a route from simulated or sampled information to an optimization problem without requiring direct evaluation of the intractable likelihood.

They develop predictive approximate Bayesian computation, or P-ABC, and provide a probabilistically approximately correct bound guaranteeing learning consistency. A numerical experiment reports significant improvements over K2-ABC and DR-ABC. The contribution combines a sample-accessible optimization formulation, an algorithm built from it, and theoretical support for its learning behavior, with empirical evidence against the two named alternatives.
summary.tldr: P-ABC formulates likelihood-intractable Bayesian inference as sample-based saddle-point optimization with a learning-consistency guarantee.

title: Predictive Approximate Bayesian Computation via Saddle Points

abstract: Deep structured models are widely used for tasks like semantic segmentation, where explicit correlations between variables provide important prior information which generally helps to reduce the data needs of deep nets. However, current deep structured models are restricted by oftentimes very local neighborhood structure, which cannot be increased for computational complexity reasons, and by the fact that the output configuration, or a representation thereof, cannot be transformed further. Very recent approaches which address those issues include graphical model inference inside deep nets so as to permit subsequent non-linear output space transformations. However, optimization of those formulations is challenging and not well understood. Here, we develop a novel model which generalizes existing approaches, such as structured prediction energy networks, and discuss a formulation which maintains applicability of existing inference techniques.

paragraphs: Structured prediction treats related output variables jointly, as in semantic segmentation, where predictions across an image have useful relationships. Encoding those correlations supplies prior information that can reduce the data needs of deep networks. Existing deep structured models, however, often restrict interactions to small neighborhoods because larger structures are computationally expensive.

A second restriction concerns what happens after a structured output or its representation has been produced. Many formulations cannot apply further nonlinear transformations to it. Recent approaches insert graphical model inference inside a deep network to permit such processing, but their optimization is challenging and remains insufficiently understood. The paper addresses this combination of representational and optimization difficulties.

The authors develop a model that generalizes existing approaches, including structured prediction energy networks. They also discuss a formulation that preserves the applicability of existing inference techniques. Its contribution is a broader framework for combining structured relationships with nonlinear output processing while retaining access to established inference machinery. This matters because richer output representations must still support the computations needed to make predictions.
summary.tldr: A generalized deep structured model supports nonlinear output transformations while preserving applicability of existing inference techniques.

title: Deep Structured Prediction with Nonlinear Output Transformations

abstract: Recent years have witnessed substantial progress in understanding the behavior of EM for mixture models that are correctly specified. Given that model misspecification is common in practice, it is important to understand EM in this more general setting. We provide non-asymptotic guarantees for population and sample-based EM for parameter estimation under a few specific univariate settings of misspecified Gaussian mixture models. Due to misspecification, the EM iterates no longer converge to the true model and instead converge to the projection of the true model over the set of models being searched over. We provide two classes of theoretical guarantees: first, we characterize the bias introduced due to the misspecification; and second, we prove that population EM converges at a geometric rate to the model projection under a suitable initialization condition. This geometric convergence rate for population EM imply a statistical complexity of order $1/\sqrt{n}$ when running EM with $n$ samples. We validate our theoretical findings in different cases via several numerical examples.

paragraphs: Expectation-maximization is widely used to estimate mixture models, but its behavior changes when the assumed model family does not contain the true data-generating model. This paper studies that mismatch in several specific one-dimensional Gaussian-mixture settings. It provides finite-sample-oriented guarantees for both population EM and EM run on observed samples.

Under misspecification, the relevant convergence target is a projection of the true model onto the family being searched. The authors characterize the bias introduced by that mismatch, separating the consequences of choosing an imperfect model family from the process of optimizing within it. They also prove geometric convergence of population EM to the projection under a suitable initialization condition.

The population convergence result leads to a statistical complexity of order one over the square root of n when EM uses n samples. Numerical examples validate the theoretical findings across different cases. The results explain both where EM converges and how quickly, with their stated scope restricted to the particular univariate misspecified settings and initialization condition analyzed.
summary.tldr: For specific misspecified univariate Gaussian mixtures, the paper characterizes EM’s bias and proves geometric population convergence under suitable initialization.

title: Theoretical guarantees for EM under misspecified Gaussian mixture models

abstract: This manuscript contributes a general and practical framework for casting a Markov process model of a system at equilibrium as a structural causal model, and carrying out counterfactual inference. Markov processes mathematically describe the mechanisms in the system, and predict the system’s equilibrium behavior upon intervention, but do not support counterfactual inference. In contrast, structural causal models support counterfactual inference, but do not identify the mechanisms. This manuscript leverages the benefits of both approaches. We define the structural causal models in terms of the parameters and the equilibrium dynamics of the Markov process models, and counterfactual inference flows from these settings. The proposed approach alleviates the identifiability drawback of the structural causal models, in that the counterfactual inference is consistent with the counterfactual trajectories simulated from the Markov process model. We showcase the benefits of this framework in case studies of complex biomolecular systems with nonlinear dynamics. We illustrate that, in presence of Markov process model misspecification, counterfactual inference leverages prior data, and therefore estimates the outcome of an intervention more accurately than a direct simulation.

paragraphs: Markov process models describe a system's mechanisms and predict equilibrium behavior under interventions. Structural causal models support counterfactual questions about what would have happened under a different intervention, but do not by themselves identify those mechanisms. This paper develops a framework that combines these capabilities for systems described at equilibrium.

The authors construct structural causal models from the parameters and equilibrium dynamics of Markov process models. Counterfactual inference then follows from that construction. The resulting inferences agree with counterfactual trajectories simulated from the Markov process model, alleviating the structural causal model's identifiability difficulty. The agreement is tied to the mechanistic model used in the construction.

Case studies examine complex biomolecular systems with nonlinear dynamics. They also illustrate an advantage when the Markov process model is misspecified: counterfactual inference can use prior data and thereby estimate intervention outcomes more accurately than direct simulation. This finding highlights how observations can improve intervention estimates even when the underlying mechanistic description is imperfect.
summary.tldr: The framework converts equilibrium Markov process models into structural causal models to support counterfactual inference consistent with their modeled dynamics.

title: Integrating Markov processes with structural causal modeling enables counterfactual inference in complex systems

abstract: The classical low rank approximation problem is to find a rank $k$ matrix $UV$ (where $U$ has $k$ columns and $V$ has $k$ rows) that minimizes the Frobenius norm of $A - UV$. Although this problem can be solved efficiently, we study an NP-hard variant of this problem that involves weights and regularization. A previous paper of [Razenshteyn et al. '16] derived a polynomial time algorithm for weighted low rank approximation with constant rank. We derive provably sharper guarantees for the regularized version by obtaining parameterized complexity bounds in terms of the statistical dimension rather than the rank, allowing for a rank-independent runtime that can be significantly faster. Our improvement comes from applying sharper matrix concentration bounds, using a novel conditioning technique, and proving structural theorems for regularized low rank problems.

paragraphs: Low-rank approximation represents a matrix as a product of two smaller matrices while keeping reconstruction error small. The classical version can be solved efficiently. This paper studies a harder variant that adds weights and regularization, for which the general problem is NP-hard. The goal is to sharpen guarantees for algorithms solving that variant.

Earlier weighted approximation results provided polynomial-time algorithms when the target rank was constant. The new analysis instead expresses parameterized complexity through statistical dimension. This change allows a runtime guarantee independent of rank and can produce a significant speed advantage. The benefit is stated as a possibility arising from the different complexity parameter, rather than a universal improvement for every input.

The sharper guarantees come from stronger matrix concentration bounds, a new conditioning technique, and structural results about regularized low-rank problems. Together, these tools explain how regularization can support a more favorable analysis. The contribution is primarily algorithmic and theoretical: it identifies a way to characterize computational difficulty more finely than target rank alone.
summary.tldr: Statistical-dimension bounds give regularized weighted low-rank approximation rank-independent runtime guarantees that can be substantially faster.

title: Regularized Weighted Low Rank Approximation

abstract: We study the sample complexity of approximate policy iteration (PI) for the Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR), building on a recent line of work using LQR as a testbed to understand the limits of reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms on continuous control tasks. Our analysis quantifies the tension between policy improvement and policy evaluation, and suggests that policy evaluation is the dominant factor in terms of sample complexity. Specifically, we show that to obtain a controller that is within $\varepsilon$ of the optimal LQR controller, each step of policy evaluation requires at most $(n+d)^3/\varepsilon^2$ samples, where $n$ is the dimension of the state vector and $d$ is the dimension of the input vector. On the other hand, only $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ policy improvement steps suffice, resulting in an overall sample complexity of $(n+d)^3 \varepsilon^{-2} \log(1/\varepsilon)$. We furthermore build on our analysis and construct a simple adaptive procedure based on $\varepsilon$-greedy exploration which relies on approximate PI as a sub-routine and obtains $T^{2/3}$ regret, improving upon a recent result of Abbasi-Yadkori et al. 2019.
