paragraphs: VPP addresses conditional 3D generation, where inputs such as text or images guide the creation of a shape. The paper examines how the choice of 3D representation affects generation quality, speed, and the tasks a model can support. Its solution progressively combines a structured voxel representation with a sparse point representation.

This pairing supports efficient generation across multiple object categories. The architecture also includes a masked-generation Transformer, allowing the approach to serve generation, editing, completion, and pre-training tasks.

Their experiments show high-fidelity, diverse shapes across different categories, together with strong representation-transfer performance. These findings support the progressive representation as a way to combine efficient generation with broader downstream utility. The contribution centers on coordinating complementary 3D representations within one generation pipeline, with the reported results demonstrating both speed and versatility.
summary.tldr: VPP progressively combines voxel and point representations to generate diverse 3D shapes efficiently and support editing, completion, and pre-training.

title: VPP: Efficient Conditional 3D Generation via Voxel-Point Progressive Representation

abstract: By now Bayesian methods are routinely used in practice for solving inverse problems. In inverse problems the parameter or signal of interest is observed only indirectly, as an image of a given map, and the observations are typically further corrupted with noise. Bayes offers a natural way to regularize these problems via the prior distribution and provides a probabilistic solution, quantifying the remaining uncertainty in the problem. However, the computational costs of standard, sampling based Bayesian approaches can be overly large in such complex models. Therefore, in practice variational Bayes is becoming increasingly popular. Nevertheless, the theoretical understanding of these methods is still relatively limited, especially in context of inverse problems.In our analysis we investigate variational Bayesian methods for Gaussian process priors to solve linear inverse problems. We consider both mildly and severely ill-posed inverse problems and work with the popular inducing variable variational Bayes approach proposed by Titsias [Titsias, 2009]. We derive posterior contraction rates for the variational posterior in general settings and show that the minimax estimation rate can be attained by correctly tunned procedures. As specific examples we consider a collection of inverse problems including the heat equation, Volterra operator and Radon transform and inducing variable methods based on population and empirical spectral features.

paragraphs: Inverse problems recover a hidden signal from indirect, usually noisy observations. Bayesian methods use prior distributions to regularize this recovery and express remaining uncertainty, but sampling-based computation can be expensive. This paper examines the theoretical behavior of a more computationally practical alternative: variational inference with Gaussian process priors.

The analysis focuses on inducing-variable variational methods for linear inverse problems. It covers both mildly and severely ill-posed settings, where recovering the underlying signal can be increasingly difficult. The authors derive posterior contraction rates, describing how quickly the approximate posterior concentrates around the true signal as information accumulates.

They show that correctly tuned procedures can attain the minimax estimation rate, the benchmark for best achievable worst-case estimation accuracy in the setting. This is a conditional result about suitable tuning, rather than a guarantee for every variational approximation. Examples include inverse problems involving the heat equation, the Volterra operator, and the Radon transform, with inducing variables based on population or empirical spectral features.
summary.tldr: Properly tuned inducing-variable Gaussian process approximations can achieve minimax estimation rates for linear inverse problems.

title: Variational Gaussian processes for linear inverse problems

abstract: It is well known that Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) may attain minimax suboptimal rates in terms of the mean squared error (Birgé and Massart, 1993). In this paper, we prove that, under relatively mild assumptions, the suboptimality of ERM must be due to its bias. Namely, the variance error term of ERM (in terms of the bias and variance decomposition) enjoys the minimax rate. In the fixed design setting, we provide an elementary proof of this result using the probabilistic method. Then, we extend our proof to the random design setting for various models. In addition, we provide a simple proof of Chatterjee’s admissibility theorem (Chatterjee, 2014, Theorem 1.4), which states that in the fixed design setting, ERM cannot be ruled out as an optimal method, and then we extend this result to the random design setting. We also show that our estimates imply stability of ERM, complementing the main result of Caponnetto and Rakhlin (2006) for non-Donsker classes. Finally, we highlight the somewhat irregular nature of the loss landscape of ERM in the non-Donsker regime, by showing that functions can be close to ERM, in terms of $L_2$ distance, while still being far from almost-minimizers of the empirical loss.

paragraphs: Empirical risk minimization selects a model by minimizing loss on observed data, yet its mean squared error can fall short of the minimax rate. This paper separates that error into bias and variance. Under relatively mild assumptions, it proves that the variance term achieves the minimax rate, so any rate suboptimality must arise from bias.

The authors give an elementary probabilistic proof for fixed design and extend the argument to various random-design models. They also simplify a proof of an admissibility result, under which empirical risk minimization cannot be ruled out as optimal in the fixed-design setting, and extend that result to random design. Their estimates additionally imply stability results for non-Donsker classes.

A final result reveals an irregular relationship between prediction-space proximity and empirical loss in the non-Donsker regime. Functions can be close to an empirical risk minimizer in L2 distance while remaining far from nearly minimizing the training loss. Together, the findings distinguish variance control, admissibility, and local loss behavior instead of treating them as equivalent forms of quality.
summary.tldr: Under relatively mild assumptions, empirical risk minimization's variance achieves the minimax rate, making bias responsible for any rate suboptimality.

title: On the Variance, Admissibility, and Stability of Empirical Risk Minimization

abstract: Data poisoning considers cases when an adversary manipulates the behavior of machine learning algorithms through malicious training data. Existing threat models of data poisoning center around a single metric, the number of poisoned samples. In consequence, if attackers can poison more samples than expected with affordable overhead, as in many practical scenarios, they may be able to render existing defenses ineffective in a short time. To address this issue, we leverage timestamps denoting the birth dates of data, which are often available but neglected in the past. Benefiting from these timestamps, we propose a temporal threat model of data poisoning with two novel metrics, earliness and duration, which respectively measure how long an attack started in advance and how long an attack lasted. Using these metrics, we define the notions of temporal robustness against data poisoning, providing a meaningful sense of protection even with unbounded amounts of poisoned samples when the attacks are temporally bounded. We present a benchmark with an evaluation protocol simulating continuous data collection and periodic deployments of updated models, thus enabling empirical evaluation of temporal robustness. Lastly, we develop and also empirically verify a baseline defense, namely temporal aggregation, offering provable temporal robustness and highlighting the potential of our temporal threat model for data poisoning.

paragraphs: Data poisoning manipulates a learning system through malicious training examples. Defenses commonly measure attacker power by the number of poisoned samples, but that protection can become inadequate if an attacker can cheaply supply more. This paper develops a different threat model using timestamps that record when data were created.

The model introduces earliness and duration, describing how far in advance an attack began and how long it lasted. These quantities support definitions of temporal robustness. Crucially, the resulting protection can remain meaningful even when the number of poisoned samples is unbounded, provided the attack is bounded in time. The temporal restriction is therefore central to the proposed guarantee.

The authors introduce a benchmark and evaluation protocol that simulate continuous data collection and periodic deployment of updated models. They also develop temporal aggregation, a baseline defense with provable temporal robustness, and verify it empirically. Together, the threat model, evaluation setting, and defense establish a way to study poisoning resistance in systems that repeatedly learn from newly arriving data.
summary.tldr: A timestamp-based poisoning threat model enables robustness guarantees against attacks bounded in time, even with unbounded poisoned-sample counts.

title: Temporal Robustness against Data poisoning

abstract: Sparse deep learning has become a popular technique for improving the performance of deep neural networks in areas such as uncertainty quantification, variable selection, and large-scale network compression. However, most existing research has focused on problems where the observations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), and there has been little work on the problems where the observations are dependent, such as time series data and sequential data in natural language processing. This paper aims to address this gap by studying the theory for sparse deep learning with dependent data. We show that sparse recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can be consistently estimated, and their predictions are asymptotically normally distributed under appropriate assumptions, enabling the prediction uncertainty to be correctly quantified. Our numerical results show that sparse deep learning outperforms state-of-the-art methods, such as conformal predictions, in prediction uncertainty quantification for time series data. Furthermore, our results indicate that the proposed method can consistently identify the autoregressive order for time series data and outperform existing methods in large-scale model compression. Our proposed method has important practical implications in fields such as finance, healthcare, and energy, where both accurate point estimates and prediction uncertainty quantification are of concern.

paragraphs: Sparse deep learning has been used for uncertainty estimation, variable selection, and network compression, but much of its theory assumes independent observations. Time series violate that assumption because observations depend on one another. This paper develops a theoretical treatment of sparse deep learning for dependent data, focusing on recurrent neural networks.

Under appropriate assumptions, the authors show that sparse recurrent networks can be estimated consistently and that their predictions become normally distributed asymptotically. These properties provide a basis for correctly quantifying prediction uncertainty in the studied setting. The asymptotic statement concerns behavior as data grow, and its validity depends on the assumptions used in the analysis.

Numerical results show better time-series uncertainty quantification than state-of-the-art methods including conformal prediction. The results also indicate consistent identification of autoregressive order and stronger large-scale model compression than existing methods. The contribution connects sparse modeling to several goals at once: predicting dependent observations, assessing uncertainty, identifying relevant temporal structure, and reducing model size. This combination is relevant where both point predictions and their uncertainty matter.
summary.tldr: The paper develops conditional statistical guarantees for sparse recurrent networks on dependent data and reports gains in uncertainty quantification and compression.

title: Sparse Deep Learning for Time Series Data: Theory and Applications

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a decentralized machine learning paradigm that enables collaborative model training across dispersed nodes without having to force individual nodes to share data.However, its broad adoption is hindered by the high communication costs of transmitting a large number of model parameters. This paper presents EvoFed, a novel approach that integrates Evolutionary Strategies (ES) with FL to address these challenges.EvoFed employs a concept of `fitness-based information sharing’, deviating significantly from the conventional model-based FL. Rather than exchanging the actual updated model parameters, each node transmits a distance-based similarity measure between the locally updated model and each member of the noise-perturbed model population. Each node, as well as the server, generates an identical population set of perturbed models in a completely synchronized fashion using the same random seeds. With properly chosen noise variance and population size, perturbed models can be combined to closely reflect the actual model updated using the local dataset, allowing the transmitted similarity measures (or fitness values) to carry nearly the complete information about the model parameters.As the population size is typically much smaller than the number of model parameters, the savings in communication load is large. The server aggregates these fitness values and is able to update the global model. This global fitness vector is then disseminated back to the nodes, each of which applies the same update to be synchronized to the global model. Our analysis shows that EvoFed converges, and our experimental results validate that at the cost of increased local processing loads, EvoFed achieves performance comparable to FedAvg while reducing overall communication requirements drastically in various practical settings.

This paper presents EvoFed, a novel approach that integrates Evolutionary Strategies (ES) with FL to address these challenges.EvoFed employs a concept of `fitness-based information sharing’, deviating significantly from the conventional model-based FL. Rather than exchanging the actual updated model parameters, each node transmits a distance-based similarity measure between the locally updated model and each member of the noise-perturbed model population. Each node, as well as the server, generates an identical population set of perturbed models in a completely synchronized fashion using the same random seeds. With properly chosen noise variance and population size, perturbed models can be combined to closely reflect the actual model updated using the local dataset, allowing the transmitted similarity measures (or fitness values) to carry nearly the complete information about the model parameters.As the population size is typically much smaller than the number of model parameters, the savings in communication load is large. The server aggregates these fitness values and is able to update the global model. This global fitness vector is then disseminated back to the nodes, each of which applies the same update to be synchronized to the global model. Our analysis shows that EvoFed converges, and our experimental results validate that at the cost of increased local processing loads, EvoFed achieves performance comparable to FedAvg while reducing overall communication requirements drastically in various practical settings.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a shared model across nodes that keep their data locally, but exchanging large parameter updates can be expensive. EvoFed reduces that communication by sending fitness values describing local updates. Its central idea is to express an update through comparisons with a shared population of perturbed models.

Every node and the server generate identical perturbed models using synchronized random seeds. Each node measures how close its locally updated model is to each population member and sends those scores. With suitable noise variance and population size, combinations of the perturbed models can closely represent the local update. When the population is much smaller than the parameter count, the score vector is substantially cheaper to transmit.

The server aggregates fitness vectors and distributes the result so all nodes apply the same global update. The paper provides convergence analysis and reports performance comparable to FedAvg with sharply reduced communication across tested settings. These savings come with increased local computation, making the method an explicit exchange of processing work for communication efficiency.
summary.tldr: EvoFed exchanges fitness scores over synchronized perturbed models to reduce federated-learning communication at the cost of more local computation.

title: EvoFed: Leveraging Evolutionary Strategies for Communication-Efficient Federated Learning

abstract: Several recent unsupervised learning methods use probabilistic approaches to solve combinatorial optimization (CO) problems based on the assumption of statistically independent solution variables. We demonstrate that this assumption imposes performance limitations in particular on difficult problem instances. Our results corroborate that an autoregressive approach which captures statistical dependencies among solution variables yields superior performance on many popular CO problems. We introduce Subgraph Tokenization in which the configuration of a set of solution variables is represented by a single token. This tokenization technique alleviates the drawback of the long sequential sampling procedure which is inherent to autoregressive methods without sacrificing expressivity. Importantly, we theoretically motivate an annealed entropy regularization and show empirically that it is essential for efficient and stable learning.

paragraphs: Some learning-based approaches to combinatorial optimization model solution variables as statistically independent. The paper shows that this assumption can limit performance, especially on difficult instances. Its results support autoregressive modeling, which captures dependencies between variables, as a stronger approach across many common combinatorial optimization problems.

Autoregressive models have a computational drawback: generating a solution involves a long sequence of sampling decisions. The proposed Subgraph Tokenization groups a set of solution variables into a single token representing their joint configuration. This reduces the burden of sequential sampling while preserving expressivity, allowing dependency-aware modeling to use larger units of generation.

The authors also theoretically motivate entropy regularization whose strength is annealed during learning. Their experiments find this component essential for efficient and stable training in the studied setting. The contribution combines three connected ideas: representing dependencies, shortening generation through grouped configurations, and managing the learning process through annealed regularization. Together, they address both the performance limits of independent-variable models and the practical cost of an autoregressive alternative.
summary.tldr: Dependency-aware autoregressive modeling, subgraph tokens, and annealed entropy regularization improve learning-based combinatorial optimization.

title: Variational Annealing on Graphs for Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: In this work, we study the effect of occlusion on video action recognition. Tofacilitate this study, we propose three benchmark datasets and experiment withseven different video action recognition models. These datasets include two synthetic benchmarks, UCF-101-O and K-400-O, which enabled understanding the effects of fundamental properties of occlusion via controlled experiments. We also propose a real-world occlusion dataset, UCF-101-Y-OCC, which helps in further validating the findings of this study. We find several interesting insights such as 1) transformers are more robust than CNN counterparts, 2) pretraining make modelsrobust against occlusions, and 3) augmentation helps, but does not generalize well to real-world occlusions. In addition, we propose a simple transformer based compositional model, termed as CTx-Net, which generalizes well under this distribution shift. We observe that CTx-Net outperforms models which are trained using occlusions as augmentation, performing significantly better under natural occlusions. We believe this benchmark will open up interesting future research in robust video action recognition

paragraphs: Video action recognition becomes harder when parts of a scene or action are hidden. This paper studies that problem with three benchmarks and seven recognition models. Two synthetic datasets, UCF-101-O and K-400-O, allow controlled investigation of occlusion properties. A real-world dataset, UCF-101-Y-OCC, checks whether the findings extend to naturally occurring occlusions.

The experiments find that transformers are more robust than their CNN counterparts and that pretraining improves robustness to occlusion. They also reveal a gap between synthetic augmentation and real-world performance: adding occlusions during training helps, but the improvement does not generalize well to natural occlusions. This makes the real-world benchmark an important complement to controlled tests.

The authors additionally introduce CTx-Net, a simple transformer-based compositional model. In their evaluation, it generalizes well under the occlusion-related distribution shift and outperforms models trained with occlusion augmentation, especially under natural occlusions. The work supplies both a testing framework and a model result, showing why robustness should be examined across controlled and naturally occurring forms of hidden visual information.
summary.tldr: Three occlusion benchmarks expose robustness gaps in video recognition, while CTx-Net improves performance under natural occlusions.

title: Revealing the unseen: Benchmarking video action recognition under occlusion

abstract: For any two point sets $A,B \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ of size up to $n$, the Chamfer distance from $A$ to $B$ is defined as $\texttt{CH}(A,B)=\sum_{a \in A} \min_{b \in B} d_X(a,b)$, where $d_X$ is the underlying distance measure (e.g., the Euclidean or Manhattan distance). The Chamfer distance is a popular measure of dissimilarity between point clouds, used in many machine learning, computer vision, and graphics applications, and admits a straightforward $O(d n^2)$-time brute force algorithm. Further, Chamfer distance is often used as a proxy for the more computationally demanding Earth-Mover (Optimal Transport) Distance. However, the \emph{quadratic} dependence on $n$ in the running time makes the naive approach intractable for large datasets.We overcome this bottleneck and present the first $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate algorithm for estimating Chamfer distance with a near-linear running time. Specifically, our algorithm runs in time $O(nd \log (n)/\epsilon^2)$ and is implementable. Our experiments demonstrate that it is both accurate and fast on large high-dimensional datasets. We believe that our algorithm will open new avenues for analyzing large high-dimensional point clouds. We also give evidence that if the goal is to report a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate mapping from $A$ to $B$ (as opposed to just its value), then any sub-quadratic time algorithm is unlikely to exist.

paragraphs: The directed Chamfer distance measures how far one point cloud lies from another by adding each source point's distance to its nearest target point. Computing it through all pairwise comparisons costs time quadratic in the number of points. That cost makes a widely used geometric comparison expensive for large, high-dimensional datasets.

The paper gives an implementable algorithm that estimates the distance within a multiplicative factor of 1 + epsilon. Its runtime is O(nd log(n)/epsilon²), where n bounds the size of each point set and d is the dimension. This replaces quadratic growth in point count with near-linear growth, while making the cost of tighter approximation explicit.

Experiments show that the estimator is accurate and fast on large high-dimensional datasets. The authors also distinguish estimating the distance value from returning a corresponding approximate mapping between point sets. They provide evidence that a subquadratic algorithm for the mapping problem is unlikely, emphasizing that the computational advance concerns the aggregate distance estimate.
summary.tldr: An implementable near-linear-time algorithm approximates Chamfer distance, with experiments supporting its accuracy and speed.

title: Near-Linear Time Algorithm for the Chamfer Distance

abstract: In diffusion models, UNet is the most popular network backbone, since its long skip connects (LSCs) to connect distant network blocks can aggregate long-distant information and alleviate vanishing gradient. Unfortunately, UNet often suffers from unstable training in diffusion models which can be alleviated by scaling its LSC coefficients smaller. However, theoretical understandings of the instability of UNet in diffusion models and also the performance improvement of LSC scaling remain absent yet. To solve this issue, we theoretically show that the coefficients of LSCs in UNet have big effects on the stableness of the forward and backward propagation and robustness of UNet. Specifically, the hidden feature and gradient of UNet at any layer can oscillate and their oscillation ranges are actually large which explains the instability of UNet training. Moreover, UNet is also provably sensitive to perturbed input, and predicts an output distant from the desired output, yielding oscillatory loss and thus oscillatory gradient. Besides, we also observe the theoretical benefits of the LSC coefficient scaling of UNet in the stableness of hidden features and gradient and also robustness. Finally, inspired by our theory, we propose an effective coefficient scaling framework ScaleLong that scales the coefficients of LSC in UNet and better improve the training stability of UNet. Experimental results on CIFAR10, CelebA, ImageNet and COCO show that our methods are superior to stabilize training, and yield about 1.5x training acceleration on different diffusion models with UNet or UViT backbones.

paragraphs: UNets are widely used inside diffusion models, and their long skip connections carry information between distant network blocks. Although these connections help information and gradients travel through the network, training can still be unstable. This paper investigates why reducing the coefficients on those connections can improve stability.

The theoretical analysis shows that skip-connection coefficients strongly affect forward activations, backward gradients, and robustness to input perturbations. Hidden features and gradients can oscillate over large ranges. Input sensitivity can also produce outputs far from their desired values, contributing to oscillating losses and gradients. The analysis identifies benefits from scaling the connections in each of these areas.

Motivated by these results, the authors introduce ScaleLong, a framework for scaling long skip-connection coefficients. Experiments on CIFAR10, CelebA, ImageNet, and COCO report more stable training and roughly 1.5-fold training acceleration across tested diffusion models with UNet or UViT backbones. The work connects a specific architectural adjustment to both a theoretical explanation and observed training improvements.
summary.tldr: ScaleLong rescales long skip connections to stabilize diffusion-model training, with theoretical support and reported acceleration of about 1.5 times.

title: ScaleLong: Towards More Stable Training of Diffusion Model via Scaling Network Long Skip Connection

abstract: This paper studies the problem of learning the large-scale Gaussian graphical models that are multivariate totally positive of order two ($\text{MTP}_2$). By introducing the concept of bridge, which commonly exists in large-scale sparse graphs, we show that the entire problem can be equivalently optimized through (1) several smaller-scaled sub-problems induced by a \emph{bridge-block decomposition} on the thresholded sample covariance graph and (2) a set of explicit solutions on entries corresponding to \emph{bridges}. From practical aspect, this simple and provable discipline can be applied to break down a large problem into small tractable ones, leading to enormous reduction on the computational complexity and substantial improvements for all existing algorithms. The synthetic and real-world experiments demonstrate that our proposed method presents a significant speed-up compared to the state-of-the-art benchmarks.

By introducing the concept of bridge, which commonly exists in large-scale sparse graphs, we show that the entire problem can be equivalently optimized through (1) several smaller-scaled sub-problems induced by a \emph{bridge-block decomposition} on the thresholded sample covariance graph and (2) a set of explicit solutions on entries corresponding to \emph{bridges}. paragraphs: This paper studies learning large Gaussian graphical models under the mathematical constraint called multivariate total positivity of order two, or MTP2. Its focus is computational: a large optimization problem can be expensive even when the underlying graph is sparse. The authors look for graph structure that allows the work to be divided without changing the problem being solved.

Their method uses bridges in the thresholded sample covariance graph. A bridge is a connection whose removal separates parts of a graph. The authors prove that a bridge-block decomposition turns the original optimization into smaller subproblems, together with explicit solutions for entries associated with bridges. The decomposition is an equivalent reformulation of the full problem.

This provides a way to apply existing algorithms to smaller, more tractable pieces while handling bridge entries directly. The authors report substantial computational reductions and significant speedups over state-of-the-art benchmarks on synthetic and real-world data. The key contribution is a provable decomposition strategy that can improve the computational efficiency of existing methods for this model class.
summary.tldr: A provably equivalent bridge-block decomposition accelerates learning of large MTP2 Gaussian graphical models by splitting them into smaller problems.

title: Learning Large-Scale MTP$_2$ Gaussian Graphical Models via Bridge-Block Decomposition

abstract: Animals survive in dynamic environments changing at arbitrary timescales, but such data distribution shifts are a challenge to neural networks. To adapt to change, neural systems may change a large number of parameters, which is a slow process involving forgetting past information. In contrast, animals leverage distribution changes to segment their stream of experience into tasks and associate them with internal task abstracts. Animals can then respond flexibly by selecting the appropriate task abstraction. However, how such flexible task abstractions may arise in neural systems remains unknown. Here, we analyze a linear gated network where the weights and gates are jointly optimized via gradient descent, but with neuron-like constraints on the gates including a faster timescale, non-negativity, and bounded activity. We observe that the weights self-organize into modules specialized for tasks or sub-tasks encountered, while the gates layer forms unique representations that switch the appropriate weight modules (task abstractions). We analytically reduce the learning dynamics to an effective eigenspace, revealing a virtuous cycle: fast adapting gates drive weight specialization by protecting previous knowledge, while weight specialization in turn increases the update rate of the gating layer. Task switching in the gating layer accelerates as a function of curriculum block size and task training, mirroring key findings in cognitive neuroscience. We show that the discovered task abstractions support generalization through both task and subtask composition, and we extend our findings to a non-linear network switching between two tasks. Overall, our work offers a theory of cognitive flexibility in animals as arising from joint gradient descent on synaptic and neural gating in a neural network architecture.

summary.tldr: Fast, bounded gates and jointly learned weights can self-organize into reusable task modules that support flexible switching and composition.

title: Flexible task abstractions emerge in linear networks with fast and bounded units

abstract: We present a formulation of flow matching as variational inference, which we refer to as variational flow matching (VFM). We use this formulation to develop CatFlow, a flow matching method for categorical data that is easy to implement, computationally efficient, and achieves strong results on graph generation tasks. In VFM, the objective is to approximate the posterior probability path, which is a distribution over possible end points of a trajectory. VFM admits both the original flow matching objective and the CatFlow objective as special cases. We also relate VFM to score-based models, in which the dynamics are stochastic rather than deterministic, and derive a bound on the model likelihood based on a reweighted VFM objective. We evaluate CatFlow on one abstract graph generation task and two molecular generation tasks. In all cases, CatFlow exceeds or matches performance of the current state-of-the-art models.

Its learning objective approximates a posterior probability path: a distribution over the possible endpoints of a trajectory. This provides a probabilistic perspective on what the model learns as it constructs a generative flow.

The framework includes both the original flow-matching objective and a new categorical-data objective as special cases. The authors use the latter to develop CatFlow, a method described as straightforward to implement and computationally efficient. They also connect VFM to score-based models with stochastic dynamics and derive a model-likelihood bound from a reweighted VFM objective.

CatFlow is evaluated on one abstract graph-generation task and two molecular-generation tasks. It matches or exceeds the current state of the art in each of those evaluations. The contribution therefore combines a unifying theoretical formulation with a practical categorical generation method. The experimental findings show that this formulation supports strong graph-generation performance across the three studied tasks.
summary.tldr: Variational flow matching unifies flow objectives and yields CatFlow, a categorical generator that matches or exceeds leading results on three graph-generation tasks.

title: Variational Flow Matching for Graph Generation

abstract: Inference on large language models (LLMs) can be expensive in terms of thecompute and memory costs involved, especially when long sequence lengths areused. In particular, the self-attention mechanism used in LLM inference contributessignificantly to these costs, which has sparked an interest in approximating the self-attention computation to reduce such costs. In this work, we propose to approximateself-attention by focusing on the dimensionality of key vectors computed in theattention block. Our analysis reveals that key vectors lie in a significantly lower-dimensional space, consistently across several datasets and models. Exploiting thisobservation, we propose Loki, a novel sparse attention method that ranks and selectstokens in the KV-cache based on attention scores computed in low-dimensionalspace. Our evaluations show that Loki is able to speed up the attention computationdue to reduced data movement (load/store) and compute costs while maintainingthe efficacy of the models better than other popular approximation methods.

paragraphs: Long input sequences can make language-model inference expensive because self-attention requires substantial computation and memory access. Loki tackles this cost by examining the key vectors used inside attention. The authors find that these vectors occupy a substantially lower-dimensional space, an observation that holds consistently across several evaluated models and datasets.

The method uses that lower-dimensional representation to calculate attention scores for ranking and selecting tokens from the key-value cache. This provides a cheaper way to decide which cached tokens deserve attention. The low-dimensional calculation is therefore central to token selection, connecting a structural observation about the vectors to a sparse attention procedure.

In the reported evaluations, Loki accelerates attention by reducing both computation and the movement of data through load and store operations. It also preserves model effectiveness better than the popular approximation methods included in those evaluations. The result supports exploiting the observed geometry of key vectors to make attention more efficient, with the stated evidence applying across the tested models and datasets.
summary.tldr: Loki uses low-dimensional key representations to select cached tokens cheaply, speeding attention while preserving model effectiveness in evaluations.

title: Loki: Low-rank Keys for Efficient Sparse Attention

abstract: We propose ESPACE, an LLM compression technique based on dimensionality reduction of activations. Unlike prior works on weight-centric tensor decomposition, ESPACE projects activations onto a pre-calibrated set of principal components. The activation-centrality of the approach enables retraining LLMs with no loss of expressivity; while at inference, weight decomposition is obtained as a byproduct of matrix multiplication associativity. Theoretical results on the construction of projection matrices with optimal computational accuracy are provided. Experimentally, we find ESPACE enables 50% compression of GPT3, Llama2, and Nemotron4 models with small accuracy degradation, as low as a 0.18 perplexity increase on GPT3-22B. At lower compression rates of 20% to 40%, ESPACE drives GPT3 models to outperforming their baseline, by up to a 0.38 decrease in perplexity for GPT3-8B. ESPACE also reduces GEMM execution time and prefill inference latency on existing hardware. Comparison with related works on compressing Llama2-7B via matrix factorization shows that ESPACE is a first step in advancing the state-of-the-art in tensor decomposition compression of LLMs.

It projects these values onto a calibrated set of principal components. This changes the starting point of compression from directly decomposing model weights to reducing the dimensions used to represent activations.

The authors state that this activation-centered formulation allows retraining without losing expressivity. During inference, regrouping matrix multiplications produces a weight decomposition as a consequence of the formulation. The paper also provides theoretical results for constructing projection matrices with optimal computational accuracy, linking the compression mechanism to its mathematical properties.

summary.tldr: ESPACE compresses language models through activation projections, achieving substantial compression with small accuracy losses and faster inference operations.

title: ESPACE: Dimensionality Reduction of Activations for Model Compression

abstract: Multi-block minimax bilevel optimization has been studied recently due to its great potential in multi-task learning, robust machine learning, and few-shot learning. However, due to the complex three-level optimization structure, existing algorithms often suffer from issues such as high computing costs due to the second-order model derivatives or high memory consumption in storing all blocks' parameters. In this paper, we tackle these challenges by proposing two novel fully first-order algorithms named FOSL and MemCS. FOSL features a fully single-loop structure by updating all three variables simultaneously, and MemCS is a memory-efficient double-loop algorithm with cold-start initialization. We provide a comprehensive convergence analysis for both algorithms under full and partial block participation, and show that their sample complexities match or outperform those of the same type of methods in standard bilevel optimization. We evaluate our methods in two applications: the recently proposed multi-task deep AUC maximization and a novel rank-based robust meta-learning. Our methods consistently improve over existing methods with better performance over various datasets.

FOSL features a fully single-loop structure by updating all three variables simultaneously, and MemCS is a memory-efficient double-loop algorithm with cold-start initialization. We evaluate our methods in two applications: the recently proposed multi-task deep AUC maximization and a novel rank-based robust meta-learning. Our methods consistently improve over existing methods with better performance over various datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies multi-block minimax bilevel optimization, a framework relevant to multi-task learning, robust learning, and few-shot learning. Its three-level optimization structure makes computation and storage difficult. Existing approaches can incur expensive second-order derivatives or require storing parameters for all blocks, creating separate obstacles to practical use.

The authors propose two algorithms that use only first-order information. FOSL updates all three variables simultaneously in a single loop. MemCS uses a double-loop structure with cold-start initialization to improve memory efficiency. These designs address the nested optimization problem through different update organizations while avoiding reliance on second-order model derivatives.

The paper analyzes convergence when all blocks participate and when only some participate. Its sample complexity results match or improve on comparable method types in standard bilevel optimization. Experiments on multi-task deep AUC maximization and rank-based robust meta-learning report consistent improvements across the evaluated datasets. Together, the analysis and applications support first-order methods as effective tools for the studied, more complex optimization structure.
summary.tldr: FOSL and MemCS use first-order updates to address computation and memory costs in minimax bilevel optimization.

title: First-Order Minimax Bilevel Optimization

abstract: While recent advancements in large multimodal models (LMMs) have significantly improved their abilities in image quality assessment (IQA) relying on absolute quality rating, how to transfer reliable relative quality comparison outputs to continuous perceptual quality scores remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce an all-around LMM-based NR-IQA model, which is capable of producing qualitatively comparative responses and effectively translating these discrete comparison outcomes into a continuous quality score. Specifically, during training, we present to generate scaled-up comparative instructions by comparing images from the same IQA dataset, allowing for more flexible integration of diverse IQA datasets. Utilizing the established large-scale training corpus, we develop a human-like visual quality comparator. During inference, moving beyond binary choices, we propose a soft comparison method that calculates the likelihood of the test image being preferred over multiple predefined anchor images. The quality score is further optimized by maximum a posteriori estimation with the resulting probability matrix. Extensive experiments on nine IQA datasets validate that the Compare2Score effectively bridges text-defined comparative levels during training with converted single image quality scores for inference, surpassing state-of-the-art IQA models across diverse scenarios. Moreover, we verify that the probability-matrix-based inference conversion not only improves the rating accuracy of Compare2Score but also zero-shot general-purpose LMMs, suggesting its intrinsic effectiveness.

paragraphs: Compare2Score addresses the gap between judging which image looks better and assigning a continuous quality score to an individual image. The paper trains a large multimodal model to make visual quality comparisons, then converts those comparisons into numerical assessments. This connects language-based judgments with the scores needed for image quality assessment.

Training instructions are constructed by comparing images within the same quality-assessment dataset. This allows comparative examples from different datasets to be combined more flexibly. During inference, the model compares a test image with several predefined anchor images. Rather than recording only a winner, it estimates the probability that the test image is preferred to each anchor.

These probabilities form a matrix used in maximum a posteriori estimation to obtain the final quality score. Experiments on nine datasets report performance above state-of-the-art assessment models across diverse settings. The same probability-based conversion also improves ratings from general-purpose multimodal models used zero-shot, suggesting that the conversion procedure contributes value beyond the specifically trained comparator.
summary.tldr: Compare2Score turns multimodal image comparisons into continuous quality scores using probabilistic comparisons with anchor images.

title: Adaptive Image Quality Assessment via Teaching Large Multimodal Model to Compare

abstract: Quantitative analysis of cardiac motion is crucial for assessing cardiac function. This analysis typically uses imaging modalities such as MRI and Echocardiograms that capture detailed image sequences throughout the heartbeat cycle. Previous methods predominantly focused on the analysis of image pairs lacking consideration of the motion dynamics and spatial variability. Consequently, these methods often overlook the long-term relationships and regional motion characteristic of cardiac. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the GPTrack, a novel unsupervised framework crafted to fully explore the temporal and spatial dynamics of cardiac motion. The GPTrack enhances motion tracking by employing the sequential Gaussian Process in the latent space and encoding statistics by spatial information at each time stamp, which robustly promotes temporal consistency and spatial variability of cardiac dynamics. Also, we innovatively aggregate sequential information in a bidirectional recursive manner, mimicking the behavior of diffeomorphic registration to better capture consistent long-term relationships of motions across cardiac regions such as the ventricles and atria. Our GPTrack significantly improves the precision of motion tracking in both 3D and 4D medical images while maintaining computational efficiency. The code is available at: https://github.com/xmed-lab/GPTrack.

paragraphs: Heart motion unfolds across an entire heartbeat and differs between anatomical regions. Tracking it through isolated image pairs can miss both longer temporal relationships and regional variation. GPTrack addresses this problem with an unsupervised framework that uses image sequences to model the spatial and temporal structure of cardiac movement together.

The framework applies a sequential Gaussian process within a latent representation and incorporates spatial information into the statistics encoded at each time point. This promotes consistency over time while retaining differences in movement across the heart. A bidirectional recursive mechanism also combines information along the sequence in both directions, helping capture relationships that extend beyond a single pair of images.

The authors describe this aggregation as mimicking diffeomorphic registration to capture consistent motion relationships across regions such as ventricles and atria. They report significantly improved tracking precision in both 3D and 4D medical images while maintaining computational efficiency. The central finding is that explicitly modeling sequence structure and regional variability can improve cardiac tracking within the evaluated imaging settings.
summary.tldr: GPTrack combines latent Gaussian processes with bidirectional sequence aggregation to improve cardiac motion tracking while retaining computational efficiency.

title: Bidirectional Recurrence for Cardiac Motion Tracking with Gaussian Process Latent Coding

abstract: An image editing model should be able to perform diverse edits, ranging from object replacement, changing attributes or style, to performing actions or movement, which require many forms of reasoning. Current *general* instruction-guided editing models have significant shortcomings with action and reasoning-centric edits.Object, attribute or stylistic changes can be learned from visually static datasets. On the other hand, high-quality data for action and reasoning-centric edits is scarce and has to come from entirely different sources that cover e.g. physical dynamics, temporality and spatial reasoning.To this end, we meticulously curate the **A**U**RO**R**A** Dataset (**A**ction-**R**easoning-**O**bject-**A**ttribute), a collection of high-quality training data, human-annotated and curated from videos and simulation engines.We focus on a key aspect of quality training data: triplets (source image, prompt, target image) contain a single meaningful visual change described by the prompt, i.e., *truly minimal* changes between source and target images.To demonstrate the value of our dataset, we evaluate an **A**U**RO**R**A**-finetuned model on a new expert-curated benchmark (**A**U**RO**R**A-Bench**) covering 8 diverse editing tasks.Our model significantly outperforms previous editing models as judged by human raters.For automatic evaluations, we find important flaws in previous metrics and caution their use for semantically hard editing tasks.Instead, we propose a new automatic metric that focuses on discriminative understanding.We hope that our efforts : (1) curating a quality training dataset and an evaluation benchmark, (2) developing critical evaluations, and (3) releasing a state-of-the-art model, will fuel further progress on general image editing.

paragraphs: Instruction-guided image editing includes changes that require understanding actions, movement, and spatial relationships. Static image datasets can teach object or style changes, but provide less suitable material for these other demands. This paper introduces AURORA, a dataset curated from videos and simulation engines with human annotation.

Its central data-quality requirement is that each source image, instruction, and target image describe a single meaningful visual change. Keeping that change minimal makes the requested transformation clear: the target should demonstrate the instruction without introducing unrelated changes. Videos and simulation supply examples involving temporal behavior, physical dynamics, and spatial reasoning that static sources may lack.

The authors fine-tune an editing model on AURORA and evaluate it using AURORA-Bench, an expert-curated benchmark covering eight editing tasks. Human raters judge the resulting model significantly better than previous editing models. The paper also identifies flaws in existing automatic metrics for semantically difficult edits and proposes a metric centered on discriminative understanding. Its contribution therefore joins carefully controlled training examples with evaluation designed to assess whether a requested edit was actually understood.
summary.tldr: AURORA uses carefully curated video and simulation examples to improve action- and reasoning-focused image editing, with gains judged by human raters.

title: Learning Action and Reasoning-Centric Image Editing from Videos and Simulation

abstract: With the widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs), the prevalence of iterative interactions among these models is anticipated to increase. Notably, recent advancements in multi-round on-policy self-improving methods allow LLMs to generate new examples for training subsequent models. At the same time, multi-agent LLM systems, involving automated interactions among agents, are also increasing in prominence. Thus, in both short and long terms, LLMs may actively engage in an evolutionary process. We draw parallels between the behavior of LLMs and the evolution of human culture, as the latter has been extensively studied by cognitive scientists for decades. Our approach involves leveraging Iterated Learning (IL), a Bayesian framework that elucidates how subtle biases are magnified during human cultural evolution, to explain some behaviors of LLMs. This paper outlines key characteristics of agents' behavior in the Bayesian-IL framework, including predictions that are supported by experimental verification with various LLMs. This theoretical framework could help to more effectively predict and guide the evolution of LLMs in desired directions.

paragraphs: Language models increasingly produce material that other models consume, including examples used to train later models. Repeated interactions among agents create another setting where model outputs influence subsequent behavior. This paper examines these processes through an analogy with cultural evolution, where information passes between people and changes across successive rounds.

The authors use Bayesian iterated learning, a framework developed to explain how small biases can become amplified during cultural transmission. They apply it to language models to characterize agent behavior across repeated learning and interaction. The focus is on how successive stages can reshape tendencies, rather than viewing each model's behavior as an isolated outcome.

The paper derives behavioral predictions within this framework and reports experimental support from several language models. This gives the cultural-evolution analogy a theoretical structure and connects its predictions to observed model behavior. The authors suggest that the framework could help anticipate and guide the evolution of language models. That prospective use remains a possibility supported by the analysis, while the stated empirical contribution is verification of predictions across the tested models.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian iterated-learning framework explains aspects of bias amplification across language-model interactions, with predictions supported by experiments.

title: Bias Amplification in Language Model Evolution: An Iterated Learning Perspective

abstract: We present the Noisy Ostracods, a noisy dataset for genus and species classificationof crustacean ostracods with specialists’ annotations. Over the 71466 specimenscollected, 5.58% of them are estimated to be noisy (possibly problematic) at genuslevel. The dataset is created to addressing a real-world challenge: creating aclean fine-grained taxonomy dataset. The Noisy Ostracods dataset has diversenoises from multiple sources. Firstly, the noise is open-set, including new classesdiscovered during curation that were not part of the original annotation. Thedataset has pseudo-classes, where annotators misclassified samples that shouldbelong to an existing class into a new pseudo-class. The Noisy Ostracods datasetis highly imbalanced with a imbalance factor ρ = 22429. This presents a uniquechallenge for robust machine learning methods, as existing approaches have notbeen extensively evaluated on fine-grained classification tasks with such diversereal-world noise. Initial experiments using current robust learning techniqueshave not yielded significant performance improvements on the Noisy Ostracodsdataset compared to cross-entropy training on the raw, noisy data. On the otherhand, noise detection methods have underperformed in error hit rate comparedto naive cross-validation ensembling for identifying problematic labels. Thesefindings suggest that the fine-grained, imbalanced nature, and complex noisecharacteristics of the dataset present considerable challenges for existing noiserobustalgorithms. By openly releasing the Noisy Ostracods dataset, our goalis to encourage further research into the development of noise-resilient machinelearning methods capable of effectively handling diverse, real-world noise in finegrainedclassification tasks. The dataset, along with its evaluation protocols, can beaccessed at https://github.com/H-Jamieu/Noisy_ostracods.

paragraphs: Noisy Ostracods turns the practical work of building a clean biological taxonomy dataset into a machine-learning benchmark. It contains 71,466 crustacean specimens annotated by specialists for genus and species classification. An estimated 5.58% of genus-level annotations are potentially problematic, making label reliability a central part of the recognition task.

The errors come from several sources. Some specimens belong to classes discovered during curation that were absent from the original labels. Others were assigned to supposed new classes even though they belong to existing ones. The dataset also has extremely uneven class frequencies, with a reported imbalance factor of 22,429, combining rare categories with subtle visual distinctions and varied annotation problems.

Initial experiments find no significant improvement from the tested robust-learning methods over cross-entropy training on the noisy data. Tested noise detectors also identify errors less effectively, by error hit rate, than simple cross-validation ensembling. These findings make the dataset a demanding evaluation resource for methods intended to handle complex, naturally occurring label noise.
summary.tldr: Noisy Ostracods exposes difficulties for existing noise-robust learning methods through fine-grained categories, extreme imbalance, and real annotation errors.

title: Noisy Ostracods: A Fine-Grained, Imbalanced Real-World Dataset for Benchmarking Robust Machine Learning and Label Correction Methods

abstract: We propose the first learning scheme for functional differential equations (FDEs).FDEs play a fundamental role in physics, mathematics, and optimal control.However, the numerical analysis of FDEs has faced challenges due to its unrealistic computational costs and has been a long standing problem over decades.Thus, numerical approximations of FDEs have been developed, but they often oversimplify the solutions. To tackle these two issues, we propose a hybrid approach combining physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) with the *cylindrical approximation*. The cylindrical approximation expands functions and functional derivatives with an orthonormal basis and transforms FDEs into high-dimensional PDEs. To validate the reliability of the cylindrical approximation for FDE applications, we prove the convergence theorems of approximated functional derivatives and solutions.Then, the derived high-dimensional PDEs are numerically solved with PINNs.Through the capabilities of PINNs, our approach can handle a broader class of functional derivatives more efficiently than conventional discretization-based methods, improving the scalability of the cylindrical approximation.As a proof of concept, we conduct experiments on two FDEs and demonstrate that our model can successfully achieve typical $L^1$ relative error orders of PINNs $\sim 10^{-3}$.Overall, our work provides a strong backbone for physicists, mathematicians, and machine learning experts to analyze previously challenging FDEs, thereby democratizing their numerical analysis, which has received limited attention.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a learning scheme for functional differential equations, which arise in physics, mathematics, and optimal control. Its starting problem is a tradeoff: numerical analysis can be prohibitively expensive, while existing approximations often simplify solutions too much. The authors combine a mathematical approximation with physics-informed neural networks to address both concerns.

The mathematical component is cylindrical approximation. It represents functions and functional derivatives using an orthonormal basis, turning the original functional differential equations into high-dimensional partial differential equations. This transformation makes the problem accessible to a different numerical solver, although the resulting equations still require a method capable of handling many dimensions.

The authors prove convergence theorems for the approximated functional derivatives and solutions, providing theoretical support for the transformation. They then use physics-informed neural networks to solve the resulting equations numerically. The abstract reports that this combination handles a broader class of functional derivatives more efficiently than conventional discretization methods, improving the approximation’s scalability.

Experiments on two functional differential equations provide a proof of concept. The reported relative L1 errors are around one thousandth, an order the authors describe as typical for physics-informed neural networks. These results demonstrate numerical success on the two tested equations, while the convergence results provide a mathematical foundation for the approximation underlying the approach.
summary.tldr: The paper combines cylindrical approximation with physics-informed neural networks to solve functional differential equations, proving approximation convergence and demonstrating accuracy on two examples.

title: Physics-informed Neural Networks for Functional Differential Equations: Cylindrical Approximation and Its Convergence Guarantees

abstract: Advances in 3D reconstruction have enabled high-quality 3D capture, but require a user to collect hundreds to thousands of images to create a 3D scene. We present CAT3D, a method for creating anything in 3D by simulating this real-world capture process with a multi-view diffusion model. Given any number of input images and a set of target novel viewpoints, our model generates highly consistent novel views of a scene. These generated views can be used as input to robust 3D reconstruction techniques to produce 3D representations that can be rendered from any viewpoint in real-time. CAT3D can create entire 3D scenes in as little as one minute, and outperforms existing methods for single image and few-view 3D scene creation.

paragraphs: High-quality 3D reconstruction often depends on collecting hundreds or thousands of photographs of a scene. CAT3D reduces this capture burden by generating additional views computationally. It treats image generation as a way to simulate the photographs that a reconstruction system would otherwise need a person to collect.

The method uses a multi-view diffusion model that receives input images and a set of requested camera viewpoints. It generates views intended to remain highly consistent with one another, which matters because they must describe the same scene from different positions. These generated images then become inputs to robust 3D reconstruction techniques.

The resulting 3D representations support real-time rendering from arbitrary viewpoints. The authors report creating entire scenes in as little as one minute and outperforming existing methods for scene creation from a single image or a few views. The timing is a best-case capability stated in the abstract, rather than a universal runtime. The central contribution is connecting coherent view generation to reconstruction so that scene creation requires less manual image capture.
summary.tldr: CAT3D generates consistent additional viewpoints from input images and uses them to reconstruct 3D scenes, sometimes in as little as one minute.

title: CAT3D: Create Anything in 3D with Multi-View Diffusion Models

abstract: Our work tackles the computational challenges of contrastive learning methods, particularly for the pretraining of Vision Transformers (ViTs). Despite the effectiveness of contrastive learning, the substantial computational resources required for training often hinder their practical application. To mitigate this issue, we propose an acceleration framework, leveraging ViT's unique ability to generalize across inputs of varying sequence lengths. Our method employs a mix of sequence compression strategies, including randomized token dropout and flexible patch scaling, to reduce the cost of gradient estimation and accelerate convergence. We further provide an in-depth analysis of the gradient estimation error of various acceleration strategies as well as their impact on downstream tasks, offering valuable insights into the trade-offs between acceleration and performance. We also propose a novel procedure to identify an optimal acceleration schedule to adjust the sequence compression ratios to the training progress, ensuring efficient training without sacrificing downstream performance. Our approach significantly reduces computational overhead across various self-supervised learning algorithms on large-scale datasets. In ImageNet, our method achieves speedups of 4$\times$ in MoCo, 3.3$\times$ in SimCLR, and 2.5$\times$ in DINO, demonstrating substantial efficiency gains.

paragraphs: Self-supervised vision training can learn useful representations but demands substantial computation. This paper accelerates that process by exploiting a property of Vision Transformers: they can handle inputs with different sequence lengths. The approach reduces the number of tokens processed during training, making gradient estimation cheaper while aiming to preserve the representations needed for downstream tasks.

The framework combines randomized token dropout with flexible patch scaling. These strategies compress image-token sequences in different ways. The authors analyze how acceleration strategies affect gradient-estimation error and downstream performance, making the tradeoff between cheaper updates and useful learning explicit. They also introduce a procedure for selecting an acceleration schedule that changes the compression ratio as training progresses.

Across the investigated self-supervised algorithms and large datasets, the method substantially reduces computational overhead while preserving downstream performance. On ImageNet, the reported speedups are fourfold for MoCo, 3.3-fold for SimCLR, and 2.5-fold for DINO. These results show that adjusting input sequence length throughout pretraining can produce substantial efficiency gains across several training approaches.
summary.tldr: Scheduling token compression during Vision Transformer pretraining delivers substantial reported speedups while preserving downstream performance.

title: Accelerating Augmentation Invariance Pretraining

abstract: In this work, we propose an Implicit Regularization Enhancement (IRE) framework to accelerate the discovery of flat solutions in deep learning, thereby improving generalization and convergence. Specifically, IRE decouples the dynamics of flat and sharp directions, which boosts the sharpness reduction along flat directions while maintaining the training stability in sharp directions. We show that IRE can be practically incorporated with *generic base optimizers* without introducing significant computational overload. Experiments show that IRE consistently improves the generalization performance for image classification tasks across a variety of benchmark datasets (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet) and models (ResNets and ViTs). Surprisingly, IRE also achieves a $2\times$ *speed-up* compared to AdamW in the pre-training of Llama models (of sizes ranging from 60M to 229M) on datasets including Wikitext-103, Minipile, and Openwebtext. Moreover, we provide theoretical guarantees, showing that IRE can substantially accelerate the convergence towards flat minima in Sharpness-aware Minimization (SAM).

paragraphs: This paper proposes Implicit Regularization Enhancement, or IRE, to help neural network training reach flat solutions more quickly. The approach distinguishes directions in parameter space where the training objective changes gently from directions where it changes sharply. Its purpose is to improve generalization and convergence by treating these different training dynamics separately.

IRE accelerates sharpness reduction along flat directions while maintaining stability along sharp ones. The authors describe it as a framework that can be incorporated into generic base optimizers without substantial computational overhead. This makes the contribution an enhancement to optimization procedures rather than a method tied to a single network architecture.

Image classification experiments report consistent generalization improvements across CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, ResNets, and vision transformers. In pretraining Llama models ranging from 60 million to 229 million parameters, the authors report a twofold speedup over AdamW on the studied datasets. They also provide theoretical guarantees of faster convergence toward flat minima for Sharpness-aware Minimization. That theoretical result has a specific optimizer setting, alongside the broader empirical evidence.
summary.tldr: IRE separates flat and sharp optimization dynamics, improving generalization and accelerating training in the reported experiments.

title: Improving Generalization and Convergence by Enhancing Implicit Regularization

abstract: Guidance is a crucial technique for extracting the best performance out of image-generating diffusion models. Traditionally, a constant guidance weight has been applied throughout the sampling chain of an image. We show that guidance is clearly harmful toward the beginning of the chain (high noise levels), largely unnecessary toward the end (low noise levels), and only beneficial in the middle. We thus restrict it to a specific range of noise levels, improving both the inference speed and result quality. This limited guidance interval improves the record FID in ImageNet-512 significantly, from 1.81 to 1.40. We show that it is quantitatively and qualitatively beneficial across different sampler parameters, network architectures, and datasets, including the large-scale setting of Stable Diffusion XL. We thus suggest exposing the guidance interval as a hyperparameter in all diffusion models that use guidance.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate images through a sequence of steps that move from high noise toward a finished result. Guidance is used to improve generation, commonly with the same strength throughout that sequence. This paper investigates whether applying guidance at every stage is actually useful.

The authors find a distinct pattern: guidance harms generation at the high-noise beginning, contributes little near the low-noise end, and helps in the middle. They therefore activate it only within a selected interval of noise levels. This changes when guidance operates, making its timing an additional control over the generation process.

Restricting guidance improves both inference speed and output quality in the reported experiments. On ImageNet-512, the reported record FID improves from 1.81 to 1.40. The authors find quantitative and qualitative benefits across sampler settings, network architectures, and datasets, including Stable Diffusion XL. These findings motivate exposing the guidance interval as a configurable hyperparameter so that users can adjust where guidance contributes during sampling.
summary.tldr: Applying diffusion guidance only at intermediate noise levels improves generation quality and speed across the settings studied.

title: Applying Guidance in a Limited Interval Improves Sample and Distribution Quality in Diffusion Models

abstract: This paper investigates score-based diffusion models when the underlying target distribution is concentrated on or near low-dimensional manifolds within the higher-dimensional space in which they formally reside, a common characteristic of natural image distributions. Despite previous efforts to understand the data generation process of diffusion models, existing theoretical support remains highly suboptimal in the presence of low-dimensional structure, which we strengthen in this paper. For the popular Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM), we find that the dependency of the error incurred within each denoising step on the ambient dimension $d$ is in general unavoidable. We further identify a unique design of coefficients that yields a converges rate at the order of $O(k^{2}/\sqrt{T})$ (up to log factors), where $k$ is the intrinsic dimension of the target distribution and $T$ is the number of steps. This represents the first theoretical demonstration that the DDPM sampler can adapt to unknown low-dimensional structures in the target distribution, highlighting the critical importance of coefficient design. All of this is achieved by a novel set of analysis tools that characterize the algorithmic dynamics in a more deterministic manner.

paragraphs: Data can have many coordinates while varying along relatively few underlying directions. This paper studies diffusion models when their target distribution lies on or near such a low-dimensional structure. Its central question is whether a sampler can benefit from that structure without knowing it beforehand, despite operating in a much larger surrounding space.

The authors analyze the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model, or DDPM. They establish that the error from an individual denoising step generally cannot avoid depending on the surrounding dimension. However, they identify a particular, unique coefficient design whose overall convergence rate depends on the intrinsic dimension k as O(k²/√T), apart from logarithmic factors, with T denoising steps.

These findings distinguish the behavior of individual steps from the convergence of the complete sampling process. The stated result shows that DDPM can adapt to unknown low-dimensional structure with the identified coefficients. New analysis tools characterize its dynamics in a more deterministic way, making coefficient choice central to the theoretical explanation of this adaptation.
summary.tldr: A particular DDPM coefficient design yields convergence governed by unknown intrinsic data dimension despite unavoidable ambient-dimension effects within individual steps.

title: Adapting to Unknown Low-Dimensional Structures in Score-Based Diffusion Models

abstract: In open-ended domains like art, autonomous agents must generate ideas that are both original and internally coherent, yet current Large Language Models (LLMs) either default to familiar cultural patterns or sacrifice coherence when pushed toward novelty. We address this by introducing the Cultural Alien Sampler (CAS), a concept-selection method that explicitly separates compositional fit from cultural typicality. CAS uses two GPT-2 models fine-tuned on WikiArt concepts: a Concept Coherence Model that scores whether concepts plausibly co-occur within artworks, and a Cultural Context Model that estimates how typical those combinations are within individual artists’ bodies of work. CAS targets combinations that are high in coherence and low in typicality, yielding ideas that maintain internal consistency while deviating from learned conventions and embedded cultural context. In a human evaluation (N = 100), our approach outperforms random selection and GPT-4o baselines and achieves performance comparable to human art students in both perceived originality and harmony. Additionally, a quantitative study shows that our method produces more diverse outputs and explores a broader conceptual space than its GPT-4o counterpart, demonstrating that artificial cultural alienness can unlock creative potential in autonomous agents.

paragraphs: The Cultural Alien Sampler addresses a tension in generating artistic ideas: familiar combinations can be coherent but predictable, while unusual combinations can lose internal consistency. Its solution is to evaluate these qualities separately, making originality a targeted departure from learned conventions rather than simply selecting concepts at random.

The method uses two GPT-2 models fine-tuned on WikiArt concepts. One estimates whether concepts plausibly belong together in an artwork. The other estimates how typical their combination is within individual artists’ work. The sampler favors combinations with strong compositional fit and low cultural typicality, seeking ideas that make sense together while avoiding familiar pairings.

In a human evaluation involving one hundred participants, the approach exceeded random selection and GPT-4o baselines and performed comparably to human art students on perceived originality and harmony. A separate quantitative analysis found greater diversity and broader conceptual exploration than GPT-4o. These results support the usefulness of separating coherence from typicality for the artistic concept-selection setting studied.
summary.tldr: Separately scoring conceptual fit and cultural typicality helps generate artistic ideas judged both original and harmonious.

title: Cultural Alien Sampler: Open-ended Art Generation Balancing Originality and Coherence

abstract: To fix the `bias in, bias out' problem in fair machine learning, it is important to steer feature distributions of data or internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs) to \emph{ideal} ones that guarantee group-fair outcomes. Previous work on fair generative models and representation steering could greatly benefit from provable fairness guarantees on the model output. We define a distribution as \emph{ideal} if the minimizer of any cost-sensitive risk on it is guaranteed to have exact group-fair outcomes (e.g., demographic parity, equal opportunity)---in other words, it has no fairness-utility trade-off. We formulate an optimization program for optimal steering by finding the nearest \emph{ideal} distribution in KL-divergence, and provide efficient algorithms for it when the underlying distributions come from well-known parametric families (e.g., normal, log-normal). Empirically, our optimal steering techniques on both synthetic and real-world datasets improve fairness without diminishing utility (and sometimes even improve utility). We demonstrate affine steering of LLM representations to reduce bias in multi-class classification, e.g., occupation prediction from a short biography in Bios dataset (De-Arteaga et al.). Furthermore, we steer internal representations of LLMs towards desired outputs so that it works equally well across different groups.
