paragraphs: This paper analyzes what happens near a solution when using proximal variance-reduced stochastic gradient methods, concentrating on SAGA and Prox-SVRG. The central assumption is that the nonsmooth part of the objective is partly smooth relative to a smooth manifold. This gives the problem a locally smooth structure that the algorithms can eventually discover.

The authors provide a unified account with two stages. First, the sequence of iterates identifies the relevant smooth manifold after finitely many iterations. Then it enters a local regime of linear convergence. The result explains how an optimization problem containing a nonsmooth component can still exhibit predictable, faster local behavior under the stated structural assumption.

The analysis also motivates acceleration after this structure becomes available. Possibilities include adapting algorithm settings to better local parameters and applying higher-order deterministic or stochastic methods that can achieve superlinear convergence. Examples from machine learning demonstrate the results. These acceleration possibilities build on the local analysis, rather than asserting that the original methods always converge superlinearly.
summary.tldr: Under partial smoothness, SAGA and Prox-SVRG identify a smooth manifold and then converge locally at a linear rate.

title: Local Convergence Properties of SAGA/Prox-SVRG and Acceleration

abstract: We consider the problem of learning from sparse and underspecified rewards, where an agent receives a complex input, such as a natural language instruction, and needs to generate a complex response, such as an action sequence, while only receiving binary success-failure feedback. Such success-failure rewards are often underspecified: they do not distinguish between purposeful and accidental success. Generalization from underspecified rewards hinges on discounting spurious trajectories that attain accidental success, while learning from sparse feedback requires effective exploration. We address exploration by using a mode covering direction of KL divergence to collect a diverse set of successful trajectories, followed by a mode seeking KL divergence to train a robust policy. We propose Meta Reward Learning (MeRL) to construct an auxiliary reward function that provides more refined feedback for learning. The parameters of the auxiliary reward function are optimized with respect to the validation performance of a trained policy. The MeRL approach outperforms an alternative method for reward learning based on Bayesian Optimization, and achieves the state-of-the-art on weakly-supervised semantic parsing. It improves previous work by 1.2% and 2.4% on WikiTableQuestions and WikiSQL datasets respectively.

paragraphs: Binary success or failure can be an ambiguous teaching signal for an agent producing complex responses. A successful action sequence might reflect the intended reasoning, or might work accidentally. This paper addresses both the difficulty of discovering successful trajectories when feedback is sparse and the difficulty of learning transferable behavior from those successes.

For exploration, the authors use a mode-covering direction of KL divergence to gather diverse successful trajectories, followed by a mode-seeking direction to train a robust policy. They then introduce Meta Reward Learning, or MeRL, which learns an auxiliary reward that gives more detailed feedback. The reward parameters are optimized according to the validation performance of the resulting trained policy.

This ties reward learning to whether the policy generalizes, helping address the problem of spurious successes. MeRL outperforms a reward-learning alternative based on Bayesian optimization and achieves the reported state of the art in weakly supervised semantic parsing. The abstract reports improvements over previous work of 1.2% on WikiTableQuestions and 2.4% on WikiSQL, supporting the usefulness of validation-guided rewards in those tasks.
summary.tldr: MeRL learns auxiliary rewards from validation performance to help agents generalize from sparse feedback that can reward accidental success.

title: Learning to Generalize from Sparse and Underspecified Rewards

abstract: Learning high-quality node embeddings is a key building block for machine learning models that operate on graph data, such as social networks and recommender systems. However, existing graph embedding techniques are unable to cope with fairness constraints, e.g., ensuring that the learned representations do not correlate with certain attributes, such as age or gender. Here, we introduce an adversarial framework to enforce fairness constraints on graph embeddings. Our approach is compositional —meaning that it can flexibly accommodate different combinations of fairness constraints during inference. For instance, in the context of social recommendations, our framework would allow one user to request that their recommendations are invariant to both their age and gender, while also allowing another user to request invariance to just their age. Experiments on standard knowledge graph and recommender system benchmarks highlight the utility of our proposed framework.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings turn nodes into representations used by systems such as recommenders and models of social networks. The paper addresses fairness constraints on those representations, including requests that they not correlate with attributes such as age or gender. Its motivation is that useful graph representations should be able to accommodate such constraints alongside their predictive role.

The authors introduce an adversarial framework whose central feature is compositionality. Different fairness constraints can be combined during inference, allowing the requested combination to vary across uses of the same framework. In the recommendation example, one user could request invariance to both age and gender, while another could request invariance only to age.

Experiments on knowledge-graph and recommender-system benchmarks demonstrate the framework’s utility. The contribution is therefore more specific than applying one fixed fairness restriction during representation learning: it supports flexible combinations at inference time. The fairness objective here concerns the stated attribute-related constraints on representations and recommendations, which is the particular form of fairness the framework is designed to address.
summary.tldr: An adversarial graph-embedding framework allows different combinations of attribute-related fairness constraints to be requested at inference time.

title: Compositional Fairness Constraints for Graph Embeddings

abstract: Naive mean field variational methods are the state of-the-art approach to inference in topic modeling. We show that these methods suffer from an instability that can produce misleading conclusions. Namely, for certain regimes of the model parameters, variational inference outputs a non-trivial decomposition into topics. However -for the same parameter values- the data contain no actual information about the true topic decomposition, and the output of the algorithm is uncorrelated with it. In particular, the estimated posterior mean is wrong, and estimated credible regions do not achieve the nominal coverage. We discuss how this instability is remedied by more accurate mean field approximations.

In particular, the estimated posterior mean is wrong, and estimated credible regions do not achieve the nominal coverage. We discuss how this instability is remedied by more accurate mean field approximations.

paragraphs: Topic modeling seeks to recover an underlying organization of data into topics. Naive mean field variational inference is a widely used way to approximate the associated uncertainty. This paper shows that, in certain ranges of model parameters, the approximation can produce an apparently meaningful topic decomposition even when the data contain no information about the true decomposition.

In those regimes, the algorithm's output is uncorrelated with the actual topics. The issue therefore reaches beyond finding an imperfect version of an identifiable pattern: the method can present structure where the available data do not support recovering that structure. A nontrivial output alone is not evidence that the true topics have been learned.

The instability also affects uncertainty estimates. The estimated posterior mean is incorrect, and credible regions fail to attain their nominal coverage. The authors discuss how more accurate mean field approximations remedy the instability. These findings identify a specific failure mode of the naive approximation, with consequences for both the reported topic structure and the confidence attached to it.
summary.tldr: In certain parameter regimes, naive mean field inference reports unsupported topic structure and miscalibrated uncertainty.

title: An Instability in Variational Inference for Topic Models

abstract: Conditional kernel mean embeddings form an attractive nonparametric framework for representing conditional means of functions, describing the observation processes for many complex models. However, the recovery of the original underlying function of interest whose conditional mean was observed is a challenging inference task. We formalize deconditional kernel mean embeddings as a solution to this inverse problem, and show that it can be naturally viewed as a nonparametric Bayes' rule. Critically, we introduce the notion of task transformed Gaussian processes and establish deconditional kernel means as their posterior predictive mean. This connection provides Bayesian interpretations and uncertainty estimates for deconditional kernel mean embeddings, explains their regularization hyperparameters, and reveals a marginal likelihood for kernel hyperparameter learning. These revelations further enable practical applications such as likelihood-free inference and learning sparse representations for big data.

paragraphs: This paper studies an inverse problem: recovering a function when the available information consists of its conditional averages. Conditional kernel mean embeddings provide a flexible way to represent those averages without committing to a fixed parametric model. Recovering the function behind them, however, requires a way to reverse the averaging relationship.

The authors formalize deconditional kernel mean embeddings for this purpose and interpret them as a nonparametric version of Bayes’ rule. Their central connection is to task transformed Gaussian processes. They show that deconditional kernel means correspond to the posterior predictive mean in this probabilistic framework, linking the reconstruction method to Bayesian inference.

That connection supplies more than an alternative interpretation. It provides uncertainty estimates, explains the role of regularization parameters, and exposes a marginal likelihood for learning kernel hyperparameters. The resulting framework therefore connects function recovery, uncertainty, and parameter selection within one account. The abstract identifies likelihood-free inference and sparse representations for large datasets as practical applications enabled by these developments.
summary.tldr: The paper gives deconditional kernel mean embeddings a Gaussian-process interpretation that supports function recovery, uncertainty estimation, and hyperparameter learning.

title: Bayesian Deconditional Kernel Mean Embeddings

abstract: Obtaining continuous representations of structural data such as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) has gained attention in machine learning and artificial intelligence. However, embedding complex DAGs in which both ancestors and descendants of nodes are exponentially increasing is difficult. Tackling in this problem, we develop Disk Embeddings, which is a framework for embedding DAGs into quasi-metric spaces. Existing state-of-the-art methods, Order Embeddings and Hyperbolic Entailment Cones, are instances of Disk Embedding in Euclidean space and spheres respectively. Furthermore, we propose a novel method Hyperbolic Disk Embeddings to handle exponential growth of relations. The results of our experiments show that our Disk Embedding models outperform existing methods especially in complex DAGs other than trees.

paragraphs: Representing a directed acyclic graph with continuous embeddings becomes difficult when both ancestor and descendant relationships grow exponentially. The paper targets this structural challenge, which extends beyond the simpler setting of trees. Its goal is to give complex directed relationships a suitable geometric representation.

The authors introduce Disk Embeddings, a framework that embeds these graphs into quasi-metric spaces. They show that Order Embeddings and Hyperbolic Entailment Cones fit within this framework through Euclidean space and spheres, respectively. This provides a common formulation for methods that otherwise appear to use different geometric constructions.

Within that framework, the paper proposes Hyperbolic Disk Embeddings specifically to handle exponential growth in relationships. Experiments show that the Disk Embedding models outperform existing methods, with particularly strong results on complex graphs that are not trees. The findings support matching the embedding geometry to the graph’s relational structure. The contribution includes both a unifying perspective on earlier methods and a new construction aimed at harder graph structures.
summary.tldr: Disk Embeddings unify existing graph embeddings and introduce a hyperbolic construction that performs especially well on complex directed acyclic graphs.

title: Hyperbolic Disk Embeddings for Directed Acyclic Graphs

abstract: We introduce Act2Vec, a general framework for learning context-based action representation for Reinforcement Learning. Representing actions in a vector space help reinforcement learning algorithms achieve better performance by grouping similar actions and utilizing relations between different actions. We show how prior knowledge of an environment can be extracted from demonstrations and injected into action vector representations that encode natural compatible behavior. We then use these for augmenting state representations as well as improving function approximation of Q-values. We visualize and test action embeddings in three domains including a drawing task, a high dimensional navigation task, and the large action space domain of StarCraft II.

We show how prior knowledge of an environment can be extracted from demonstrations and injected into action vector representations that encode natural compatible behavior. We then use these for augmenting state representations as well as improving function approximation of Q-values. We visualize and test action embeddings in three domains including a drawing task, a high dimensional navigation task, and the large action space domain of StarCraft II.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can benefit from recognizing that different actions are related. Act2Vec learns context based vector representations of actions so that similar actions can be grouped and their relationships used by a learning algorithm. The aim is to make action relationships part of the information available for learning.

The framework extracts prior knowledge of an environment from demonstrations and incorporates it into action vectors that encode compatible behavior. Those representations are then used in two ways: to augment state representations and to improve approximation of Q-values. This gives the learned action structure a role both in representing the agent's situation and in estimating the value of its choices.

The authors visualize and test the embeddings in a drawing task, a high dimensional navigation task, and StarCraft II, which supplies a large action space setting. The work presents action representations as a means of improving reinforcement learning performance through relationships between actions. Its demonstrations across these domains examine the usefulness of that representation strategy in different kinds of decision problems.
summary.tldr: Act2Vec learns action embeddings from demonstrations and uses action relationships to enrich state representations and improve Q-value approximation.

title: The Natural Language of Actions

abstract: This paper studies the statistical theory of off-policy evaluation with function approximation in batch data reinforcement learning problem. We consider a regression-based fitted Q-iteration method, show that it is equivalent to a model-based method that estimates a conditional mean embedding of the transition operator, and prove that this method is information-theoretically optimal and has nearly minimal estimation error. In particular, by leveraging contraction property of Markov processes and martingale concentration, we establish a finite-sample instance-dependent error upper bound and a nearly-matching minimax lower bound. The policy evaluation error depends sharply on a restricted $\chi^2$-divergence over the function class between the long-term distribution of target policy and the distribution of past data. This restricted $\chi^2$-divergence characterizes the statistical limit of off-policy evaluation and is both instance-dependent and function-class-dependent. Further, we provide an easily computable confidence bound for the policy evaluator, which may be useful for optimistic planning and safe policy improvement.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a target policy would perform using data collected previously under other behavior. This paper studies the statistical accuracy of that task with linear function approximation and a fixed batch of reinforcement-learning data. It analyzes regression-based fitted Q-iteration, connecting a practical evaluation procedure to the information available in the dataset.

The authors show that this procedure is equivalent to a model-based method estimating a conditional mean embedding of the transition operator. They derive a finite-sample error upper bound and a nearly matching minimax lower bound. Together, these results establish that the method's estimation error is nearly as small as the statistical limits permit in the studied setting.

A restricted chi-squared divergence captures the mismatch between the target policy's long-term distribution and the distribution of historical data. Its restriction to the function class makes the difficulty depend on both the particular problem and the chosen representation. The paper also provides a computable confidence bound that may support optimistic planning and safe policy improvement.
summary.tldr: Fitted Q-iteration achieves nearly minimal off-policy evaluation error, governed by distribution mismatch measured through the chosen function class.

title: Minimax-Optimal Off-Policy Evaluation with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: This paper employs a formal connection of machine learning with thermodynamics to characterize the quality of learnt representations for transfer learning. We discuss how information-theoretic functionals such as rate, distortion and classification loss of a model lie on a convex, so-called equilibrium surface. We prescribe dynamical processes to traverse this surface under constraints, e.g., an iso-classification process that trades off rate and distortion to keep the classification loss unchanged. We demonstrate how this process can be used for transferring representations from a source dataset to a target dataset while keeping the classification loss constant. Experimental validation of the theoretical results is provided on standard image-classification datasets.

These capture different aspects of the information a model retains and how well that information supports its task.

They prescribe dynamical processes that move along the surface while respecting constraints. One example is an iso-classification process, which trades off rate and distortion while keeping classification loss unchanged.

The paper demonstrates how this process can transfer representations from a source dataset to a target dataset while preserving classification loss. Experiments on standard image-classification datasets validate the theoretical results. The contribution is a framework for reasoning about representation changes through explicit tradeoffs, together with a process that maintains a specified task-related quantity during transfer.
summary.tldr: A thermodynamic framework describes how to transfer representations while trading off information-related quantities and keeping classification loss constant.

title: A Free-Energy Principle for Representation Learning

abstract: In this work, we propose ParaNet, a non-autoregressive seq2seq model that converts text to spectrogram. It is fully convolutional and brings 46.7 times speed-up over the lightweight Deep Voice 3 at synthesis, while obtaining reasonably good speech quality. ParaNet also produces stable alignment between text and speech on the challenging test sentences by iteratively improving the attention in a layer-by-layer manner. Furthermore, we build the parallel text-to-speech system by applying various parallel neural vocoders, which can synthesize speech from text through a single feed-forward pass. We also explore a novel VAE-based approach to train the inverse autoregressive flow (IAF) based parallel vocoder from scratch, which avoids the need for distillation from a separately trained WaveNet as previous work.

summary.tldr: ParaNet enables fast parallel text-to-spectrogram synthesis with stable alignments and combines with parallel vocoders for feed-forward speech generation.

title: Non-Autoregressive Neural Text-to-Speech

abstract: Environments with procedurally generated content serve as important benchmarks for testing systematic generalization in deep reinforcement learning. In this setting, each level is an algorithmically created environment instance with a unique configuration of its factors of variation. Training on a prespecified subset of levels allows for testing generalization to unseen levels. What can be learned from a level depends on the current policy, yet prior work defaults to uniform sampling of training levels independently of the policy. We introduce Prioritized Level Replay (PLR), a general framework for selectively sampling the next training level by prioritizing those with higher estimated learning potential when revisited in the future. We show TD-errors effectively estimate a level’s future learning potential and, when used to guide the sampling procedure, induce an emergent curriculum of increasingly difficult levels. By adapting the sampling of training levels, PLR significantly improves sample-efficiency and generalization on Procgen Benchmark—matching the previous state-of-the-art in test return—and readily combines with other methods. Combined with the previous leading method, PLR raises the state-of-the-art to over 76% improvement in test return relative to standard RL baselines.

This paper observes that a level’s usefulness changes as the agent’s policy changes, whereas uniform sampling chooses levels without accounting for what the agent currently has the potential to learn.

Prioritized Level Replay selects which training levels to revisit according to their estimated future learning potential. The authors show that temporal-difference errors provide an effective estimate for this purpose. Using those errors to guide sampling produces an emergent curriculum of increasingly difficult levels, adapting the training distribution as learning progresses.

That percentage describes the combined method’s comparison with those baselines, rather than PLR’s standalone gain.
summary.tldr: Prioritized Level Replay improves reinforcement-learning efficiency and generalization by revisiting levels with greater estimated learning potential.

title: Prioritized Level Replay

abstract: Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs) are a class of generative models that transform a prior distribution to a model distribution by solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE). We propose to train CNFs on manifolds by minimizing probability path divergence (PPD), a novel family of divergences between the probability density path generated by the CNF and a target probability density path. PPD is formulated using a logarithmic mass conservation formula which is a linear first order partial differential equation relating the log target probabilities and the CNF’s defining vector field. PPD has several key benefits over existing methods: it sidesteps the need to solve an ODE per iteration, readily applies to manifold data, scales to high dimensions, and is compatible with a large family of target paths interpolating pure noise and data in finite time. Theoretically, PPD is shown to bound classical probability divergences. Empirically, we show that CNFs learned by minimizing PPD achieve state-of-the-art results in likelihoods and sample quality on existing low-dimensional manifold benchmarks, and is the first example of a generative model to scale to moderately high dimensional manifolds.

This paper develops a training objective for these models on manifolds. Instead of focusing only on the final distribution, it compares the model’s evolving density with a target sequence of densities connecting noise and data.

They also demonstrate scaling to moderately high-dimensional manifolds, presented as the first such generative-model example. These results support the training formulation’s usefulness beyond the low-dimensional settings used in established benchmarks.
summary.tldr: Probability path divergence trains continuous normalizing flows on manifolds without solving an ODE at each training iteration.

title: Matching Normalizing Flows and Probability Paths on Manifolds

abstract: The accelerated proximal point method (APPA), also known as "Catalyst", is a well-established reduction from convex optimization to approximate proximal point computation (i.e., regularized minimization). This reduction is conceptually elegant and yields strong convergence rate guarantees. However, these rates feature an extraneous logarithmic term arising from the need to compute each proximal point to high accuracy. In this work, we propose a novel Relaxed Error Criterion for Accelerated Proximal Point (RECAPP) that eliminates the need for high accuracy subproblem solutions. We apply RECAPP to two canonical problems: finite-sum and max-structured minimization. For finite-sum problems, we match the best known complexity, previously obtained by carefully-designed problem-specific algorithms. For minimizing max_y f(x,y) where f is convex in x and strongly-concave in y, we improve on the best known (Catalyst-based) bound by a logarithmic factor.

paragraphs: The accelerated proximal point method, also known as Catalyst, solves a convex optimization problem through a sequence of regularized subproblems. This is an elegant way to obtain strong convergence guarantees. However, requiring very accurate solutions to those subproblems introduces an extra logarithmic factor in the overall computational bounds.

RECAPP changes the criterion used to decide whether a subproblem has been solved accurately enough. Its relaxed error requirement removes the need for high-accuracy intermediate solutions. The significance is that the outer accelerated procedure can retain strong guarantees without paying for more precision than it needs at every stage.

The authors apply the method to finite-sum optimization and max-structured minimization. For finite sums, RECAPP matches the best known complexity, previously achieved through carefully specialized algorithms. For objectives formed by maximizing a function that is convex in the minimization variable and strongly concave in the maximization variable, it improves the previous Catalyst-based bound by a logarithmic factor. These results show the value of changing the subproblem accuracy requirement within a general reduction.
summary.tldr: RECAPP relaxes intermediate accuracy requirements in accelerated proximal optimization, matching or improving leading complexity bounds.

title: RECAPP: Crafting a More Efficient Catalyst for Convex Optimization

abstract: We investigate a natural but surprisingly unstudied approach to the multi-armed bandit problem under safety risk constraints. Each arm is associated with an unknown law on safety risks and rewards, and the learner’s goal is to maximise reward whilst not playing unsafe arms, as determined by a given threshold on the mean risk. We formulate a pseudo-regret for this setting that enforces this safety constraint in a per-round way by softly penalising any violation, regardless of the gain in reward due to the same. This has practical relevance to scenarios such as clinical trials, where one must maintain safety for each round rather than in an aggregated sense. We describe doubly optimistic strategies for this scenario, which maintain optimistic indices for both safety risk and reward. We show that schema based on both frequentist and Bayesian indices satisfy tight gap-dependent logarithmic regret bounds, and further that these play unsafe arms only logarithmically many times in total. This theoretical analysis is complemented by simulation studies demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed schema, and probing the domains in which their use is appropriate.

paragraphs: In this bandit problem, each action has unknown reward and safety-risk distributions. An action is considered unsafe when its mean risk exceeds a specified threshold. The learner seeks high rewards while avoiding unsafe actions, so uncertainty about safety is part of the exploration problem.

The paper defines a pseudo-regret measure that penalizes safety violations on individual rounds, regardless of any reward gained on those rounds. This captures a concern that aggregate reward or average performance alone could obscure. The proposed strategies maintain optimistic indices for both safety and reward, allowing both kinds of uncertainty to guide action selection.

The authors analyze versions using frequentist and Bayesian indices. They prove tight gap-dependent logarithmic regret bounds and show that unsafe actions are selected only logarithmically many times in total. This is a bound on the frequency of unsafe choices, rather than a guarantee that none occur during learning. Simulations demonstrate the strategies' effectiveness and investigate where they are appropriate, complementing the theoretical account of reward learning under per-round safety penalties.
summary.tldr: Strategies optimistic about both safety and reward achieve logarithmic regret and logarithmically many unsafe selections under the analyzed bounds.

title: Strategies for Safe Multi-Armed Bandits with Logarithmic Regret and Risk

abstract: Wasserstein gradient flow has emerged as a promising approach to solve optimization problems over the space of probability distributions. A recent trend is to use the well-known JKO scheme in combination with input convex neural networks to numerically implement the proximal step. The most challenging step, in this setup, is to evaluate functions involving density explicitly, such as entropy, in terms of samples. This paper builds on the recent works with a slight but crucial difference: we propose to utilize a variational formulation of the objective function formulated as maximization over a parametric class of functions. Theoretically, the proposed variational formulation allows the construction of gradient flows directly for empirical distributions with a well-defined and meaningful objective function. Computationally, this approach replaces the computationally expensive step in existing methods, to handle objective functions involving density, with inner loop updates that only require a small batch of samples and scale well with the dimension. The performance and scalability of the proposed method are illustrated with the aid of several numerical experiments involving high-dimensional synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: Wasserstein gradient flow provides a way to optimize over probability distributions. Recent numerical approaches combine the JKO scheme with input-convex neural networks, but objectives involving densities, such as entropy, create a difficult computational step. Evaluating those terms from samples can be especially demanding as the dimension increases.

This paper reformulates the objective variationally, expressing it as a maximization over a parameterized family of functions. The change allows gradient flows to be constructed directly for empirical distributions while keeping the objective well defined and meaningful. This is a theoretical benefit of working with the new formulation, alongside its computational purpose.

Computationally, the reformulation replaces the expensive treatment of density-dependent objectives with inner-loop updates that use small sample batches and scale well with dimension. Numerical experiments on high-dimensional synthetic and real datasets illustrate performance and scalability. The contribution is therefore a different way to express and evaluate the objective, making sample-based distribution optimization more practical within this gradient-flow approach.
summary.tldr: A variational objective enables Wasserstein gradient flows directly on empirical distributions and replaces costly density calculations with sample-based inner updates.

title: Variational Wasserstein gradient flow

abstract: Inductive transfer learning aims to learn from a small amount of training data for the target task by utilizing a pre-trained model from the source task. Most strategies that involve large-scale deep learning models adopt initialization with the pre-trained model and fine-tuning for the target task. However, when using over-parameterized models, we can often prune the model without sacrificing the accuracy of the source task. This motivates us to adopt model pruning for transfer learning with deep learning models. In this paper, we propose PAC-Net, a simple yet effective approach for transfer learning based on pruning. PAC-Net consists of three steps: Prune, Allocate, and Calibrate (PAC). The main idea behind these steps is to identify essential weights for the source task, fine-tune on the source task by updating the essential weights, and then calibrate on the target task by updating the remaining redundant weights. Under the various and extensive set of inductive transfer learning experiments, we show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance by a large margin.

paragraphs: Inductive transfer learning uses a model trained on a source task to learn a target task from limited data. A common approach initializes the target model with the pretrained weights and fine-tunes them. PAC-Net starts from the observation that over-parameterized models can often be pruned without reducing their source-task accuracy.

Its procedure has three stages: pruning, allocation, and calibration. It identifies weights essential to the source task, then fine-tunes those essential weights on source data. Finally, it adapts to the target task by updating the remaining redundant weights. This assigns different roles to the weights used for retaining source-task capability and those available for target-task adaptation.

Across the paper’s extensive transfer-learning experiments, PAC-Net achieves reported state-of-the-art performance by a large margin. The findings support using pruning to organize the transfer process, beyond its role in reducing a model’s size. The motivation depends on the availability of redundant capacity, which the abstract describes as a frequent property of over-parameterized models rather than a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: PAC-Net uses pruning to separate source-essential weights from redundant weights that can be adapted to a target task.

title: PAC-Net: A Model Pruning Approach to Inductive Transfer Learning

abstract: The task of approximating an arbitrary convex function arises in several learning problems such as convex regression, learning with a difference of convex (DC) functions, and learning Bregman or $f$-divergences. In this paper, we develop and analyze an approach for solving a broad range of convex function learning problems that is faster than state-of-the-art approaches. Our approach is based on a 2-block ADMM method where each block can be computed in closed form. For the task of convex Lipschitz regression, we establish that our proposed algorithm converges with iteration complexity of $ O(n\sqrt{d}/\epsilon)$ for a dataset $\bm X \in \mathbb R^{n\times d}$ and $\epsilon > 0$. Combined with per-iteration computation complexity, our method converges with the rate $O(n^3 d^{1.5}/\epsilon+n^2 d^{2.5}/\epsilon+n d^3/\epsilon)$. This new rate improves the state of the art rate of $O(n^5d^2/\epsilon)$ if $d = o( n^4)$. Further we provide similar solvers for DC regression and Bregman divergence learning. Unlike previous approaches, our method is amenable to the use of GPUs. We demonstrate on regression and metric learning experiments that our approach is over 100 times faster than existing approaches on some data sets, and produces results that are comparable to state of the art.

This paper develops faster solvers for a broad range of these problems. Its approach uses a two-block alternating direction method of multipliers, with each block update available in closed form.

For convex Lipschitz regression on n examples with d features, the authors establish an iteration bound of O(n√d/ε). The improvement therefore comes with an explicit relationship between dataset size and dimension.

In regression and metric-learning experiments, the approach runs more than 100 times faster than existing methods on some datasets while producing results comparable to the state of the art.
summary.tldr: Closed-form two-block optimization updates accelerate convex function learning, with theoretical improvements and large speedups on some datasets.

title: Faster Algorithms for Learning Convex Functions

abstract: Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) are instances of Graph Neural Networks that leverage the graph to send messages over the edges. This inductive bias leads to a phenomenon known as over-squashing, where a node feature is insensitive to information contained at distant nodes. Despite recent methods introduced to mitigate this issue, an understanding of the causes for over-squashing and of possible solutions are lacking. In this theoretical work, we prove that: (i) Neural network width can mitigate over-squashing, but at the cost of making the whole network more sensitive; (ii) Conversely, depth cannot help mitigate over-squashing: increasing the number of layers leads to over-squashing being dominated by vanishing gradients; (iii) The graph topology plays the greatest role, since over-squashing occurs between nodes at high commute time. Our analysis provides a unified framework to study different recent methods introduced to cope with over-squashing and serves as a justification for a class of methods that fall under graph rewiring.

paragraphs: Message passing neural networks update graph nodes by exchanging information along edges. Over-squashing occurs when a node’s representation becomes insensitive to information at distant nodes. This theoretical paper separates the roles of network width, depth, and graph topology to explain why that loss of influence happens and which changes can address it.

The analysis shows that greater width can mitigate over-squashing, but increases the sensitivity of the whole network. Increasing depth does not resolve the issue in the analysis: as layers are added, vanishing gradients come to dominate over-squashing. These results distinguish the effects of giving messages more representational capacity from simply extending the sequence of message-passing operations.

Graph topology has the greatest role in the authors’ account. They connect over-squashing to pairs of nodes with high commute time, relating the problem to the graph’s connectivity. The framework unifies the study of several mitigation methods and provides theoretical justification for a class of graph-rewiring approaches, which address information flow by changing graph connections.
summary.tldr: The analysis connects over-squashing primarily to graph topology, showing that width has a sensitivity cost and added depth cannot resolve it.

title: On Over-Squashing in Message Passing Neural Networks: The Impact of Width, Depth, and Topology

abstract: In reinforcement learning and imitation learning, an object of central importance is the state distribution induced by the policy. It plays a crucial role in the policy gradient theorem, and references to it–along with the related state-action distribution–can be found all across the literature. Despite its importance, the state distribution is mostly discussed indirectly and theoretically, rather than being modeled explicitly. The reason being an absence of appropriate density estimation tools. In this work, we investigate applications of a normalizing flow based model for the aforementioned distributions. In particular, we use a pair of flows coupled through the optimality point of the Donsker-Varadhan representation of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, for distribution matching based imitation learning. Our algorithm, Coupled Flow Imitation Learning (CFIL), achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark tasks with a single expert trajectory and extends naturally to a variety of other settings, including the subsampled and state-only regimes.

paragraphs: Imitation learning asks an agent to reproduce demonstrated behavior. One way to express that goal is to match the distribution of states, or state–action pairs, produced by an expert. These distributions describe where a policy takes the agent and what it does there. The paper makes them explicit modeling targets, addressing a quantity often discussed mainly through theory.

The proposed Coupled Flow Imitation Learning method uses normalizing flows to model these distributions. Its central construction links two flows through a mathematical representation of Kullback–Leibler divergence, a measure of distributional difference. Specifically, the coupling uses the optimality point of the Donsker–Varadhan representation. This supplies a principled connection between the density models and the distribution-matching objective.

On benchmark tasks, CFIL achieves reported state-of-the-art performance using a single expert trajectory. The method also extends naturally to demonstrations that are subsampled or contain only states. These findings make explicit distribution modeling relevant to imitation settings where expert demonstrations are scarce or provide incomplete behavioral information.
summary.tldr: CFIL couples two normalizing flows to match expert behavior, achieving leading benchmark performance with a single demonstration trajectory.

title: A Coupled Flow Approach to Imitation Learning

abstract: Propensity-based weighting methods have been widely studied and demonstrated competitive performance in debiased recommendations. Nevertheless, there are still many questions to be addressed. How to estimate the propensity more conducive to debiasing performance? Which metric is more reasonable to measure the quality of the learned propensities? Is it better to make the cross-entropy loss as small as possible when learning propensities? In this paper, we first discuss the potential problems of the previously widely adopted metrics for learned propensities, and propose balanced-mean-squared-error (BMSE) metric for debiased recommendations. Based on BMSE, we propose IPS-V2 and DR-V2 as the estimators of unbiased loss, and theoretically show that IPS-V2 and DR-V2 have greater propensity balancing and smaller variance without sacrificing additional bias. We further propose a co-training method for learning balanced representation and unbiased prediction. Extensive experiments are conducted on three real-world datasets including a large industrial dataset, and the results show that our approach boosts the balancing property and results in enhanced debiasing performance.

paragraphs: Propensity-based weighting is used to reduce bias in recommendation, but learning propensities raises a further question: how should their quality be judged? The paper examines whether commonly used metrics, including the pursuit of smaller cross-entropy loss, adequately reflect their usefulness for debiasing. It focuses on the balancing behavior that the learned propensities produce.

The authors introduce balanced mean squared error, or BMSE, as a metric for this purpose. Building on it, they propose IPS-V2 and DR-V2 loss estimators. Their theoretical analysis shows stronger propensity balancing and lower variance without an additional bias cost, connecting the proposed evaluation criterion to improvements in the estimators used for learning.

The paper also develops a co-training method that learns balanced representations together with unbiased predictions. Experiments use three real-world datasets, including a large industrial dataset, and report improved balancing and debiasing performance. The findings connect three parts of the recommendation pipeline: how propensity quality is measured, how weighted loss is estimated, and how representations and predictions are learned together.
summary.tldr: A balancing-focused propensity metric leads to revised estimators and co-training that improve debiasing in the reported recommendation experiments.

title: Propensity Matters: Measuring and Enhancing Balancing for Recommendation

abstract: We consider decentralized optimization problems where one aims to minimize a sum of convex smooth objective functions distributed between nodes in the network. The links in the network can change from time to time. For the setting when the amount of changes is arbitrary, lower complexity bounds and corresponding optimal algorithms are known, and the consensus acceleration is not possible. However, in practice the magnitude of network changes may be limited. We derive lower complexity bounds for several regimes of velocity of networks changes. Moreover, we show how to obtain accelerated communication rates for a certain class of time-varying graphs using a specific consensus algorithm.

paragraphs: In decentralized optimization, different network nodes hold different parts of a shared objective. The paper considers minimizing the sum of smooth convex functions when communication links can change over time. Reaching agreement across nodes is part of the challenge, and the pattern of network changes affects how quickly communication can accomplish it.

When network changes are unrestricted, existing complexity results rule out consensus acceleration. This paper asks whether that conclusion changes when the network evolves more slowly. The authors derive lower complexity bounds for several regimes describing the speed of network changes, giving limits that distinguish these different settings.

They also construct a specific consensus algorithm that achieves accelerated communication rates for a certain class of changing graphs. This provides a qualified positive answer to the title's question: acceleration is possible within the identified graph class. The work therefore makes the restrictions on network evolution central to understanding both achievable communication rates and fundamental obstacles.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes limits for several network-change regimes and shows that communication acceleration is possible for a particular class of time-varying graphs.

title: Is Consensus Acceleration Possible in Decentralized Optimization over Slowly Time-Varying Networks?

abstract: Ad hoc teamwork requires an agent to cooperate with unknown teammates without prior coordination. Many works propose to abstract teammate instances into high-level representation of types and then pre-train the best response for each type. However, most of them do not consider the distribution of teammate instances within a type. This could expose the agent to the hidden risk of type confounding. In the worst case, the best response for an abstract teammate type could be the worst response for all specific instances of that type. This work addresses the issue from the lens of causal inference. We first theoretically demonstrate that this phenomenon is due to the spurious correlation brought by uncontrolled teammate distribution. Then, we propose our solution, CTCAT, which disentangles such correlation through an instance-wise teammate feedback rectification. This operation reweights the interaction of teammate instances within a shared type to reduce the influence of type confounding. The effect of CTCAT is evaluated in multiple domains, including classic ad hoc teamwork tasks and real-world scenarios. Results show that CTCAT is robust to the influence of type confounding, a practical issue that directly hazards the robustness of our trained agents but was unnoticed in previous works.

paragraphs: Ad hoc teamwork asks an agent to cooperate with unfamiliar teammates without arranging a strategy beforehand. A common approach groups teammates into broad types and trains a response for each type. This paper shows why that abstraction can be misleading when training ignores how individual teammates are distributed within each group.

The problem, called type confounding, can be severe: in the worst case, the response judged best for a type can be worst for every individual assigned to it. Through causal analysis, the authors attribute this phenomenon to spurious correlations introduced by an uncontrolled distribution of teammate instances. The apparent value of a response can therefore reflect which teammates produced the feedback rather than reliable guidance for cooperation.

Their method, CTCAT, adjusts feedback at the level of individual teammate instances. It reweights interactions within a shared type to reduce the influence of the confounding correlation. Evaluations across classic teamwork tasks and real-world scenarios show robustness to type confounding. The findings make the composition of teammate groups an explicit concern when training agents to cooperate with new partners.
summary.tldr: CTCAT reweights feedback from individual teammates to reduce misleading correlations hidden inside broad teammate types.

title: Controlling Type Confounding in Ad Hoc Teamwork with Instance-wise Teammate Feedback Rectification

abstract: Current fake audio detection algorithms have achieved promising performances on most datasets. However, their performance may be significantly degraded when dealing with audio of a different dataset. The orthogonal weight modification to overcome catastrophic forgetting does not consider the similarity of genuine audio across different datasets. To overcome this limitation, we propose a continual learning algorithm for fake audio detection to overcome catastrophic forgetting, called Regularized Adaptive Weight Modification (RAWM). When fine-tuning a detection network, our approach adaptively computes the direction of weight modification according to the ratio of genuine utterances and fake utterances. The adaptive modification direction ensures the network can effectively detect fake audio on the new dataset while preserving its knowledge of old model, thus mitigating catastrophic forgetting. In addition, genuine audio collected from quite different acoustic conditions may skew their feature distribution, so we introduce a regularization constraint to force the network to remember the old distribution in this regard. Our method can easily be generalized to related fields, like speech emotion recognition. We also evaluate our approach across multiple datasets and obtain a significant performance improvement on cross-dataset experiments.

paragraphs: A fake-audio detector can perform well on one dataset and deteriorate on another. Updating it for new data also raises the problem of catastrophic forgetting: learning the new dataset can erode previously acquired knowledge. This paper proposes Regularized Adaptive Weight Modification, or RAWM, to improve adaptation while retaining earlier detection capabilities.

RAWM adjusts the direction of weight updates according to the proportion of genuine and fake utterances during fine-tuning. This addresses a limitation of orthogonal weight modification, which does not account for similarities in genuine audio across datasets. The adaptive direction is designed to support learning about new fake audio while preserving knowledge from the previous model.

The method also adds a regularization constraint to retain the earlier feature distribution when genuine audio comes from substantially different acoustic conditions. Across multiple datasets, the authors report significant improvements in cross-dataset experiments. The two components address related sources of forgetting: changes in how the detector learns and shifts in genuine-audio features. The authors also describe applicability to related areas such as speech emotion recognition.
summary.tldr: RAWM combines adaptive weight updates and distribution-preserving regularization to reduce forgetting when fake-audio detectors learn new datasets.

title: Do You Remember? Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting for Fake Audio Detection

abstract: Despite the recent advancements in offline RL, no unified algorithm could achieve superior performance across a broad range of tasks. Offline value function learning, in particular, struggles with sparse-reward, long-horizon tasks due to the difficulty of solving credit assignment and extrapolation errors that accumulates as the horizon of the task grows. On the other hand, models that can perform well in long-horizon tasks are designed specifically for goal-conditioned tasks, which commonly perform worse than value function learning methods on short-horizon, dense-reward scenarios. To bridge this gap, we propose a hierarchical planner designed for offline RL called PlanDQ. PlanDQ incorporates a diffusion-based planner at the high level, named D-Conductor, which guides the low-level policy through sub-goals. At the low level, we used a Q-learning based approach called the Q-Performer to accomplish these sub-goals. Our experimental results suggest that PlanDQ can achieve superior or competitive performance on D4RL continuous control benchmark tasks as well as AntMaze, Kitchen, and Calvin as long-horizon tasks.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning methods face different difficulties depending on task structure. Value-function learning struggles when rewards are sparse and success requires a long sequence of decisions, because credit assignment and extrapolation errors become harder to manage. Methods specialized for long-horizon, goal-conditioned tasks can perform worse in shorter tasks with frequent rewards.

PlanDQ combines two approaches in a hierarchical planner. At the high level, a diffusion-based D-Conductor proposes subgoals that guide the policy. At the low level, a Q-learning-based Q-Performer works to accomplish those subgoals. This division gives long-range planning and local execution distinct roles within the same offline learning system.

Experiments suggest superior or competitive performance on D4RL continuous-control benchmarks and on the long-horizon AntMaze, Kitchen, and Calvin tasks. These results support the proposed combination across the evaluated task types, rather than establishing universal superiority. The paper’s contribution is a practical architecture for bridging the performance gap between methods suited to sparse, delayed rewards and those effective with shorter horizons and denser rewards.
summary.tldr: PlanDQ combines diffusion-based subgoal planning with Q-learning execution to achieve competitive results across short- and long-horizon offline RL tasks.

title: PlanDQ: Hierarchical Plan Orchestration via D-Conductor and Q-Performer

abstract: Detecting text generated by modern large language models is thought to be hard, as both LLMs and humans can exhibit a wide range of complex behaviors. However, we find that a score based on contrasting two closely related language models is highly accurate at separating human-generated and machine-generated text. Based on this mechanism, we propose a novel LLM detector that only requires simple calculations using a pair of pre-trained LLMs. The method, called Binoculars, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy without any training data. It is capable of spotting machine text from a range of modern LLMs without any model-specific modifications. We comprehensively evaluate Binoculars on a number of text sources and in varied situations. Over a wide range of document types, Binoculars detects over 90% of generated samples from ChatGPT (and other LLMs) at a false positive rate of 0.01%, despite not being trained on any ChatGPT data. Code available at https://github.com/ahans30/Binoculars.

paragraphs: Human writing and language-model output can both exhibit complex and varied behavior, making automated detection difficult. Binoculars approaches the task by contrasting two closely related pretrained language models. The authors find that a score derived from this comparison separates human and machine text accurately in their evaluations.

The detector needs only simple calculations using the two models and requires no detector training data. It can also detect output from multiple modern language models without modifications tailored to each generating model. This makes the comparison score the central mechanism for transferring detection across different sources of generated text.

Across a wide range of document types, the reported detector identifies more than 90% of generated samples from ChatGPT and other models at a false-positive rate of 0.01%. It achieves this without training on ChatGPT data. These empirical results support the usefulness of paired-model comparison for accurate zero-shot detection across the text sources and situations examined.
summary.tldr: Binoculars compares two pretrained language models to detect generated text accurately without detector training data or generator-specific modifications.

title: Spotting LLMs With Binoculars: Zero-Shot Detection of Machine-Generated Text

abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are general-purpose parallel-sequential computers. The program of an RNN is its weight matrix. How to learn useful representations of RNN weights that facilitate RNN analysis as well as downstream tasks? While the mechanistic approach directly looks at some RNN’s weights to predict its behavior, the functionalist approach analyzes its overall functionality–specifically, its input-output mapping. We consider several mechanistic approaches for RNN weights and adapt the permutation equivariant Deep Weight Space layer for RNNs. Our two novel functionalist approaches extract information from RNN weights by ’interrogating’ the RNN through probing inputs. We develop a theoretical framework that demonstrates conditions under which the functionalist approach can generate rich representations that help determine RNN behavior. We create and release the first two ’model zoo’ datasets for RNN weight representation learning. One consists of generative models of a class of formal languages, and the other one of classifiers of sequentially processed MNIST digits. With the help of an emulation-based self-supervised learning technique we compare and evaluate the different RNN weight encoding techniques on multiple downstream applications. On the most challenging one, namely predicting which exact task the RNN was trained on, functionalist approaches show clear superiority.

paragraphs: An RNN's weight matrix determines how it processes sequences, but turning those weights into a useful description of its behavior is challenging. This paper compares two perspectives. Mechanistic methods inspect the weights directly, while functionalist methods study the input-output behavior that those weights produce.

The authors examine several mechanistic approaches and adapt a permutation-equivariant Deep Weight Space layer to recurrent networks. They also introduce two functionalist methods that probe an RNN with inputs and encode information from its responses. A theoretical framework establishes conditions under which these behavioral probes can produce rich representations useful for determining how the RNN behaves.

For evaluation, the paper introduces two RNN model-zoo datasets: formal-language generators and classifiers that process MNIST digits sequentially. An emulation-based self-supervised technique supports comparisons across downstream applications. Functionalist methods clearly outperform the alternatives on the hardest reported task, identifying the exact task used to train an RNN. This finding gives behavioral probing a particularly strong role in recovering information about a network's training task.
summary.tldr: Probing RNN behavior produces useful weight representations and clearly improves identification of training tasks in the paper's hardest evaluation.

title: Learning Useful Representations of Recurrent Neural Network Weight Matrices

abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are potent frameworks for knowledge representation and reasoning. Nevertheless, KGs are inherently incomplete, leaving numerous uncharted relationships and facts awaiting discovery. Deep learning methodologies have proven effective in enhancing KG completion by framing it as a link prediction task, where the goal is to discern the validity of a triple comprising a head, relation, and tail. The significance of structural information in assessing the validity of a triple within a KG is well-established. However, quantifying this structural information poses a challenge. We need to pinpoint the metric that encapsulates the structural information of a triple and smoothly incorporate this metric into the link prediction learning process. In this study, we recognize the critical importance of the intersection among the $k$-hop neighborhoods of the head, relation, and tail when determining the validity of a triple. To address this, we introduce a novel randomized algorithm designed to efficiently generate intersection features for candidate triples. Our experimental results demonstrate that a straightforward fully-connected network leveraging these intersection features can surpass the performance of established KG embedding models and even outperform graph neural network baselines. Additionally, we highlight the substantial training time efficiency gains achieved by our network trained on intersection features.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs contain entities and relationships, but many valid facts are missing. Completion methods often assess candidate triples consisting of a head, a relation, and a tail. Graph structure provides useful evidence for deciding whether a triple is valid; the challenge is expressing that evidence in a form a predictor can use efficiently.

The authors focus on intersections among the k-hop neighborhoods of the head, relation, and tail. These overlaps provide explicit structural features for candidate triples. A new randomized algorithm generates the intersection features efficiently, allowing the prediction model to operate directly on this representation of the surrounding graph.

The resulting predictor is a straightforward fully connected network. In the reported experiments, it surpasses established knowledge graph embedding models and graph neural network baselines, while also delivering substantial training-time savings. The findings show that the choice of structural features can make a relatively simple predictor highly effective, with neighborhood intersections capturing useful information for the tested completion tasks.
summary.tldr: Efficient neighborhood-intersection features let a simple network outperform established knowledge graph completion baselines in the reported experiments.

title: Knowledge Graphs Can be Learned with Just Intersection Features

abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has proven effective in aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences, but gathering high-quality preference labels is expensive. RL from AI Feedback (RLAIF), introduced in Bai et al. (2022b), offers a promising alternative that trains the reward model (RM) on preferences generated by an off-the-shelf LLM. Across the tasks of summarization, helpful dialogue generation, and harmless dialogue generation, we show that RLAIF achieves comparable performance to RLHF. Furthermore, we take a step towards "self-improvement" by demonstrating that RLAIF can outperform a supervised fine-tuned baseline even when the AI labeler is the same size as the policy, or even the exact same checkpoint as the initial policy. Finally, we introduce direct-RLAIF (d-RLAIF) - a technique that circumvents RM training by obtaining rewards directly from an off-the-shelf LLM during RL, which achieves superior performance to canonical RLAIF. Our results suggest that RLAIF can achieve performance on-par with using human feedback, offering a potential solution to the scalability limitations of RLHF.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback depends on preference labels that can be expensive to collect. This paper examines whether preferences supplied by an existing language model can provide a scalable alternative. In the standard AI-feedback approach, those preferences train a reward model, which then guides reinforcement learning.

Across summarization, helpful dialogue, and harmless dialogue tasks, the authors find performance comparable to learning from human feedback. They also show improvement over a supervised fine-tuned baseline when the AI labeler has the same size as the policy, or even starts from the exact same checkpoint. These results provide evidence toward self-improvement without requiring a larger labeling model in those experiments.

The paper additionally introduces direct-RLAIF, which obtains rewards from an existing language model during reinforcement learning and avoids training a separate reward model. This variant outperforms canonical RLAIF in the reported evaluation. Together, the findings suggest that AI feedback can match human-feedback performance on the studied tasks and may ease the scaling constraints associated with collecting human preferences.
summary.tldr: AI feedback matches human-feedback performance on the studied tasks, and directly using language-model rewards further improves the AI-feedback approach.

title: RLAIF vs. RLHF: Scaling Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback with AI Feedback

abstract: Decision making demands intricate interplay between perception, memory, and reasoning to discern optimal policies. Conventional approaches to decision making face challenges related to low sample efficiency and poor generalization. In contrast, foundation models in language and vision have showcased rapid adaptation to diverse new tasks. Therefore, we advocate for the construction of foundation agents as a transformative shift in the learning paradigm of agents. This proposal is underpinned by the formulation of foundation agents with their fundamental characteristics and challenges motivated by the success of large language models (LLMs). Moreover, we specify the roadmap of foundation agents from large interactive data collection or generation, to self-supervised pretraining and adaptation, and knowledge and value alignment with LLMs. Lastly, we pinpoint critical research questions derived from the formulation and delineate trends for foundation agents supported by real-world use cases, addressing both technical and theoretical aspects to propel the field towards a more comprehensive and impactful future.

paragraphs: Decision-making agents must combine perception, memory, and reasoning to choose effective actions. Conventional learning approaches often need many examples and struggle to transfer to new situations. This position paper argues that the rapid adaptation demonstrated by language and vision foundation models motivates a similar foundation-model approach to agents.

The authors formulate what foundation agents should be, describe their fundamental characteristics, and identify challenges suggested by the experience of large language models. They propose a development roadmap beginning with collecting or generating large amounts of interactive data, followed by self-supervised pretraining and adaptation. The roadmap also includes aligning agents with the knowledge and values represented by language models.

The paper's contribution is a research agenda for building broadly adaptable decision makers. It identifies technical and theoretical questions and connects emerging directions to real-world use cases. Its claim is that foundation agents offer a promising shift in how agents are learned; the abstract presents an argument and roadmap rather than reporting a particular agent's measured gains. This framing organizes the work needed to pursue that proposed shift.
summary.tldr: This position paper proposes foundation agents and a roadmap for broadly adaptable decision-making systems.

title: Position: Foundation Agents as the Paradigm Shift for Decision Making

abstract: Sequential decision-making algorithms such as reinforcement learning (RL) in real-world scenarios inevitably face environments with partial observability. This paper scrutinizes the effectiveness of a popular architecture, namely Transformers, in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) and reveals its theoretical limitations. We establish that regular languages, which Transformers struggle to model, are reducible to POMDPs. This poses a significant challenge for Transformers in learning POMDP-specific inductive biases, due to their lack of inherent recurrence found in other models like RNNs. This paper casts doubt on the prevalent belief in Transformers as sequence models for RL and proposes to introduce a point-wise recurrent structure. The Deep Linear Recurrent Unit (LRU) emerges as a well-suited alternative for Partially Observable RL, with empirical results highlighting the sub-optimal performance of the Transformer and considerable strength of LRU.

paragraphs: This paper questions how well Transformers suit decision-making when the environment is only partially observable. In a partially observable Markov decision process, the agent’s immediate observation does not fully reveal its situation. The authors examine whether a popular sequence architecture has the structural properties needed to learn effectively in this setting.

Their theoretical argument shows that regular-language problems, which Transformers struggle to model, can be reduced to these decision problems. This connects a known modeling difficulty to partially observable reinforcement learning. The authors identify the absence of inherent recurrence as a challenge for learning the relevant inductive biases, contrasting Transformers with recurrent models.

They propose adding a point-wise recurrent structure and identify the Deep Linear Recurrent Unit as a suitable alternative. Empirical results show suboptimal Transformer performance and considerable strength for this recurrent approach in the evaluated settings. The paper thus combines a theoretical warning with experimental evidence for revisiting architecture choices, rather than treating general sequence-modeling popularity as sufficient evidence of suitability for partially observable control.
summary.tldr: Theoretical and empirical results expose Transformer difficulties in partially observable reinforcement learning and support a recurrent alternative.

title: Rethinking Transformers in Solving POMDPs

abstract: We study regret minimization in online episodic linear Markov Decision Processes, and propose a policy optimization algorithm that is computationally efficient, and obtains rate optimal $\widetilde O (\sqrt K)$ regret where $K$ denotes the number of episodes. Our work is the first to establish the optimal rate (in terms of $K$) of convergence in the stochastic setting with bandit feedback using a policy optimization based approach, and the first to establish the optimal rate in the adversarial setup with full information feedback, for which no algorithm with an optimal rate guarantee was previously known.

paragraphs: The paper studies online reinforcement learning in episodic linear Markov decision processes. An agent improves its behavior over repeated episodes, and regret measures the accumulated cost of its learning decisions relative to the comparison used by the problem. The goal is an efficient policy optimization method whose regret grows at the best possible rate with experience.

The proposed algorithm achieves regret scaling with the square root of the number of episodes, up to logarithmic factors. The authors establish optimality specifically in that episode-count dependence. Computational efficiency is also part of the result, connecting the statistical rate to an algorithm intended to be feasible to run.

Two feedback settings are covered. In the stochastic setting with bandit feedback, this is the first stated optimal episode-dependent rate achieved through policy optimization. In the adversarial setting with full information, the paper establishes an optimal rate where no algorithm previously had such a guarantee. The distinction matters: the adversarial result uses richer feedback, so the two guarantees concern different learning conditions.
summary.tldr: An efficient policy optimization algorithm achieves optimal episode-dependent regret rates for two specified linear MDP feedback settings.

title: Rate-Optimal Policy Optimization for Linear Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Sample-efficiency and reliability remain major bottlenecks toward wide adoption of reinforcement learning algorithms in continuous settings with high-dimensional perceptual inputs. Toward addressing these challenges, we introduce a new theoretical framework, RichCLD (“Rich-Observation RL with Continuous Latent Dynamics”), in which the agent performs control based on high-dimensional observations, but the environment is governed by low-dimensional latent states and Lipschitz continuous dynamics. Our main contribution is a new algorithm for this setting that is provably statistically and computationally efficient. The core of our algorithm is a new representation learning objective; we show that prior representation learning schemes tailored to discrete dynamics do not naturally extend to the continuous setting. Our new objective is amenable to practical implementation, and empirically, we find that it compares favorably to prior schemes in a standard evaluation protocol. We further provide several insights into the statistical complexity of the RichCLD framework, in particular proving that certain notions of Lipschitzness that admit sample-efficient learning in the absence of rich observations are insufficient in the rich-observation setting.

paragraphs: RichCLD studies reinforcement learning in environments where an agent observes high-dimensional inputs but the underlying state is low-dimensional. The framework assumes continuous latent dynamics with Lipschitz regularity, a condition controlling how sharply the dynamics can change. This setting separates the complexity of what the agent sees from the smaller state governing the environment.

The authors introduce an algorithm that is provably efficient in both statistical and computational terms within this framework. Its core is a new representation-learning objective. They show that objectives designed for discrete dynamics do not transfer naturally to continuous dynamics, making the representation objective a substantive part of the solution.

The objective is suitable for practical implementation and compares favorably with previous schemes under a standard evaluation protocol. The paper also establishes limits on which smoothness assumptions suffice: certain notions of Lipschitzness that permit sample-efficient learning without rich observations are insufficient when observations are rich. The guarantees consequently depend on the framework’s structure, rather than following from continuity or smoothness alone.
summary.tldr: RichCLD provides an efficient RL algorithm for rich observations with continuous low-dimensional latent dynamics, while clarifying which regularity assumptions are insufficient.

title: Rich-Observation Reinforcement Learning with Continuous Latent Dynamics

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in problem-solving. However, their proficiency in solving mathematical problems remains inadequate. We propose MathScale, a simple and scalable method to create high-quality mathematical reasoning data using frontier LLMs (e.g., GPT-3.5). Inspired by the cognitive mechanism in human mathematical learning, it first extracts topics and knowledge points from seed math questions and then build a concept graph, which is subsequently used to generate new math questions. MathScale exhibits effective scalability along the size axis of the math dataset that we generate. As a result, we create a mathematical reasoning dataset (MathScaleQA) containing two million math question-answer pairs. To evaluate mathematical reasoning abilities of LLMs comprehensively, we construct MWPBench, a benchmark of Math Word Problems, which is a collection of 9 datasets (including GSM8K and MATH) covering K-12, college, and competition level math problems. We apply MathScaleQA to fine-tune open-source LLMs (e.g., LLaMA-2 and Mistral), resulting in significantly improved capabilities in mathematical reasoning. Evaluated on MWPBench, MathScale-7B achieves state-of-the-art performance across all datasets, surpassing its best peers of equivalent size by 42.8% in micro average accuracy and 43.6% in macro average accuracy, respectively.

Using this process, the authors create MathScaleQA, a dataset containing two million question-answer pairs. title: MathScale: Scaling Instruction Tuning for Mathematical Reasoning

abstract: We study the game modification problem, where a benevolent game designer or a malevolent adversary modifies the reward function of a zero-sum Markov game so that a target deterministic or stochastic policy profile becomes the unique Markov perfect Nash equilibrium and has a value within a target range, in a way that minimizes the modification cost. We characterize the set of policy profiles that can be installed as the unique equilibrium of a game and establish sufficient and necessary conditions for successful installation. We propose an efficient algorithm that solves a convex optimization problem with linear constraints and then performs random perturbation to obtain a modification plan with a near-optimal cost.

We characterize the set of policy profiles that can be installed as the unique equilibrium of a game and establish sufficient and necessary conditions for successful installation.
