paragraphs: This paper asks how to change the rewards of a zero-sum Markov game so that players settle on a desired policy profile. The objective is demanding: the target must become the unique Markov perfect Nash equilibrium, its value must lie within a specified range, and the reward changes should cost as little as possible.

The setting allows either deterministic or stochastic target policies and can represent the actions of a benevolent designer or a malicious adversary. A central contribution is characterizing which policy profiles can actually be installed as the unique equilibrium. The paper supplies both necessary and sufficient conditions, making feasibility an explicit part of the problem rather than assuming every requested modification can succeed.

For constructing a modification, the authors propose an efficient algorithm that solves a convex optimization problem with linear constraints and then applies a random perturbation. The resulting modification plan has near-optimal cost. This combines a characterization of attainable outcomes with a procedure for approaching the cheapest reward change that achieves the specified equilibrium and value requirements.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes feasible equilibrium-changing reward modifications and constructs near-minimum-cost plans for zero-sum Markov games.

title: Minimally Modifying a Markov Game to Achieve Any Nash Equilibrium and Value

abstract: Fine-tuning pretrained large models to downstream tasks is an important problem, which however suffers from huge memory overhead due to large-scale parameters. This work strives to reduce memory overhead in fine-tuning from perspectives of activation function and layer normalization. To this end, we propose the Approximate Backpropagation (Approx-BP) theory, which provides the theoretical feasibility of decoupling the forward and backward passes. We apply our Approx-BP theory to backpropagation training and derive memory-efficient alternatives of GELU and SiLU activation functions, which use derivative functions of ReLUs in the backward pass while keeping their forward pass unchanged. In addition, we introduce a Memory-Sharing Backpropagation strategy, which enables the activation memory to be shared by two adjacent layers, thereby removing activation memory usage redundancy. Our method neither induces extra computation nor reduces training efficiency. We conduct extensive experiments with pretrained vision and language models, and the results demonstrate that our proposal can reduce up to $\sim$$30%$ of the peak memory usage. Our code is released at github.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning large pretrained models requires substantial memory. This paper targets memory associated with activation functions and layer normalization, examining how backpropagation can be changed to reduce that overhead. Its approach combines a theoretical basis for using different forward and backward computations with a strategy for sharing stored activations.

Approximate Backpropagation provides a feasibility argument for decoupling the two passes. The resulting alternatives to GELU and SiLU preserve their forward computations but use ReLU derivative functions during the backward pass. Memory-Sharing Backpropagation then allows two adjacent layers to share activation memory, removing redundant storage. These mechanisms address how training computations use and retain intermediate information.

Experiments on pretrained vision and language models show peak memory reductions of up to approximately 30%. The authors also report that the method adds no computation and does not reduce training efficiency. The result supports changing backward computations and sharing activations as useful ways to lower fine-tuning memory requirements. The reported memory saving is a maximum observed reduction across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Approximate activation gradients and shared activation storage reduce fine-tuning peak memory by up to about 30% without reported training-efficiency loss.

title: Reducing Fine-Tuning Memory Overhead by Approximate and Memory-Sharing Backpropagation

abstract: Using multiple input streams simultaneously to train multimodal neural networks is intuitively advantageous but practically challenging. A key challenge is unimodal bias, where a network overly relies on one modality and ignores others during joint training. We develop a theory of unimodal bias with multimodal deep linear networks to understand how architecture and data statistics influence this bias. This is the first work to calculate the duration of the unimodal phase in learning as a function of the depth at which modalities are fused within the network, dataset statistics, and initialization. We show that the deeper the layer at which fusion occurs, the longer the unimodal phase. A long unimodal phase can lead to a generalization deficit and permanent unimodal bias in the overparametrized regime. Our results, derived for multimodal linear networks, extend to nonlinear networks in certain settings. Taken together, this work illuminates pathologies of multimodal learning under joint training, showing that late and intermediate fusion architectures can give rise to long unimodal phases and permanent unimodal bias. Our code is available at: https://yedizhang.github.io/unimodal-bias.html.

paragraphs: Training on several input modalities does not ensure that a network will use all of them. It may rely heavily on one stream while neglecting the others, producing unimodal bias. This paper develops a theory using multimodal deep linear networks to explain how architecture, dataset statistics, and initialization influence that behavior.

The authors calculate how long the unimodal learning phase lasts as a function of those factors, including the depth at which modalities are fused. Their analysis shows that fusing streams deeper in the network lengthens this phase. This connects an architectural decision about where information meets to the timing of how different modalities are learned.

A prolonged unimodal phase can cause weaker generalization and permanent unimodal bias in the overparameterized regime. Although the core results concern linear networks, they extend to nonlinear networks in certain settings. The findings identify a possible training pathology of late and intermediate fusion: combining modalities deeper can leave learning dominated by one stream for a long time.
summary.tldr: A theory of multimodal linear networks links deeper fusion to longer unimodal learning phases that can impair generalization and become permanent.

title: Understanding Unimodal Bias in Multimodal Deep Linear Networks

abstract: Despite advancing language model (LM) alignment, direct preference optimization (DPO) falls short in LM reasoning with the free lunch from reinforcement learning (RL). As the breakthrough, this work proposes a new RL-free preference optimization method aiming to achieve DPO along with learning another LM, whose response generation policy holds the asymptotic equivalence with AlphaZero-like search, the apex of algorithms for complex reasoning missions like chess Go. While circumventing explicit value and reward modeling, the neural implicit tree search executed by the extra LM remains seeking to equip DPO with reasoning procedure technically akin to AlphaZero. Our experiments demonstrate that our methodology outperforms both regular DPO variants in human preference alignment, and MCTS-based LMs in mathematical reasoning and planning tasks.

paragraphs: Direct preference optimization trains language models using preferences between responses, but the paper argues that its alignment benefits do not fully provide the reasoning advantages associated with reinforcement learning. The proposed method aims to combine preference optimization with a search-like response-generation process while remaining free of reinforcement learning.

The approach learns an additional language model alongside the preference optimization procedure. Its response-generation policy has a stated asymptotic equivalence to AlphaZero-like search, allowing the authors to frame it as neural implicit tree search. The method avoids explicit value and reward models. The asymptotic qualification is central: the theoretical connection describes a limiting relationship between policies.

Experiments evaluate both preference alignment and reasoning. The method outperforms regular DPO variants in human preference alignment and language models using Monte Carlo tree search on mathematical reasoning and planning tasks. These results support the proposed combination of preference learning and implicit search behavior, with the theoretical connection explaining why the additional model is relevant to reasoning.
summary.tldr: An RL-free preference method learns an additional language model whose generation policy is asymptotically equivalent to AlphaZero-like search.

title: Language Models as Implicit Tree Search

abstract: Crystalline materials often exhibit a high level of symmetry. However, most generative models do not account for symmetry, but rather model each atom without any constraints on its position or element. We propose a generative model, Wyckoff Diffusion (WyckoffDiff), which generates symmetry-based descriptions of crystals. This is enabled by considering a crystal structure representation that encodes all symmetry, and we design a novel neural network architecture which enables using this representation inside a discrete generative model framework. In addition to respecting symmetry by construction, the discrete nature of our model enables fast generation. We additionally present a new metric, Fréchet Wrenformer Distance, which captures the symmetry aspects of the materials generated, and we benchmark WyckoffDiff against recently proposed generative models for crystal generation. As a proof-of-concept study, we use WyckoffDiff to find new materials below the convex hull of thermodynamical stability.

paragraphs: Crystal structures often contain substantial symmetry, yet many generative models describe atoms without constraining their positions or elements through that symmetry. WyckoffDiff instead generates symmetry-based descriptions of crystals. Its representation encodes all symmetry, making symmetry a built-in part of the generated description.

The authors develop a neural-network architecture that makes this representation usable within a discrete generative framework. The model respects symmetry by construction, and its discrete formulation enables fast generation. That demonstration connects symmetry-aware generation with a materials-discovery objective. The contribution spans representation, architecture, and evaluation, treating crystal symmetry as a core modeling requirement throughout.
summary.tldr: WyckoffDiff generates symmetry-respecting crystal descriptions and demonstrates a proof-of-concept search for materials below the thermodynamic stability convex hull.

title: WyckoffDiff – A Generative Diffusion Model for Crystal Symmetry

abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have raised concerns about generating inappropriate content, such as "nudity". Despite efforts to erase undesirable concepts through unlearning techniques, these unlearned models remain vulnerable to adversarial inputs that can potentially regenerate such content. To safeguard unlearned models, we propose a novel inference-time defense strategy that mitigates the impact of adversarial inputs. Specifically, we first reformulate the challenge of ensuring robustness in unlearned diffusion models as a robust regression problem. Building upon the naive median smoothing for regression robustness, which employs isotropic Gaussian noise, we develop a generalized median smoothing framework that incorporates anisotropic noise. Based on this framework, we introduce a token-wise Adaptive Median Smoothing method that dynamically adjusts noise intensity according to each token’s relevance to target concepts. Furthermore, to improve inference efficiency, we explore implementations of this adaptive method at the text-encoding stage. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach enhances adversarial robustness while preserving model utility and inference efficiency, outperforming baseline defense techniques.

paragraphs: Removing an unwanted concept from a text-to-image model does not necessarily prevent adversarial prompts from bringing it back. This paper studies that vulnerability in models that have already undergone unlearning. Its contribution is a defense applied during inference, aimed at reducing the effect of adversarial inputs while keeping the model useful for ordinary generation.

The authors formulate the robustness problem as robust regression and extend median smoothing. The starting approach uses isotropic Gaussian noise, which treats directions uniformly. Their generalized framework permits anisotropic noise, allowing perturbations to vary across directions. The resulting Adaptive Median Smoothing method adjusts noise intensity separately for each token according to its relevance to the concepts targeted for removal.

This adaptive treatment makes concept relevance part of the defense itself. The authors also explore applying the method during text encoding to improve inference efficiency. Their experiments report stronger adversarial robustness than baseline defenses while preserving utility and efficiency. These findings support the method as an additional safeguard for unlearned models, rather than establishing that unwanted content becomes impossible to generate.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Median Smoothing varies noise by token relevance to improve the adversarial robustness of unlearned image generators at inference time.

title: Adaptive Median Smoothing: Adversarial Defense for Unlearned Text-to-Image Diffusion Models at Inference Time

abstract: Time series forecasting fundamentally relies on accurately modeling complex interdependencies and shared patterns within time series data. Recent advancements, such as Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks (STGNNs) and Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), have demonstrated promising results by effectively capturing intricate spatial and temporal dependencies across diverse real-world datasets. However, these models typically require large volumes of training data and often struggle in data-scarce scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose a framework named Few-shot Spatio-Temporal Large Language Models (FSTLLM), aimed at enhancing model robustness and predictive performance in few-shot settings. FSTLLM leverages the contextual knowledge embedded in Large Language Models (LLMs) to provide reasonable and accurate predictions. In addition, it supports the seamless integration of existing forecasting models to further boost their predicative capabilities. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the adaptability and consistently superior performance of FSTLLM over major baseline models by a significant margin. Our code is available at: https://github.com/JIANGYUE61610306/FSTLLM.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting requires recognizing patterns over time and relationships among the series being predicted. The paper focuses on situations with little training data, where spatio-temporal graph networks and time-series foundation models can struggle despite their strengths on larger datasets. FSTLLM is designed to improve forecasting robustness and predictive performance in these few-shot settings.

The framework draws on contextual knowledge already embedded in large language models to support predictions. This brings pretrained model knowledge into a forecasting problem where task-specific observations are scarce. FSTLLM also supports integration with existing forecasting models, allowing the framework to augment their predictive capabilities within the same approach.

Experiments on real-world datasets report consistently superior performance over major baselines by a significant margin, along with adaptability across the evaluated data. The stated contribution is therefore a framework for making forecasting more effective when examples are limited. Its support for existing forecasters also matters practically: the approach can build on forecasting models already used to capture spatial and temporal dependencies.
summary.tldr: FSTLLM uses pretrained language-model knowledge to improve spatio-temporal forecasting when training data are scarce.

title: FSTLLM: Spatio-Temporal LLM for Few Shot Time Series Forecasting

abstract: While Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate impressive abilities over high-level perception and reasoning, their robustness in the wild remains limited, often falling short on tasks that are intuitive and effortless for humans. We examine the hypothesis that these deficiencies stem from the absence of core knowledge—rudimentary cognitive abilities innate to humans from early childhood. To explore the core knowledge representation in MLLMs, we introduce CoreCognition, a large-scale benchmark encompassing 12 core knowledge concepts grounded in developmental cognitive science. We evaluate 230 models with 11 different prompts, leading to a total of 2,530 data points for analysis. Our experiments uncover four key findings, collectively demonstrating core knowledge deficits in MLLMs: they consistently underperform and show reduced, or even absent, scalability on low-level abilities relative to high-level ones. Finally, we propose Concept Hacking, a novel controlled evaluation method, that reveals MLLMs fail to progress toward genuine core knowledge understanding, but instead rely on shortcut learning as they scale. Project page at https://williamium3000.github.io/core-knowledge/.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can perform impressive high-level tasks while struggling with abilities that humans find intuitive. This paper investigates whether those difficulties reflect deficits in core knowledge: basic cognitive abilities present early in human development. It makes those abilities an explicit evaluation target.

The authors introduce CoreCognition, a large benchmark covering 12 concepts drawn from developmental cognitive science. They evaluate 230 models using 11 prompts, producing 2,530 data points for analysis. The experiments find that models underperform on low-level abilities and that scaling produces weaker, or sometimes absent, improvements on those abilities compared with high-level ones.

The paper also introduces Concept Hacking, a controlled evaluation method intended to distinguish conceptual understanding from shortcut learning. Its results indicate that the evaluated models increasingly rely on shortcuts rather than progressing toward genuine core knowledge understanding as they scale. These findings question whether improvements on sophisticated tasks necessarily indicate stronger basic cognition, and provide a focused way to examine that gap.
summary.tldr: CoreCognition finds persistent basic cognitive deficits in multimodal models, with controlled evaluations indicating shortcut learning as models scale.

title: Core Knowledge Deficits in Multi-Modal Language Models

abstract: Large Language Models’ safety-aligned behaviors, such as refusing harmful queries, can be represented by linear directions in activation space. Previous research modeled safety behavior with a single direction, limiting mechanistic understanding to an isolated safety feature. In this work, we discover that safety-aligned behavior is jointly controlled by multi-dimensional directions. Namely, we study the vector space of representation shifts during safety fine-tuning on Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks. By studying orthogonal directions in the space, we first find that a dominant direction governs the model’s refusal behavior, while multiple smaller directions represent distinct and interpretable features like hypothetical narrative and role-playing. We then measure how different directions promote or suppress the dominant direction, showing the important role of secondary directions in shaping the model’s refusal representation. Finally, we demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens in harmful queries can mitigate these directions to bypass the learned safety capability, providing new insights on understanding safety alignment vulnerability from a multi-dimensional perspective.

Finally, we demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens in harmful queries can mitigate these directions to bypass the learned safety capability, providing new insights on understanding safety alignment vulnerability from a multi-dimensional perspective.

This paper examines representation changes during safety fine-tuning of Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks and finds a multidimensional structure underlying the resulting safety-aligned behavior.

By analyzing orthogonal directions, the authors identify a dominant direction governing refusal and several smaller directions associated with interpretable features, including hypothetical narratives and role-playing. They then measure how these secondary directions promote or suppress the dominant one. This shows that refusal behavior depends on interactions among multiple representational features in the studied model.

The authors also demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens from harmful queries can weaken these directions and bypass the learned safety behavior. This finding links the internal representation analysis to an observed vulnerability. The contribution is a more detailed mechanistic account of alignment in this setting: secondary features can shape refusal even when one direction appears to dominate the overall behavior.
summary.tldr: An analysis of safety-tuned Llama 3 8B finds that multiple interacting activation directions shape refusal and help explain alignment vulnerabilities.

title: The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Orthogonal Safety Directions

abstract: We introduce PaperBench, a benchmark evaluating the ability of AI agents to replicate state-of-the-art AI research. Agents must replicate 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight and Oral papers from scratch, including understanding paper contributions, developing a codebase, and successfully executing experiments. For objective evaluation, we develop rubrics that hierarchically decompose each replication task into smaller sub-tasks with clear grading criteria. In total, PaperBench contains 8,316 individually gradable tasks. Rubrics are co-developed with the author(s) of each ICML paper for accuracy and realism. To enable scalable evaluation, we also develop an LLM-based judge to automatically grade replication attempts against rubrics, and assess our judge’s performance by creating a separate benchmark for judges. We evaluate several frontier models on PaperBench, finding that the best-performing tested agent, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) with open-source scaffolding, achieves an average replication score of 21.0%. Finally, we recruit top ML PhDs to attempt a subset of PaperBench, finding that models do not yet outperform the human baseline. We open-source our code (https://github.com/openai/preparedness) to facilitate future research in understanding the AI engineering capabilities of AI agents.

title: PaperBench: Evaluating AI’s Ability to Replicate AI Research

abstract: In online platforms, incentives (e.g., discounts, coupons) are used to boost user engagement and revenue. Uplift modeling methods are developed to estimate user responses from observational data, often incorporating distribution balancing to address selection bias. However, these methods are limited by in-distribution testing data, which mirrors the training data distribution. In reality, user features change continuously due to time, geography, and other factors, especially on complex online marketing platforms. Thus, effective uplift modeling method for out-of-distribution data is crucial. To address this, we propose a novel uplift modeling method Invariant Deep Uplift Modeling, namely IDUM, which uses invariant learning to enhance out-of-distribution generalization by identifying causal factors that remain consistent across domains. IDUM further refines these features into necessary and sufficient factors and employs a masking component to reduce computational costs by selecting the most informative invariant features. A balancing discrepancy component is also introduced to mitigate selection bias in observational data. We conduct extensive experiments on public and real-world datasets to demonstrate IDUM’s effectiveness in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios in online marketing. Furthermore, we also provide theoretical analysis and related proofs to support our IDUM’s generalizability.

The stated findings suggest that stable causal features can help incentive-response models remain useful as the conditions around an online marketing platform change.
summary.tldr: IDUM combines invariant causal features and bias balancing to improve incentive-response modeling across changing user distributions.

title: Invariant Deep Uplift Modeling for Incentive Assignment in Online Marketing via Probability of Necessity and Sufficiency

abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) lies at the heart of a plethora of applications involving the interaction of a group of agents in a shared unknown environment. A prominent framework for studying MARL is Markov games, with the goal of finding various notions of equilibria in a sample-efficient manner, such as the Nash equilibrium (NE) and the coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE). However, existing sample-efficient approaches either require tailored uncertainty estimation under function approximation, or careful coordination of the players. In this paper, we propose a novel model-based algorithm, called VMG, that incentivizes exploration via biasing the empirical estimate of the model parameters towards those with a higher collective best-response values of all the players when fixing the other players’ policies, thus encouraging the policy to deviate from its current equilibrium for more exploration. VMG is oblivious to different forms of function approximation, and permits simultaneous and uncoupled policy updates of all players. Theoretically, we also establish that VMG achieves a near-optimal regret for finding both the NEs of two-player zero-sum Markov games and CCEs of multi-player general-sum Markov games under linear function approximation in an online environment, which nearly match their counterparts with sophisticated uncertainty quantification.

paragraphs: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents must learn about a shared unknown environment while responding to one another. Markov games formalize this problem, with learning often aimed at reaching an equilibrium efficiently. Existing sample-efficient methods can require specialized uncertainty estimates for the chosen function approximation or carefully coordinated updates among players.

VMG encourages exploration by changing how the environment model is estimated. It favors model parameters with larger collective best-response values: values reflecting how well each player could do when the others' policies are fixed. This bias encourages departures from the current equilibrium to gather more information. The algorithm permits simultaneous, uncoupled policy updates and does not require a separate design for each form of function approximation.

Within that setting, VMG achieves near-optimal regret for finding Nash equilibria in two-player zero-sum games and coarse correlated equilibria in multiplayer general-sum games. Its bounds nearly match those obtained using more elaborate uncertainty quantification, supporting model-estimation bias as an efficient exploration mechanism.
summary.tldr: VMG encourages multi-agent exploration through biased model estimation and achieves near-optimal regret guarantees under linear function approximation.

title: Incentivize without Bonus: Provably Efficient Model-based Online Multi-agent RL for Markov Games

abstract: Inferring properties of graph-structured data, e.g., the solubility of molecules, essentially involves learning the implicit mapping from graphs to their properties. This learning process is often costly for graph property learners like Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). To address this, we propose a paradigm called Graph Nonparametric Teaching (GraNT) that reinterprets the learning process through a novel nonparametric teaching perspective. Specifically, the latter offers a theoretical framework for teaching implicitly defined (i.e., nonparametric) mappings via example selection. Such an implicit mapping is realized by a dense set of graph-property pairs, with the GraNT teacher selecting a subset of them to promote faster convergence in GCN training. By analytically examining the impact of graph structure on parameter-based gradient descent during training, and recasting the evolution of GCNs—shaped by parameter updates—through functional gradient descent in nonparametric teaching, we show for the first time that teaching graph property learners (i.e., GCNs) is consistent with teaching structure-aware nonparametric learners. These new findings readily commit GraNT to enhancing learning efficiency of the graph property learner, showing significant reductions in training time for graph-level regression (-36.62%), graph-level classification (-38.19%), node-level regression (-30.97%) and node-level classification (-47.30%), all while maintaining its generalization performance.

summary.tldr: GraNT uses a theoretically grounded teaching strategy to select graph examples and reduce training time while maintaining generalization performance.

title: Nonparametric Teaching for Graph Property Learners

abstract: Koopman operator theory provides a framework for nonlinear dynamical system analysis and time-series forecasting by mapping dynamics to a space of real-valued measurement functions, enabling a linear operator representation. Despite the advantage of linearity, the operator is generally infinite-dimensional. Therefore, the objective is to learn measurement functions that yield a tractable finite-dimensional Koopman operator approximation. In this work, we establish a connection between Koopman operator approximation and linear Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which have recently demonstrated remarkable success in sequence modeling. We show that by considering an extended state consisting of lagged observations, we can establish an equivalence between a structured Koopman operator and linear RNN updates. Building on this connection, we present SKOLR, which integrates a learnable spectral decomposition of the input signal with a multilayer perceptron (MLP) as the measurement functions and implements a structured Koopman operator via a highly parallel linear RNN stack. Numerical experiments on various forecasting benchmarks and dynamical systems show that this streamlined, Koopman-theory-based design delivers exceptional performance. Our code is available at: https://github.com/networkslab/SKOLR.

Its practical difficulty is that this operator is generally infinite-dimensional. A forecasting model therefore needs measurement functions that support a manageable finite-dimensional approximation while retaining useful information about the dynamics.

The paper connects that approximation problem to linear recurrent neural networks. By extending the state to include lagged observations, the authors establish an equivalence between a structured Koopman operator and linear recurrent updates. title: SKOLR: Structured Koopman Operator Linear RNN for Time-Series Forecasting

abstract: While likelihood-based generative models, particularly diffusion and autoregressive models, have achieved remarkable fidelity in visual generation, the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) objective, which minimizes the forward KL divergence, inherently suffers from a mode-covering tendency that limits the generation quality under limited model capacity. In this work, we propose Direct Discriminative Optimization (DDO) as a unified framework that integrates likelihood-based generative training and GAN-type discrimination to bypass this fundamental constraint by exploiting reverse KL and self-generated negative signals. Our key insight is to parameterize a discriminator implicitly using the likelihood ratio between a learnable target model and a fixed reference model, drawing parallels with the philosophy of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Unlike GANs, this parameterization eliminates the need for joint training of generator and discriminator networks, allowing for direct, efficient, and effective finetuning of a well-trained model to its full potential beyond the limits of MLE. DDO can be performed iteratively in a self-play manner for progressive model refinement, with each round requiring less than 1% of pretraining epochs. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DDO by significantly advancing the previous SOTA diffusion model EDM, reducing FID scores from 1.79/1.58/1.96 to new records of 1.30/0.97/1.26 on CIFAR-10/ImageNet-64/ImageNet 512$\times$512 datasets without any guidance mechanisms, and by consistently improving both guidance-free and CFG-enhanced FIDs of visual autoregressive models on ImageNet 256$\times$256.

summary.tldr: DDO improves visual generation by fine-tuning likelihood-based models with an implicit discriminator and self-generated negative examples.

title: Direct Discriminative Optimization: Your Likelihood-Based Visual Generative Model is Secretly a GAN Discriminator

abstract: ML attacks on Learning with Errors (LWE) with binary or small secrets only succeed on LWE settings with very simple secrets. For example, they can recover secrets with up to three non-zero bits when models are trained on not-reduced LWE data, and three non-zero bits in the ”cruel region” [9] when BKZ pre-processing is applied. We show that larger training sets and the use of repeated examples in the training data allow the recovery of denser secrets. We empirically observe a power-law relationship between model based attempts to recover the secrets, dataset size and repeated examples. We introduce a stepwise regression technique to recover the “cool bits” of the secret. Overall, these techniques allow for the recovery of denser binary secrets: up to Hamming weight $70$ (and $8$ cruel bits) for dimension $256$ $\log_2 q=20$ and $75$ (and $7$ cruel bits) for dimension $512$ $\log_2 q=41$ (vs $33$ and $63$ Hamming weight and $3$ cruel bits in previous works). We also demonstrate our methods’ effectiveness on denser ternary secrets, showing a substantial improvement over prior work.

Earlier attacks succeeded only on relatively simple secrets, including very few nonzero bits in the difficult region remaining after preprocessing. The authors investigate how training-data scale, repeated examples, and a separate recovery procedure extend that reach.

Larger training sets and repetition allow recovery of denser secrets. The authors empirically observe a power-law relationship involving model-based recovery attempts, dataset size, and repeated examples. summary.tldr: Larger datasets, repeated training examples, and stepwise regression enable ML attacks to recover denser LWE secrets in the tested settings.

title: Improving ML Attacks on LWE with Data Repetition and Stepwise Regression

abstract: Learning-based surrogates for partial differential equations have recently matched the accuracy of classical solvers while achieving orders-of-magnitude speedups, predominantly in fluid settings and structured geometries. In contrast, robust surrogates for deformable solids remain underexplored, despite the presence of nonlinear elasticity, plasticity, and transient behavior that challenge standard architectures. We introduce a multigrid graph neural network for solid mechanics that couples an encoder-processor-decoder backbone with a physics-informed coarsening strategy. Instead of downsampling via geometric heuristics, our method scores nodes using a residual-based measure of local physical activity and preferentially retains regions of high strain or stress concentration, allocating multiscale capacity where it is most needed. This preserves long-range interactions through hierarchical message passing while improving stability over long rollouts. We evaluate on multiple datasets covering linear, nonlinear, and transient regimes, and observe consistent gains in accuracy and rollout stability compared to standard sampling baselines. Our results highlight the importance of physics-informed coarsening for scalable surrogate modeling in solid mechanics.

paragraphs: Predicting how deformable solids behave requires handling effects such as nonlinear elasticity, plasticity, and change over time. The paper introduces a multigrid graph neural surrogate for solid mechanics. Its central question is how to simplify a graph at coarser scales without discarding physically important regions.

The model combines an encoder-processor-decoder architecture with coarsening guided by physical activity. A residual-based score identifies nodes associated with high strain or concentrated stress, and the method preferentially retains them. This directs multiscale modeling capacity toward active regions instead of selecting nodes solely through geometric heuristics. Hierarchical message passing preserves interactions across long distances.

Evaluations cover multiple datasets spanning linear, nonlinear, and transient behavior. Compared with standard sampling baselines, the approach consistently improves predictive accuracy and stability when predictions are rolled forward over time. The findings connect the choice of coarse representation to simulation quality: retaining physically consequential detail can help a hierarchical model represent both local activity and longer-range effects.
summary.tldr: Physics-guided graph coarsening preserves high-strain and high-stress regions, improving solid-mechanics prediction accuracy and rollout stability in experiments.

title: Physics-Informed Coarsening for Multigrid Graph Neural Surrogates

abstract: Evaluating conditional coverage remains one of the most persistent challenges in assessing the reliability of predictive systems. Although conformal methods can give guarantees on marginal coverage, no method can guarantee to produce sets with correct conditional coverage, leaving practitioners without a clear way to interpret local deviations. To overcome sample-inefficiency and overfitting issues of existing metrics, we cast conditional coverage estimation as a classification problem. Conditional coverage is violated if and only if some classifier can achieve lower risk than the target coverage. Through the choice of a (proper) loss function, the resulting risk difference gives a conservative estimate of natural miscoverage measures such as L1 and L2 distance, and can even separate the effects of over- and under-coverage, as well as handle non-constant target coverages. We call the resulting family of metrics excess risk of the target coverage (ERT). We show experimentally that the use of modern classifiers provides much higher statistical power than simple classifiers underlying established metrics like CovGap. Additionally, we use our metric to benchmark different conformal prediction methods. Finally, we release an open-source package for ERT as well as previous conditional coverage metrics. Together, these contributions provide a new lens for understanding, diagnosing, and improving the conditional reliability of predictive systems.

paragraphs: A prediction set can include the correct answer at the desired rate overall while behaving differently for particular inputs. Conformal prediction's marginal coverage guarantees address the overall rate, but evaluating these local differences remains difficult. This paper develops diagnostics for conditional coverage by translating the problem into classification.

The central result connects coverage violations to predictive performance: conditional coverage is violated exactly when some classifier can achieve lower risk than the target-coverage reference. The authors call the resulting metrics excess risk of the target coverage, or ERT. With an appropriate loss, the risk improvement conservatively estimates discrepancies measured by L1 or L2 distance. Different choices can distinguish excessive coverage from insufficient coverage and accommodate targets that vary across inputs.

Experiments show that modern classifiers give these diagnostics much greater statistical power than the simple classifiers behind established metrics such as CovGap. The authors also compare conformal methods and release a package containing ERT and earlier metrics. The contribution makes conditional reliability more measurable; it does not turn a coverage diagnostic into a conditional guarantee.
summary.tldr: ERT uses classification performance to detect and conservatively quantify local coverage errors in conformal prediction.

title: Conditional Coverage Diagnostics for Conformal Prediction

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) using chain-of-thought reasoning often waste substantial compute by producing long, incorrect responses. Abstention can mitigate this by withholding outputs unlikely to be correct. While most abstention methods decide to withhold outputs before or after generation, dynamic mid-generation abstention considers early termination of unpromising reasoning traces at each token position. Prior work has explored empirical variants of this idea, but principled guidance for the abstention rule remains lacking. We present a formal analysis of dynamic abstention for LLMs, modeling abstention as an explicit action within a regularized reinforcement learning framework. An abstention reward parameter controls the trade-off between compute and information. We show that abstaining when the value function falls below this reward strictly outperforms natural baselines under general conditions. We further derive a principled and efficient method to approximate the value function. Empirical results on mathematical reasoning tasks support our theory and demonstrate improved selective accuracy over existing methods.
originalAbstract: Large language models (LLMs) using chain-of-thought reasoning often waste substantial compute by producing long, incorrect responses. Abstention can mitigate this by withholding outputs unlikely to be correct. While most abstention methods decide to withhold outputs before or after generation, dynamic mid-generation abstention considers early termination of unpromising reasoning traces at each token position. Prior work has explored empirical variants of this idea, but principled guidance for the abstention rule remains lacking. We present a formal analysis of dynamic abstention for LLMs, modeling abstention as an explicit action within a regularized reinforcement learning framework. An abstention reward parameter controls the trade-off between compute and information. We show that abstaining when the value function falls below this reward strictly outperforms natural baselines under general conditions. We further derive a principled and efficient method to approximate the value function. Empirical results on mathematical reasoning tasks support our theory and demonstrate improved selective accuracy over existing methods.

paragraphs: A language model can spend substantial computation completing a long reasoning trace that ultimately leads to an incorrect answer. Dynamic abstention addresses this by allowing the model to stop partway through generation. This paper develops a formal basis for deciding when to quit, extending beyond rules that only decide whether to answer before or after the full response is generated.

The authors model abstention as an explicit action in a regularized reinforcement learning framework. A reward assigned to abstaining controls the trade-off between computation and information. Their rule compares the value of the current reasoning state with that reward and stops when the value falls below it. Under general conditions, they prove that this rule strictly outperforms natural baselines.

Because applying the rule requires a value estimate, the paper also derives an efficient approximation method. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks support the theory and show improved selective accuracy over existing approaches. Selective accuracy concerns correctness among responses the system chooses to provide, making the stopping decision part of the method’s performance rather than merely an after-generation filter.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning analysis yields a value-based rule for stopping unpromising reasoning traces, with improved selective accuracy in mathematical reasoning experiments.

title: Knowing When to Quit: A Principled Framework for Dynamic Abstention in LLM Reasoning

abstract: Distributional reinforcement learning (DRL) models the full return distribution rather than expectations, but extending it to multivariate settings remains challenging. Many common metrics do not naturally generalize beyond one dimension or lose computational tractability, and the multivariate case introduces additional difficulties such as general matrix discounting, for which no contraction results are available. We introduce Sliced Distributional Reinforcement Learning (SDRL), which lifts tractable one-dimensional divergences to multivariate return distributions via projections. We prove Bellman contraction for uniform slicing under shared scalar discounting, and introduce a maximum-slicing variant with contraction under general dense discount matrices. SDRL supports a broad class of base divergences; we analyze Wasserstein, Cramér, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), and characterize which SDRL variants suit the standard single-sample Bellman update used in distributional RL. We evaluate SDRL on a toy chain problem and a gridworld image-based environment as well as a subset of Atari games. Code is available at https://github.com/BaptisteDebes/SlicedDistributionalRL

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning models the range of possible returns rather than only their expected value. Extending it to several return dimensions creates difficulties: familiar distribution comparisons may become expensive or fail to generalize naturally. Matrix-valued discounting adds another challenge because the corresponding Bellman updates need suitable contraction guarantees.

Sliced Distributional Reinforcement Learning compares multivariate return distributions through one-dimensional projections. This preserves access to tractable one-dimensional divergences. The authors prove Bellman contraction for uniform slicing when dimensions share a scalar discount, and introduce a maximum-slicing version with contraction under general dense discount matrices. These are distinct results tied to different slicing and discounting settings.

The framework supports several underlying divergences, with detailed analysis of Wasserstein, Cramér, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy choices. The paper also determines which variants fit the standard single-sample Bellman update, connecting mathematical properties to how distributional learning is implemented. Evaluations cover a toy chain, an image-based gridworld, and a subset of Atari games, examining the framework in several settings.
summary.tldr: SDRL uses one-dimensional projections to compare multivariate return distributions, with contraction results for different slicing and discounting settings.

title: Multivariate Distributional Reinforcement Learning Using Sliced Divergences

abstract: Deep attribute graph clustering aims to learn discriminative node representations by leveraging both node attributes and graph topology to partition nodes into distinct clusters. Although substantial progress has been made in attribute-graph clustering in recent years, two key challenges remain: noisy edges in the original adjacency matrix degrade the quality of information propagation, and redundant feature information across different feature views hampers the learning of discriminative representations. To address these issues, we propose a self-supervised attribute graph clustering method based on topological reconstruction and correlation decorrelation. First, we reconstruct the graph topology by computing intersections between k-nearest neighbors and the original adjacency relationships, while simultaneously leveraging global semantic information from K-means clustering to filter out noisy nodes. This reconstructed topology effectively mitigates information redundancy during feature aggregation in Graph Neural Networks. Second, unlike existing augmentation-based contrastive methods, we treat the feature representations from an auto-encoder (AE) and a graph auto-encoder (GAE) as two complementary natural views. We then apply mutual information minimization and a decorrelation constraint to suppress redundant information between views, yielding more discriminative node representations. Extensive experiments on four widely-used graph datasets—ACM, DBLP, CITE, and AMAP—demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms six state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Clustering an attributed graph requires combining information about individual nodes with information about their connections. Noisy edges can spread misleading information, while overlapping feature representations can add redundancy. This paper addresses both problems through a self-supervised method that reconstructs graph connections and reduces redundancy between two learned views.

To reconstruct topology, the method intersects nearest-neighbor relationships with the original adjacency relationships. It also uses global information from K-means clustering to filter noisy nodes. These steps refine the structure used for graph-based feature aggregation. The goal is to make the information passed between nodes more useful for separating clusters.

The two feature views come naturally from an autoencoder and a graph autoencoder. Mutual-information minimization and a decorrelation constraint suppress redundant information between them, encouraging more discriminative representations. Across ACM, DBLP, CITE, and AMAP, the method consistently outperforms six leading baselines. The results support jointly improving the graph used for aggregation and the complementarity of the representations used for clustering.
summary.tldr: Reconstructing graph connections and reducing redundancy between feature views improves clustering across four evaluated graph datasets.

title: Discriminative Attribute Graph Clustering Through Topology-Guided Contrastive Learning

abstract: Transformer-based architectures have advanced sequence modeling in language and vision, yet general-purpose representation learning for heterogeneous multivariate time series remains underexplored. We introduce CHARM (Channel-Aware Representation Model), which incorporates channel-level textual descriptions into a Transformer encoder equivariant to channel order. CHARM is trained with a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) and a novel loss promoting informative, temporally stable embeddings; latent-space prediction encourages robustness to sensor noise while description-aware gating provides interpretability through learned inter-channel relationships. Across anomaly detection, classification, and short- and long-term forecasting, the learned embeddings achieve strong performance using only a linear probe. Performance is driven primarily by the JEPA objective and conditioning architecture, with text descriptions serving as channel identifiers for cross-dataset generalization.

paragraphs: Multivariate time series contain several channels whose identities and relationships can vary across datasets. CHARM learns representations for this heterogeneous setting by combining sensor sequences with textual channel descriptions. Its Transformer encoder is equivariant to channel order, meaning that rearranging channels produces a corresponding rearrangement of the representation rather than changing their identities.

Training uses a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, which predicts in representation space, together with a loss encouraging embeddings to remain informative and stable over time. Latent prediction encourages robustness to sensor noise. A gating mechanism conditioned on descriptions also exposes learned relationships between channels, providing a way to interpret how the model combines their information.

The learned embeddings support strong results using only a linear probe for anomaly detection, classification, and forecasting over short and long horizons. The authors attribute most of the performance to the predictive objective and conditioning architecture. Text descriptions mainly function as channel identifiers that support generalization across datasets, clarifying their role within the multimodal system.
summary.tldr: CHARM combines channel descriptions with predictive representation learning to produce useful, temporally stable embeddings for heterogeneous sensor data.

title: Giving Sensors a Voice: Multimodal JEPA for Semantic Time-Series Embeddings

abstract: We study a cooperative form of multi-agent reinforcement learning with state space dynamics and agent interaction controlled by an underlying graph. Each agent has a local state and action, the evolution of the local state depends only on the states and actions in the $1$-hop neighborhood defined by the graph. Structured dynamics of this type arise in various applications, including network resource allocation, co-operative games, epidemic control, and wireless scheduling. The global state-action space scales exponentially in the number of agents, so that computing global optimal policies is intractable in the worst-case. We study conditions under which it is possible to approximate the optimal policies by a local policy for each agent that depends only on states associated with nodes within its $m$-hop neighborhood. By controlling the propagation of influences via a Dobrushin-type stability matrix, we establish that globally optimal policies can be approximated by local policies with sub-optimality gap decaying exponentially in $m$.

paragraphs: In the cooperative multi-agent systems studied here, a graph determines which agents directly affect one another. Each agent has its own state and action, and its next state depends only on its immediate neighborhood. Even with this local transition structure, the combined state-action space grows exponentially as agents are added, making global optimization intractable in the worst case.

The paper asks when an agent can make a nearly optimal decision using only states within a limited graph radius. A policy with radius m can inspect nodes up to m hops away. The analysis uses a Dobrushin-type stability matrix to control how influences propagate through the network.

Under the established conditions, local policies approximate globally optimal policies with a suboptimality gap that decreases exponentially with neighborhood radius. This gives a quantitative reason to enlarge local information gradually: each increase in reach can sharply reduce the approximation error. The guarantee is conditional on controlled influence propagation; local state transitions alone are not presented as sufficient to make every cooperative decision problem locally solvable.
summary.tldr: Under conditions controlling influence propagation, neighborhood-based policies approximate globally optimal multi-agent decisions with error decreasing exponentially in neighborhood radius.

title: Local Policies for Graph-Structured Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Safe deployment of increasingly capable AI agents may require visibility into how they make decisions. Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring can detect misbehavior in today’s reasoning models, but this “monitorability” may be fragile under different training procedures, data sources, or continued system scaling. We propose three evaluation archetypes (intervention, process, and outcome-property), a new monitorability metric, and a broad evaluation suite. We show CoT monitoring outperforms action-only monitoring in practical settings, and that frontier models are generally—but not perfectly—monitorable. We study scaling trends with pre-training model size and inference-time compute, finding longer CoTs are typically more monitorable. We find that, for a fixed capability level, using a smaller model at higher reasoning effort can yield higher monitorability, at greater inference compute cost. We further find that increasing a weak monitor’s test-time compute when monitoring a strong agent improves monitorability, and giving the monitor access to the CoT both boosts monitorability and steepens the compute–to-monitorability scaling trend. Finally, we show monitorability can be improved by asking follow-up questions and giving the follow-up CoT to the monitor.

paragraphs: This paper asks how reliably a monitor can detect problematic agent behavior from a model's chain of thought. It treats monitorability as a property to measure because changes in training, data, or scale may affect it. The authors introduce intervention, process, and outcome-property evaluation archetypes, alongside a metric and broad evaluation suite.

Their evaluations find that inspecting chain of thought outperforms monitoring actions alone in practical settings. Frontier models are generally monitorable, though imperfectly, and longer reasoning traces are typically easier to monitor. At a fixed capability level, a smaller model using more reasoning effort can provide greater monitorability, with a corresponding increase in inference computation.

The monitor's own resources also matter. Giving a weak monitor more test-time computation improves its monitoring of a stronger agent. Access to the agent's reasoning improves both monitorability and how it scales with compute. Follow-up questions provide another route: sharing the resulting follow-up reasoning with the monitor improves detection visibility. These findings identify several empirical ways to strengthen oversight.
summary.tldr: A new evaluation suite finds that reasoning access, additional compute, and follow-up questions can improve agent monitorability, though monitoring remains imperfect.

title: Monitoring Monitorability

abstract: While the auto-bidding literature predominantly considers independent bidding, we investigate the coordination problem among multiple auto-bidders in online advertising platforms. Two motivating scenarios are: collaborative bidding among multiple bidders managed by a third-party bidding agent, and strategic bid selection for multiple ad campaigns managed by a single advertiser. We formalize this coordination problem as a theoretical model and investigate the coordination mechanism where only the highest-value bidder competes with outside bidders, while other coordinated bidders refrain from competing. We demonstrate that such a coordination mechanism dominates independent bidding, improving both Return-on-Spend (RoS) compliance and the total value accrued for the participating auto-bidders or ad campaigns, for a broad class of auto-bidding algorithms. Additionally, our simulations on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical result that coordination outperforms independent bidding. These findings highlight both the theoretical potential and the practical robustness of coordinated auto-bidding in online auctions.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether automated advertising bidders benefit from coordinating their participation in auctions. It considers bidders managed by a shared third-party agent and multiple campaigns controlled by one advertiser. These settings create a common coordination question: how should participants choose bids when their aggregate value and spending compliance matter?

The authors formalize a mechanism in which only the coordinated bidder with the highest value competes against outside bidders. Other members of the coordinated group refrain from competing. Their theoretical analysis shows that this mechanism dominates independent bidding for a broad class of auto-bidding algorithms, improving both total accrued value and Return-on-Spend compliance.

Simulations using synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical advantage. The findings indicate that coordination can improve outcomes for participating bidders or campaigns under the studied model and algorithms. The contribution connects a simple participation rule with both mathematical analysis and empirical support, showing how the decision about which coordinated bidder enters can affect the group's overall auction outcomes.
summary.tldr: Allowing only the highest-value coordinated bidder to compete improves group value and Return-on-Spend compliance for a broad class of auto-bidding algorithms.

title: On the Coordination of Value-Maximizing Bidders

abstract: A truly universal AI-Generated Image (AIGI) detector must simultaneously generalize across diverse generative models and varied semantic content. Current methods learn a single, entangled forgery representation, conflating content-dependent flaws with content-agnostic artifacts, and are further constrained by outdated benchmarks. We propose OmniAID, a novel framework centered on a decoupled Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture that separates: (1) semantic flaws across distinct content domains via Routable Specialized Semantic Experts, and (2) content-agnostic universal artifacts from content-dependent flaws via a Fixed Universal Artifact Expert. A two-stage training strategy first specializes experts independently with domain-specific hard-sampling, then trains a lightweight gating network for effective input routing. By explicitly decoupling "what is generated” (content-specific flaws) from "how it is generated” (universal artifacts), OmniAID achieves robust generalization. We also introduce Mirage, a large-scale, contemporary dataset comprising a modern training set and a challenging test set. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniAID surpasses existing detectors, establishing a new standard for AIGI detection against modern, in-the-wild threats.

paragraphs: Detecting generated images requires handling variation in both image content and the models that produced it. OmniAID addresses the problem that a single forgery representation can mix content-specific flaws with artifacts that appear independently of content. That entanglement makes it harder to generalize across both sources of variation.

The framework separates these signals using a mixture of experts. Specialized semantic experts handle flaws associated with different content domains, while a fixed universal artifact expert addresses content-independent generation traces. Training first specializes the experts independently using domain-specific hard sampling, then trains a lightweight gating network to route inputs effectively among the specialized components.

The authors also introduce Mirage, a contemporary dataset with a modern training set and a challenging test set. Experiments report that OmniAID outperforms existing detectors against modern, in-the-wild generated images. The findings support separating evidence about depicted content from evidence about the generation process, with routing providing a way to combine specialized detection capabilities.
summary.tldr: OmniAID separates content-specific flaws from content-independent artifacts to improve generated-image detection across diverse content and generators.

title: OmniAID: Decoupling Semantics and Artifacts for Universal AI-Generated Image Detection in the Wild

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with combinatorial action spaces remains challenging because feasible action sets are exponentially large and governed by complex feasibility constraints, making direct policy parameterization impractical. Existing approaches embed task-specific value functions into constrained optimization programs or learn deterministic structured policies, sacrificing generality and policy expressiveness. We propose a solver-induced latent spherical flow policy that brings the expressiveness of modern generative policies to combinatorial RL while guaranteeing feasibility by design. Our method, LSFlow, learns a stochastic policy in a compact continuous latent space via spherical flow matching, and delegates feasibility to a combinatorial optimization solver that maps each latent sample to a valid structured action. To improve efficiency, we train the value network directly in the latent space, avoiding repeated solver calls during policy optimization. To address the piecewise-constant and discontinuous value landscape induced by solver-based action selection, we introduce a smoothed Bellman operator that yields stable, well-defined learning targets. Empirically, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by an average of 20.6% across a range of challenging combinatorial RL tasks.

paragraphs: Combinatorial reinforcement learning involves choosing structured actions from an exponentially large set while satisfying feasibility constraints. Directly representing every valid choice is impractical. This paper introduces LSFlow, which separates learning a flexible distribution over choices from enforcing the constraints that make a structured action valid.

LSFlow learns a stochastic policy in a compact continuous latent space using spherical flow matching. A combinatorial optimization solver converts each latent sample into a feasible action, providing feasibility by design. The value network also operates directly in latent space, avoiding repeated solver calls during policy optimization and reducing the computational burden of learning.

Solver-based action selection creates another difficulty: changes in a latent input can leave the selected action unchanged and then suddenly switch it. The resulting value landscape is piecewise constant and discontinuous. LSFlow uses a smoothed Bellman operator to obtain stable, well-defined learning targets. Across the evaluated combinatorial tasks, it outperforms leading baselines by an average of 20.6%, supporting the combination of generative policy flexibility, solver-enforced constraints, and latent-space value learning.
summary.tldr: LSFlow learns expressive stochastic policies in a continuous latent space and uses an optimization solver to guarantee feasible combinatorial actions.

title: Latent Spherical Flow Policy for Reinforcement Learning with Combinatorial Actions

abstract: High-dimensional genomics studies are frequently confounded by unmeasured biological processes that obscure disease-specific signals. While existing workflows can estimate these latent confounders, they fail to quantify how robust a discovery is to varying levels of hypothetical confounding. We introduce sensGAN, a deep-learning adversarial framework that systematically explores the confounding spectrum by learning "worst-case" latent variables that nullify the most gene associations under novel predictive-gain constraints. By identifying the minimum confounding strength required to explain away an observed effect, our method shifts the paradigm toward a formal, quantitative sensitivity analysis. In diverse simulations, sensGAN accurately recovers latent structures and outperforms existing methods in identifying confounder-sensitive genes. Applied to human Alzheimer’s disease microglia, our framework prioritizes robust disease pathways while successfully isolating signals driven by unmeasured co-occurring neurodegenerative pathologies.

paragraphs: Genomic studies can associate genes with disease even when unmeasured biological processes help explain those associations. Estimating hidden confounders does not by itself reveal how vulnerable a discovery is to hypothetical confounding. sensGAN addresses this by asking how strong an unseen influence would need to be to explain away an observed effect.

The method uses adversarial learning to search for latent variables that remove as many gene associations as possible, subject to predictive-gain constraints. These constraints let it explore different levels of confounding strength. The resulting sensitivity analysis distinguishes associations that are easily explained away from those that withstand stronger hypothetical hidden influences.

In simulations, sensGAN recovers latent structures and improves identification of confounder-sensitive genes compared with existing methods. Applied to human Alzheimer's disease microglia, it prioritizes robust disease pathways and separates signals attributed to unmeasured co-occurring neurodegenerative pathologies. The contribution is a quantitative assessment of robustness to confounding, helping interpret which observed genomic signals remain convincing across the explored confounding spectrum.
summary.tldr: sensGAN learns worst-case hidden confounders to quantify how much confounding would be needed to explain away genomic associations.

title: High-Dimensional Sensitivity Analysis for Genomic Studies: An Adversarial Framework for Learning Worst-Case Latent Confounders

abstract: Monocular-to-stereo conversion synthesizes stereoscopic content from 2D videos for immersive 3D experiences. In modern Depth-Image-Based Rendering (DIBR) approaches, stereo inpainting of disocclusions is the critical bottleneck. Training-based methods achieve superior quality but rely on scarce stereo pairs or synthetic data with domain gaps. We address this through the first self-supervised framework learning from monocular videos via cycle consistency. Our key contribution is the Geometric Reciprocity Theorem (GRT): under the nearest-neighbor DIBR formulation, the disocclusion mask when synthesizing a target view equals the mask of pixels lost when warping back from target to source, enabling analytical computation of test-time disocclusion masks directly from monocular images. This yields train-test consistency for the stated warping formulation, supporting self-supervised learning from unlimited monocular videos and substantial improvements over training-free and supervised state-of-the-art methods. Project page: https://visual-ai.github.io/grt/

paragraphs: Converting a monocular video into stereo requires synthesizing another viewpoint. Moving the viewpoint exposes regions that were hidden in the original image, leaving gaps that need to be filled. Learning to fill these disocclusions usually relies on scarce stereo pairs or synthetic examples whose appearance can differ from real footage.

The paper develops self-supervision from monocular videos using a geometric cycle. Its Geometric Reciprocity Theorem states that, under nearest-neighbor depth-image-based rendering, the target-view disocclusion mask equals the mask of pixels lost when warping back to the source. This relationship makes the relevant disocclusion masks analytically computable from monocular images and connects the training construction to the masks encountered at test time.

That consistency supports learning from abundant monocular videos without requiring paired stereo footage. The authors report substantial improvements over training-free and supervised state-of-the-art methods. The theorem’s stated nearest-neighbor warping formulation is essential to interpreting the result: it establishes the geometric relationship under that formulation, providing the foundation for the self-supervised training approach.
summary.tldr: A geometric reciprocity result enables self-supervised stereo-video training from monocular footage under a specified nearest-neighbor rendering formulation.

title: Geometric Reciprocity: Unlocking Self-Supervision for Stereoscopic Video Generation

abstract: Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) seeks a low-rank approximation $X \approx UV^T$ with nonnegative factors and is commonly solved using interior methods that enforce feasibility throughout optimization. We show that such constraint-driven approaches can impede progress in the nonconvex landscape, leading to slow convergence or convergence to suboptimal stationary points. We propose an exterior framework for NMF (eNMF) that separates low-rank approximation from nonnegativity enforcement. Our method initializes from the optimal unconstrained factorization and introduces a rotation procedure that maps unconstrained factors to an exterior point closest to the nonnegative orthant. This viewpoint yields an algorithmic framework in which simple iterative updates converge to KKT-satisfying stationary points on the boundary of the positive orthant. The exterior formulation also enables a geometric interpretation of NMF solutions, clarifying equivalence classes of factorizations under permutation and orthogonal transformations. An intriguing numerical result, involving 400 NMF experiments across both real and synthetic datasets, show that in 99% of the cases, different algorithms tend to converge towards equivalent factor matrices. We benchmark eNMF against 9 state-of-the-art NMF algorithms with 9 initialization schemes across 3 real-world and 2 synthetic datasets. eNMF consistently outperforms all 81 competitors, achieving up to 30% lower reconstruction error under equal-time settings and up to 150% speedup under equal-error settings. The downstream experiments further demonstrate substantial performance gains in audio processing and recommendation tasks, corroborating the practical benefits of the proposed exterior optimization framework. Code is available at https://github.com/roychowdhuryresearch/eNMF

paragraphs: Nonnegative matrix factorization approximates a data matrix using smaller factors whose entries cannot be negative. Many algorithms enforce that restriction at every optimization step. This paper argues that staying inside the allowed region can obstruct progress, slowing convergence or steering the search toward less useful stationary points.

It starts with the optimal unconstrained factorization, then rotates the factors toward the nonnegative region. Its iterative updates converge to boundary stationary points satisfying the relevant constrained optimality conditions; this is not a guarantee of finding a global optimum.

Improvements in audio processing and recommendation suggest that its optimization benefits can carry through to downstream tasks.
summary.tldr: eNMF approaches nonnegative factorization from outside the feasible region, improving reconstruction quality and optimization speed in the reported experiments.

title: An Exterior Method for Nonnegative Matrix Factorization

abstract: Modern learning systems excel at interpolation but struggle to generalize to unseen tasks outside the training distribution’s support. This failure occurs even in simple settings, such as handling task parameters beyond the training range, and persists despite advances in foundation models. To this end, we develop the Relational Task Extrapolator (RTE), an algorithm designed to enable systematic extrapolation to novel tasks. The key observation is that extrapolation is inherently relational: extrapolating to unseen tasks requires learning how tasks transform into one another. If a model learns the transformation between tasks A and B during training, it can apply that same transformation to relate known tasks to unseen ones at test time. RTE operationalizes this idea by decomposing each target task into a known anchor task and a transformation linking the anchor and target. It then learns a relational operator, mapping an anchor–transformation pair to predictions for the target task. We instantiate RTE across multiple task extrapolation regimes in function prediction, e.g. where target tasks use out-of-range parameters (parameter extrapolation), has greater compositional depth (length extrapolation), and/or recombine function primitives in unseen ways (compositional extrapolation). We further extend RTE to sequence prediction, integrating it into fine-tuning algorithms for foundation models. Across empirical studies, we find that RTE substantially outperforms existing approaches on extrapolation to novel, unseen tasks.

The paper approaches this problem through relationships between tasks. Its central idea is that a learned transformation between familiar tasks can also help connect a familiar task to an unfamiliar one.

This makes the relationship between tasks an explicit component of prediction, providing a mechanism for reusing transformations outside the observed task range.

They also extend the approach to sequence prediction through foundation-model fine-tuning. Across their empirical studies, RTE substantially outperforms existing approaches on unseen-task extrapolation. These results support learning task transformations as a useful strategy across several distinct forms of extrapolation.
summary.tldr: RTE predicts unseen tasks by learning transformations that connect them to known anchor tasks.

title: Learning to Extrapolate to New Tasks: A Relational Approach to Task Extrapolation

abstract: LLM-based multi-agent simulations are increasingly adopted across application domains, but remain difficult to scale due to GPU memory pressure. Each agent maintains private GPU-resident states, including models, prefix caches, and adapters, which quickly exhaust device memory as the agent count grows. We identify two key properties of these workloads: sparse agent activation and an estimable agent invocation order. Based on an analysis of representative workload classes, we introduce invocation distance, a unified abstraction that estimates the relative order in which agents will issue future LLM requests. Leveraging this abstraction, we present ScaleSim, a memory-efficient LLM serving system for large-scale multi-agent simulations. ScaleSim enables proactive prefetching and priority-based eviction, supports diverse agent-specific memory through a modular interface, and achieves up to 1.74$\times$ speedup over SGLang on simulation benchmarks. ScaleSim’s source code is available at https://github.com/PanZaifeng/KVFlow.
