paragraphs: Large simulations involving many language-model agents can exhaust GPU memory because each agent carries private state. That state can include models, cached prefixes, and adapters. ScaleSim builds on two observed workload properties: only a sparse subset of agents is active at a time, and the order of future agent requests can be estimated.

The system summarizes that order using invocation distance, which estimates how soon an agent will issue a request relative to others. It uses these estimates to bring needed state into memory proactively and to prioritize which state to evict. A modular interface supports the different kinds of memory associated with individual agents.

On simulation benchmarks, ScaleSim achieves speedups of up to 1.74 times over SGLang. The result shows how information about simulation scheduling can inform memory management and improve serving performance. Its approach draws value from sparse activation and estimable request order: the GPU can prepare for likely upcoming work instead of treating every agent's state as equally urgent to retain.
summary.tldr: ScaleSim uses estimated agent request order to prefetch and evict GPU state, improving large-scale multi-agent simulation serving.

title: ScaleSim: Serving Large-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation with Invocation Distance-Based Memory Management

abstract: Stock markets are one of the most complex systems in the modern world, where prices emerge from billions of decentralized interactions among heterogeneous participants in an ever-evolving information landscape. While high-fidelity simulation is important for understanding market dynamics, existing approaches face a persistent trade-off between structural and behavioral fidelity. To this end, we propose MarketSim, a large-scale stock market simulation framework with generative agents. MarketSim introduces a hierarchical multi-agent architecture that decouples strategic reasoning from high-frequency execution, enabling LLM agents to operate in a nanosecond-resolution, NASDAQ-like continuous double auction market. Building on this, we simulate over 15,000 heterogeneous market participants whose interactions shape and are shaped by an evolving market environment grounded in more than 12k real-world news articles, policy documents, and earnings reports. To evaluate our proposed MarketSim, we develop a comprehensive benchmark that includes stocks from 8 GICS sectors and 3 representative real-world scenarios, along with 5 stylized facts for market complexity and 5 price-related statistical metrics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MarketSim not only captures key complexity properties of real-world markets, but also outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in tracking high-frequency price dynamics with an average MAPE of 3.48%, providing a scalable testbed for market analysis.

summary.tldr: MarketSim separates agent strategy from rapid execution to simulate over 15,000 participants and reproduce tested market dynamics.

title: MarketSim: Simulating Stock Markets with Large-Scale Generative Agents

abstract: Unpaired domain translation remains a challenging task due to the need of finding a balance between faithfulness and realism. In this paper, we propose a method called Regularized Distribution Matching Distillation (RDMD) that combines the best properties of Optimal Transport (OT) and diffusion-based domain translation methods. Instead of the conventional adversarial training, RDMD utilizes diffusion-based distribution matching, addressing the common shortcomings of OT methods and providing a strong initialization for the trained models. RDMD provides efficient one-step inference, explicitly controls the input-output alignment via regularization of the transport cost and maintains high faithfulness similar to the OT methods. We prove that in theory RDMD approximates the OT map and demonstrate its empirical performance on several tasks, including unpaired image-to-image translation in pixel and latent space and unpaired text detoxification. Empirical results show that RDMD achieves a comparable or better faithfulness-realism trade-off compared to the diffusion and OT baselines.

paragraphs: Unpaired domain translation learns to transform inputs without matched examples showing the desired output for each one. A successful transformation must preserve relevant input content while looking realistic in the destination domain. Regularized Distribution Matching Distillation, or RDMD, combines optimal-transport ideas with diffusion-based distribution matching to manage that balance.

RDMD replaces conventional adversarial training with a diffusion-based matching procedure that also provides a strong initialization. A transport-cost regularizer explicitly controls alignment between inputs and outputs. After training, the model performs translation in one inference step, combining efficient execution with a mechanism for encouraging faithfulness to the original input.

The authors prove a theoretical approximation relationship between RDMD and the optimal-transport map. They evaluate the method on unpaired image translation in both pixel and latent spaces, as well as unpaired text detoxification. The reported results show a faithfulness–realism trade-off comparable to or better than diffusion and optimal-transport baselines. This supports using diffusion-based training to obtain a fast translation model with explicit control over input preservation.
summary.tldr: RDMD combines diffusion-based training with transport-cost regularization to deliver one-step translation with a competitive faithfulness–realism trade-off.

title: One-step Optimal Transport via Regularized Distribution Matching Distillation

abstract: Few shot segmentation with vision foundation models relies on high quality prompts to segment unseen categories from limited support annotations. Existing prompt construction methods depend on test-time adaptation, fixed heuristic sampling, or monolithic reinforcement learning, making it difficult to balance semantic consistency, spatial coverage, and prompt credit assignment. To address these limitations, PromptPilot is proposed as a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for point prompt optimization with frozen DINOv2 and SAM. Prompt construction is formulated as sequential decision making, where feature and physical agents propose complementary prompt modifications, and a manager agent selects actions using SAM feedback and local marginal contribution. PromptPilot functions as an inference-time optimization strategy without parameter updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed game-theoretic approach improves segmentation performance and generalization, offering a principled solution for automated prompt engineering. The code is available at https://github.com/L-AILab/PromptPilot.

paragraphs: Few-shot segmentation asks a model to identify unfamiliar categories using limited annotated examples. For promptable vision models, success depends heavily on choosing good prompts. PromptPilot focuses on point prompts, where construction must balance semantic consistency, spatial coverage, and determining which changes actually improve the segmentation result.

The method organizes prompt optimization as a sequence of decisions made by multiple agents. Feature and physical agents propose complementary changes, and a manager selects actions using SAM’s feedback and the local marginal contribution of proposed modifications. This hierarchy gives distinct agents roles in exploring prompt changes and provides a mechanism for assigning credit to their effects.

PromptPilot uses frozen DINOv2 and SAM models and operates through inference-time prompt optimization without parameter updates. Its decision framework is developed using hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning. The experiments report improved segmentation performance and generalization, supporting the idea that coordinated prompt search can make better use of fixed foundation models when only a few support annotations are available.
summary.tldr: PromptPilot coordinates multiple agents to optimize point prompts for frozen vision models, improving few-shot segmentation without inference-time parameter updates.

title: PromptPilot: Game-Theoretic Multi-Agent Prompt Optimization for Segment Anything

abstract: Dynamical systems model trajectory data generated by fixed underlying dynamics, with applications ranging from biology to physics. Especially in scientific settings, dynamical systems are not generic but often exhibit symmetries imposed by physical laws, formalized through equivariance with respect to group actions. The identification problem concerns recovering the parameters of a system from observed trajectories. In this work, we study adaptive symmetry discovery for dynamical system identification and address how a system can be identified from a single trajectory when it is equivariant with respect to an unknown symmetry group. To this end, we first show that for known symmetries, the system can be identified from a significantly shorter single trajectory than in the generic setting, and we precisely characterize this improvement. We then consider the automatic symmetry discovery setting, proposing a method to learn the symmetry group directly from a single trajectory and incorporate it into the identification procedure, achieving the same optimal trajectory length as in the known-symmetry case. Our analysis relies on tools from group representation theory and the expander properties of Cayley graphs, and may be of independent interest for the study of symmetries in dynamical systems.

paragraphs: Identifying a dynamical system means recovering its governing parameters from an observed trajectory. Scientific systems often have symmetries: transformations of the system’s state that interact predictably with its evolution. This paper asks how much those symmetries can reduce the amount of trajectory data needed, including when the symmetry group is initially unknown.

The authors first analyze the case where the symmetry is supplied. They show that identification can require a significantly shorter single trajectory than in the generic setting and precisely characterize that improvement. They then develop a method that learns the symmetry group from the trajectory and incorporates the discovered structure into parameter identification.

In the analyzed setting, discovering the symmetry achieves the same optimal trajectory length as knowing it beforehand. This makes symmetry discovery part of the statistical efficiency result, rather than merely an additional descriptive output. The analysis combines group representation theory with expansion properties of Cayley graphs to explain how structural constraints enable identification from less observation.
summary.tldr: The proposed method discovers a dynamical system’s symmetry from one trajectory and matches the optimal trajectory length available when that symmetry is known.

title: Adaptive Symmetry Discovery for Dynamical System Identification

abstract: Graph Masked Auto-Encoder (GMAE) has emerged as a prevalent self-supervised paradigm, showing superior performance in graph learning. However, existing methods mainly emphasize reconstruction outcomes and give limited specification to how neighborhood context is used for reconstruction. Our experimental investigation shows that, even when reconstruction outcomes are similar, the ways of using neighborhood context differ substantially, resulting in performance shifts. To address this issue, we propose Consistency- and Coverage-aware Graph Masked Auto-Encoder (C2-GMAE), which encourages more consistent use of neighborhood context and promotes broader training coverage in the graph. Specifically, C2-GMAE leverages positional encoding as an observable structural reference, introduces density-partitioned masking to improve coverage across regions, and amplifies heterophilic edges to reduce the attenuation of discriminative relational information during reconstruction. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that C2-GMAE improves downstream performance against GMAE baselines.

paragraphs: Graph masked auto-encoders learn by reconstructing hidden information using graph context. This paper finds that similar reconstruction outcomes can conceal substantially different uses of neighboring information, with consequences for later tasks. It therefore focuses on the reconstruction process itself, including how consistently context is used and how broadly training covers the graph.

The proposed C2-GMAE makes three changes. Positional encoding provides an observable structural reference. Density-partitioned masking promotes coverage across graph regions. Amplifying heterophilic edges helps preserve discriminative relational information that might otherwise weaken during reconstruction. Together, these mechanisms address structural guidance, training coverage, and the retention of informative relationships.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks show improved downstream performance relative to graph masked auto-encoder baselines. The finding matters because successful reconstruction alone does not fully describe the quality of a learned representation. By explicitly shaping how neighborhood evidence contributes to reconstruction, C2-GMAE improves the usefulness of those representations for the evaluated downstream tasks.
summary.tldr: C2-GMAE improves graph representations by guiding neighborhood-context use, broadening masking coverage, and preserving informative heterophilic relationships.

title: Reconstruction Outcomes Look Similar but Processes Differ: Improving Context Consistency and Coverage in Graph Masked Auto-Encoder

abstract: Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics combined with Gibbs updates (SGLD-Gibbs) provides a highly scalable approach to approximate Bayesian inference in latent variable models. However, it remains unclear how to tune the algorithm’s hyperparameters in a principled manner to ensure the uncertainty estimates are statistically meaningful. In this work, we address this gap in tuning guidance by developing a statistical scaling limit theory for SGLD-Gibbs. We derive a joint asymptotic limit for the global parameters and latent variables under appropriate space-time rescaling. We show that global parameters converge to a diffusion-type limit, while individual latent variables converge to a jump process reflecting their intermittent Gibbs updates. This joint jump-diffusion structure reveals how latent-variable randomness contributes to the stationary distribution of the global parameters. We leverage our results to provide explicit guidance on hyperparameter tuning for SGLD-Gibbs that ensures meaningful uncertainty quantification. Our empirical results show that SGLD-Gibbs with our tuning guidance leads to better parameter estimates and uncertainty quantification than stochastic variational inference.

paragraphs: Combining stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics with Gibbs updates offers a scalable way to approximate Bayesian inference in models with latent variables. The practical difficulty is choosing hyperparameters so that the resulting uncertainty estimates remain statistically meaningful. This paper develops a scaling-limit theory to explain how the algorithm’s different sources of randomness interact and to turn that explanation into tuning guidance.

Under appropriate rescaling of space and time, the authors derive a joint limiting process for global parameters and individual latent variables. Global parameters approach a diffusion-type process, while latent variables approach a jump process because their Gibbs updates occur intermittently. The contribution connects scalable computation with statistical interpretation: it explains why tuning must account for latent updates as well as the evolution of global parameters.
summary.tldr: A joint jump-diffusion theory provides principled tuning guidance for scalable Bayesian uncertainty estimation with SGLD-Gibbs.

title: Large-scale Uncertainty Quantification for Latent Variable Models Using Subsampling Markov Chain Monte Carlo

abstract: Large language model(LLM)-driven multi-agent systems(MAS) coordinate specialized agents through predefined topologies and show promise for complex tasks such as competition-level code generation. Recent studies demonstrate that carefully designed multi-agent workflows and communication graphs can significantly improve code generation performance by leveraging collaborative reasoning. However, existing methods neither adapt topology density to task difficulty nor refine the topology within an instance using execution feedback, which leads to redundant communication and performance bottlenecks. To address these issues, we propose AgentConductor: a reinforcement learning-optimized MAS with an LLM-based orchestrator agent as its core, which enables end-to-end feedback-driven dynamic generation of interaction topologies. For each query, AgentConductor infers agent roles and task difficulty, then constructs a task-adapted, density-aware layered directed acyclic graph(DAG) topology, underpinned by two key innovations. First, we design a novel topology density function to quantify communication-aware multi-agent interactions. Second, we adopt difficulty interval partitioning to avoid excessive pruning for precise topological density upper bound measurement per difficulty level and finer-grained control. Across five code datasets, AgentConductor outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 14.6% in pass@1, with 13% lower topology density and 68% lower token cost.

paragraphs: AgentConductor studies how teams of language-model agents should communicate when solving competition-level coding problems. Fixed communication structures can create redundant exchanges, especially when they do not account for task difficulty or change in response to execution feedback. The paper makes the communication structure itself something the system can adapt.

An orchestrator trained with reinforcement learning infers useful agent roles and the difficulty of each query. It then constructs a layered directed acyclic graph describing agent interactions. A topology-density measure quantifies communication, while difficulty intervals help determine appropriate density upper bounds without excessively pruning the graph. These results support adapting agent interactions through feedback as a way to improve coding performance while reducing communication and token use.
summary.tldr: AgentConductor adapts multi-agent communication to coding-task difficulty and execution feedback, improving reported performance while reducing token cost.

title: AgentConductor: Topology Evolution for Multi-Agent Competition-Level Code Generation

abstract: Diffusion models trained on different, non-overlapping subsets of a dataset often produce strikingly similar outputs when given the same noise seed. We trace this consistency to a simple linear effect: the shared Gaussian statistics across splits already predict much of the generated images. To formalize this, we develop a random matrix theory (RMT) framework that quantifies how finite datasets shape the expectation and variance of the learned denoiser and sampling map in the linear setting. For expectations, sampling variability acts as a renormalization of the noise level through a self-consistent relation $\sigma^2\to\kappa(\sigma^2)$, explaining why limited data overshrink low-variance directions and pull samples toward the dataset mean. For fluctuations, our variance formulas reveal three key factors behind cross-split disagreement: anisotropy across eigenmodes, inhomogeneity across inputs, and overall scaling with dataset size. Extending deterministic-equivalence tools to fractional matrix powers further allows us to analyze entire sampling trajectories. The theory sharply predicts the behavior of linear diffusion models, and we validate its predictions on UNet and DiT architectures in their non-memorization regime, identifying where and how samples deviates across training data split. This provides a principled baseline for reproducibility in diffusion training, linking spectral properties of data to the stability of generative outputs.
originalAbstract: Diffusion models trained on different, non-overlapping subsets of a dataset often produce strikingly similar outputs when given the same noise seed. We trace this consistency to a simple linear effect: the shared Gaussian statistics across splits already predict much of the generated images. To formalize this, we develop a random matrix theory (RMT) framework that quantifies how finite datasets shape the expectation and variance of the learned denoiser and sampling map in the linear setting. For expectations, sampling variability acts as a renormalization of the noise level through a self-consistent relation $\sigma^2\to\kappa(\sigma^2)$, explaining why limited data overshrink low-variance directions and pull samples toward the dataset mean. For fluctuations, our variance formulas reveal three key factors behind cross-split disagreement: anisotropy across eigenmodes, inhomogeneity across inputs, and overall scaling with dataset size. Extending deterministic-equivalence tools to fractional matrix powers further allows us to analyze entire sampling trajectories. The theory sharply predicts the behavior of linear diffusion models, and we validate its predictions on UNet and DiT architectures in their non-memorization regime, identifying where and how samples deviates across training data split. This provides a principled baseline for reproducibility in diffusion training, linking spectral properties of data to the stability of generative outputs.

paragraphs: Diffusion models trained on separate portions of a dataset can produce remarkably similar images when started from the same noise. This paper investigates how much of that agreement follows from shared statistical structure. Its central explanation is a linear effect: Gaussian statistics common to the training splits already account for much of the generated output.

The authors develop a random matrix theory analysis of how finite training data affect a linear denoiser and its sampling process. Limited data effectively change the noise level, causing excessive shrinkage along directions with little variation and drawing samples toward the dataset mean. Their variance analysis separates disagreement into differences across data directions, differences across inputs, and dependence on dataset size.

The framework also analyzes complete sampling trajectories. It closely predicts linear diffusion behavior, and the authors validate predictions on UNet and DiT models in a regime without memorization. These results provide a principled baseline for understanding reproducibility: some agreement across training splits can arise from shared data statistics, while their spectral structure helps explain where outputs diverge.
summary.tldr: A random matrix analysis explains much cross-split diffusion consistency through shared Gaussian statistics and predicts how finite data affect generated outputs.

title: A Random Matrix Theory Perspective on the Consistency of Diffusion Models

abstract: In open-ended domains, natural language instructions are often underspecified, mapping to multiple valid yet functionally distinct latent intents. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at generation, their interactive disambiguation remains limited by semantic blindness: they may spend clarification turns distinguishing superficial syntactic variants rather than resolving substantive intent differences. We propose Topological Active Inference (TAI), a geometric framework that recasts task disambiguation as intent-manifold contraction. TAI uses Persistent Homology to recover persistent intent clusters from sampled solutions, filtering short-lived syntactic variations while preserving robust semantic structure under mild separability assumptions. It then synthesizes clarifying questions as semantic separators and selects them with Topological Expected Information Gain (TEIG), which optimizes uncertainty reduction over intent clusters rather than individual candidates. This reduces the effective hypothesis space from $N$ sampled solutions to $K$ latent intents and yields logarithmic interaction complexity $\mathcal{O}(\log K)$ under balanced-split conditions. Experiments across code, visualization, and navigation tasks show that TAI resolves user intent with fewer turns and remains robust to noisy feedback, and smaller model scales.

paragraphs: An underspecified instruction can correspond to several genuinely different user intentions, alongside many superficial ways of expressing the same solution. Topological Active Inference aims to spend clarification turns on the meaningful differences. It treats disambiguation as progressively narrowing a geometric representation of possible intents, rather than distinguishing every sampled candidate separately.

TAI applies persistent homology to sampled solutions to recover stable intent clusters while filtering short-lived syntactic variation. This recovery relies on mild separability assumptions. It generates questions that separate those clusters and chooses among them using Topological Expected Information Gain, which measures uncertainty reduction over intents. The effective search space therefore becomes K latent intents instead of N individual solutions.

Under balanced-split conditions, the framework yields logarithmic interaction complexity, O(log K). That condition matters: the bound depends on questions dividing the remaining possibilities in a balanced way. Experiments across coding, visualization, and navigation report fewer clarification turns and robustness to noisy feedback and smaller model scales. The findings support organizing clarification around substantive intent differences rather than surface diversity among possible answers.
summary.tldr: TAI groups candidate solutions into stable intents and selects clarifying questions that reduce uncertainty over those intents.

title: Topological Active Inference for Task Disambiguation

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promising results in automating formal verification. However, existing approaches treat proof generation as a static, end-to-end prediction over source code, relying on limited verifier feedback and lacking access to concrete program behaviors. We present ExVerus, a counterexample-guided framework that enables LLMs to reason about proofs using behavioral feedback via counterexamples. When a proof fails, ExVerus automatically generates and validates counterexamples, and then guides the LLM to generalize them into inductive invariants to block these failures. Our evaluation shows that ExVerus significantly improves proof accuracy, robustness, and token efficiency over the state-of-the-art prompting-based Verus proof generator.
originalAbstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promising results in automating formal verification. However, existing approaches treat proof generation as a static, end-to-end prediction over source code, relying on limited verifier feedback and lacking access to concrete program behaviors. We present ExVerus, a counterexample-guided framework that enables LLMs to reason about proofs using behavioral feedback via counterexamples. When a proof fails, ExVerus automatically generates and validates counterexamples, and then guides the LLM to generalize them into inductive invariants to block these failures. Our evaluation shows that ExVerus significantly improves proof accuracy, robustness, and token efficiency over the state-of-the-art prompting-based Verus proof generator.

paragraphs: A language model attempting a formal proof needs useful feedback when verification fails. ExVerus focuses on giving it concrete examples of program behavior that explain the failure. This addresses a weakness of approaches that predict proofs directly from source code and receive only limited feedback from the verifier.

When a proof fails, ExVerus automatically generates counterexamples and validates them. It then guides the language model to generalize those examples into inductive invariants: conditions intended to remain true as execution proceeds. The counterexamples ground this repair process in specific failures, while the invariants aim to rule out the broader patterns those failures reveal.

The evaluation reports significant improvements in proof accuracy, robustness, and token efficiency compared with a state-of-the-art prompting-based Verus proof generator. These results support using behavioral feedback to guide proof repair. The distinctive step is moving from a concrete failing case to a general condition that can help the verifier establish correctness, giving the model a more informative basis for its next proof attempt.
summary.tldr: ExVerus turns validated counterexamples into guidance for repairing Verus proofs, improving reported accuracy, robustness, and token efficiency.

title: ExVerus: Verus Proof Repair via Counterexample Reasoning

abstract: Generating diverse responses is crucial for test-time scaling of large language models (LLMs), yet standard stochastic sampling mostly yields surface-level lexical variation, limiting semantic exploration. In this paper, we propose Exploratory Sampling (ESamp), a decoding approach that explicitly encourages semantic diversity during generation. ESamp is motivated by the well-known observation that neural networks tend to make lower-error predictions on inputs similar to those encountered before, and incur higher prediction error on novel ones. Building on this property, we train a lightweight Distiller at test time to predict deep-layer hidden representations of the LLM from its shallow-layer representations to model the LLM’s depth-wise representation transitions. During decoding, the Distiller continuously adapts to the mappings induced by the current generation context. ESamp uses the prediction error as a novelty signal to reweight candidate token extensions conditioned on the current prefix, thereby biasing decoding toward less-explored semantic patterns. ESamp is implemented with an asynchronous training–inference pipeline, with less than 5% worst case overhead (1.2% in the optimized release). Empirical results show that ESamp significantly boosts the Pass@k efficiency of reasoning models, showing superior or comparable performance to strong stochastic and heuristic baselines. Notably, ESamp achieves robust generalization across mathematics, science, and code generation benchmarks and breaks the trade-off between diversity and coherence in creative writing. Our code has released at: https://github.com/LinesHogan/tLLM.

paragraphs: Generating multiple answers helps only when those answers explore meaningfully different possibilities. Standard stochastic sampling can change wording without changing the underlying approach. Exploratory Sampling, or ESamp, introduces a decoding signal intended to encourage semantic novelty by measuring how predictable a model's internal representations are.

A lightweight Distiller learns during test time to predict deep-layer representations from shallow-layer representations. It continually adapts to the current generation context. ESamp treats larger prediction errors as a novelty signal and uses them to adjust the weights of candidate next-token extensions. This biases generation toward semantic patterns that the Distiller has less successfully modeled.

An asynchronous training and inference pipeline keeps the reported worst-case overhead below 5%, with 1.2% in the optimized release. Experiments show improved Pass@k efficiency, meaning more effective use of multiple attempts, with superior or comparable results against strong sampling baselines. The reported benefits span mathematics, science, and code generation. Creative-writing results also show gains in diversity without the usual loss of coherence, supporting internal representation novelty as a useful decoding guide.
summary.tldr: ESamp uses an adapting predictor of hidden representations to steer generation toward semantic novelty and improve multi-attempt reasoning efficiency.

title: Large Language Models Explore by Latent Distilling

abstract: Maximum entropy has become a mainstream off-policy reinforcement learning (RL) framework for balancing exploitation and exploration. However, two bottlenecks still limit further performance gains: (1) non-stationary Q-value estimation stemming from the joint injection of entropy and the concurrent updating of its temperature parameter; and (2) short-sighted local entropy tuning, which adjusts temperature solely based on current single-step entropy without accounting for cumulative entropy over time. In this paper, we broaden the maximum entropy framework by proposing a trajectory entropy-constrained reinforcement learning (TECRL) framework to address these limitations. We begin by introducing reward-entropy separation (RES) to decouple the value targets, ensuring they remain stable and unaffected by temperature fluctuations. Subsequently, the resulting entropy Q-function is leveraged to explicitly quantify expected cumulative entropy, allowing for the enforcement of a trajectory entropy constraint (TEC) to govern long-term stochasticity. We instantiate this framework as DSAC-E, a practical off-policy algorithm that builds upon the latest distributional soft actor-critic. Extensive evaluations across 10 challenging tasks in locomotion, robotic manipulation, and vision-based driving domains demonstrate that DSAC-E consistently outperforms baselines in both cumulative returns and training stability.

paragraphs: Maximum-entropy reinforcement learning balances reward seeking with randomness in action selection. The paper identifies two difficulties: updating the entropy temperature can make value-estimation targets change, and tuning temperature from current-step entropy overlooks randomness accumulated over time. TECRL addresses both by separating reward and entropy estimation and constraining entropy across trajectories.

Reward-entropy separation decouples the value targets so that temperature fluctuations do not alter them. An entropy Q-function then estimates expected cumulative entropy, allowing the algorithm to regulate longer-term stochasticity. This gives entropy control a temporal scope beyond the uncertainty of the immediate action choice.

The authors implement the framework as DSAC-E, building on distributional soft actor-critic. Across ten tasks involving locomotion, robotic manipulation, and vision-based driving, DSAC-E consistently exceeds the evaluated baselines in cumulative returns and training stability. These results support the combination of temperature-independent value targets and trajectory-level entropy control as a practical improvement to off-policy reinforcement learning in the tested domains.
summary.tldr: TECRL separates reward and entropy estimation and regulates cumulative trajectory entropy to improve reinforcement learning performance and stability.

title: Mind Your Entropy: From Maximum Entropy to Trajectory Entropy-Constrained RL

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) must resolve conflicts when modalities provide contradictory information, a behavior we term "modality following". We propose a framework that decomposes this behavior into case-specific relative preference uncertainty and stable inherent preference. Across diverse MLLMs and benchmarks, the probability of following a modality consistently decreases as its relative preference uncertainty increases, a trend robust to alternative uncertainty indices. This regularity defines a "balance point” where modality preferences are evenly matched, offering a capability-disentangled measure of modality bias. Layer-wise probing further shows that ambiguous cases near the balance point trigger middle-to-late-layer "concept oscillations," where top predictions vacillate between modality-supported answers. Finally, we demonstrate the framework’s utility for preference steering through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). We find that data efficiency is governed by preference uncertainty: training on easy samples (where one modality dominates) fails to generalize, whereas targeting the identified “boundary cases" is essential for robust preference alignment and suppressing internal vacillation.

paragraphs: When an image and accompanying text imply different answers, a multimodal model must decide which to follow. This paper separates that decision into two factors: a relatively stable preference for a modality and uncertainty specific to the current example. This distinction helps explain why observed choices cannot always be attributed to a fixed visual or textual bias.

Across the tested models and benchmarks, a modality becomes less likely to be followed as its relative preference uncertainty increases. The relationship persists with different uncertainty measures. The authors identify a balance point where neither modality is preferred, providing a way to measure bias separately from capability. Internal probing also reveals that ambiguous examples near this point produce alternating answer preferences in middle and later layers.

The framework informs supervised fine-tuning for steering preferences. In the reported experiments, easy examples with a clearly dominant modality do not generalize effectively. Targeting boundary cases is essential to the demonstrated robust alignment and reduces internal vacillation, connecting training-data selection to the model’s uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Modality choices depend on case-specific uncertainty as well as stable bias, and training on ambiguous boundary cases improves preference alignment.

title: Beyond Fixed Biases: Decoding the Role of Reasoning Uncertainty in MLLM Modality Conflicts

abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and its variants enable parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models under the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paradigm. However, their efficacy and behavior under Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) are less well understood. In particular, two structurally initialized LoRA variants, PiSSA and MiLoRA, which outperform standard LoRA under SFT, can underperform standard LoRA under RLVR and may even exhibit training instability. These observations suggest that how to initialize the low-rank matrices in RLVR remains unclear. In this work, we develop a theoretical analysis of LoRA in RLVR, showing that orthonormal initialization achieves the minimal gap between LoRA’s outcome and that of full fine-tuning. Guided by this insight, we propose geometry-preserving orthonormal initialization for low-rank adaptation in RLVR, leading to two new variants, LoRA-RLPO and LoRA-RLMO. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that our orthonormal initialization stabilizes RLVR training and outperforms standard LoRA, contrasting with PiSSA and MiLoRA. Finally, our unified analysis also explains why PiSSA and MiLoRA can underperform in RLVR, which may be of independent interest.
originalAbstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and its variants enable parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models under the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paradigm. However, their efficacy and behavior under Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) are less well understood. In particular, two structurally initialized LoRA variants, PiSSA and MiLoRA, which outperform standard LoRA under SFT, can underperform standard LoRA under RLVR and may even exhibit training instability. These observations suggest that how to initialize the low-rank matrices in RLVR remains unclear. In this work, we develop a theoretical analysis of LoRA in RLVR, showing that orthonormal initialization achieves the minimal gap between LoRA’s outcome and that of full fine-tuning. Guided by this insight, we propose geometry-preserving orthonormal initialization for low-rank adaptation in RLVR, leading to two new variants, LoRA-RLPO and LoRA-RLMO. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that our orthonormal initialization stabilizes RLVR training and outperforms standard LoRA, contrasting with PiSSA and MiLoRA. Finally, our unified analysis also explains why PiSSA and MiLoRA can underperform in RLVR, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation reduces the number of parameters updated during language-model fine-tuning, but its initialization can behave differently across training regimes. The paper observes that PiSSA and MiLoRA, which outperform standard LoRA in supervised fine-tuning, can do worse under reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. They may also become unstable, motivating a closer analysis of initialization in this setting.

The authors develop a theoretical account of LoRA under this reinforcement-learning regime. Their analysis shows that orthonormal initialization minimizes the gap between the outcome of low-rank adaptation and full fine-tuning. This finding motivates geometry-preserving initializations implemented in two variants, LoRA-RLPO and LoRA-RLMO. The same analysis also explains why the previously successful structured initializations can underperform here.

On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, the proposed initialization stabilizes training and improves performance over standard LoRA. These results show why initialization choices should be evaluated in the training regime where they will be used. Success under supervised learning does not, by itself, establish effectiveness under verifiable-reward reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: Orthonormal initialization brings LoRA closer to full fine-tuning in the paper’s analysis and improves stability and mathematical reasoning under RLVR.

title: Geometry-Preserving Orthonormal Initialization for Low-Rank Adaptation in RLVR

abstract: A new class of nonparametric algorithms for high-dimensional binary classification is proposed using cascades of low dimensional polynomial structures. Construction of polynomial cascadesis based on Minimax Probability Machine Classification (MPMC), which results in direct estimates of classificationaccuracy, and provides a simple stopping criteria that does not requireexpensive cross-validation measures. This Polynomial MPMC Cascade (PMC) algorithm is constructed in linear timewith respect to the input space dimensionality, and linear time in the numberof examples, making it a potentially attractive alternative to algorithms likesupport vector machines and standard MPMC. Experimental evidence is given showing that, compared to state-of-the-artclassifiers, PMCs are competitive; inherently fast to compute; not prone tooverfitting; and generally yield accurate estimates of the maximum error rateon unseen data.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a family of nonparametric methods for binary classification with many input features. The classifier is constructed as a cascade of low-dimensional polynomial structures. This organizes the high-dimensional classification problem around a sequence of smaller polynomial components and forms the basis of the Polynomial MPMC Cascade algorithm.

Cascade construction uses Minimax Probability Machine Classification. This supplies direct estimates of classification accuracy and a stopping criterion that avoids expensive cross-validation measures. The construction time is linear in the input dimensionality and linear in the number of examples, making the approach potentially attractive when either quantity is large.

The reported experiments find the cascades competitive with leading classifiers, fast to compute, and not prone to overfitting in the evaluated settings. Their estimates of the maximum error rate on unseen data are generally accurate. Together, these results support the method as a potentially useful alternative to SVMs and standard MPMC, combining classification with an internal basis for estimating error and deciding when to stop construction.
summary.tldr: Polynomial MPMC cascades offer efficient high-dimensional classification with accuracy estimates and a stopping rule that avoids expensive cross-validation.

abstract: We develop a penalized kernel smoothing method for the problem of selecting non-zero elements of the conditional precision matrix, known as conditional covariance selection. This problem has a key role in many modern applications such as finance and computational biology. However, it has not been properly addressed. Our estimator is derived under minimal assumptions on the underlying probability distribution and works well in the high-dimensional setting. The efficiency of the algorithm is demonstrated on both simulation studies and the analysis of the stock market.

This problem has a key role in many modern applications such as finance and computational biology. However, it has not been properly addressed. The efficiency of the algorithm is demonstrated on both simulation studies and the analysis of the stock market.

paragraphs: This paper addresses conditional covariance selection, formulated as identifying which entries of a conditional precision matrix are nonzero. The target is therefore a pattern of selected matrix entries, rather than simply an unrestricted matrix estimate. The authors motivate the problem through applications including finance and computational biology.

Their method combines kernel smoothing with a penalty to estimate this sparse structure. Kernel smoothing supplies the nonparametric component, while penalization addresses the selection of nonzero entries. The estimator is derived under what the authors describe as minimal assumptions on the underlying probability distribution, and they report that it works well in high-dimensional settings.

The algorithm is evaluated through simulation studies and an analysis of stock-market data, which demonstrate its efficiency. These evaluations connect the proposed estimation procedure to both constructed data and a stated application. The contribution is a penalized nonparametric approach to a conditional matrix-selection problem that the authors identify as insufficiently addressed, with particular emphasis on handling high dimensionality.
summary.tldr: A penalized kernel-smoothing estimator selects nonzero conditional precision-matrix entries under minimal distributional assumptions.

title: On Sparse Nonparametric Conditional Covariance Selection
